title: fix(api): raise informative TypeError for non-dataframe validate() input
issue_title: validate function should throw a more informative error for non-dataframe arguments
gold_patch:
diff --git a/pandera/api/pandas/container.py b/pandera/api/pandas/container.py
index 21406e590..5b3bbe7c1 100644
--- a/pandera/api/pandas/container.py
+++ b/pandera/api/pandas/container.py
@@ -14,7 +14,7 @@
     from typing import Self
 
 from pandera.api.dataframe.container import DataFrameSchema as _DataFrameSchema
-from pandera.api.pandas.types import PandasDtypeInputTypes
+from pandera.api.pandas.types import PandasDtypeInputTypes, is_table_or_field
 from pandera.config import get_config_context
 from pandera.engines import pandas_engine
 from pandera.errors import BackendNotFoundError
@@ -149,6 +149,19 @@ def validate(
         if not get_config_context().validation_enabled:
             return check_obj
 
+        # Fail early with an informative error for non-dataframe inputs.
+        # Without this guard, backend dispatch raises an opaque
+        # ``BackendNotFoundError`` (or ``AttributeError``) instead of clearly
+        # communicating that a dataframe-like object was expected. This mirrors
+        # the ``is_field`` guard in ``SeriesSchema.validate``. Field-like
+        # objects (e.g. ``pd.Series``) are permitted here because
+        # ``MultiIndex`` (a ``DataFrameSchema`` subclass) reuses this method to
+        # validate the index of a ``SeriesSchema``.
+        if not is_table_or_field(check_obj):
+            raise TypeError(
+                f"expected pd.DataFrame, got {type(check_obj)}"
+            )
+
         # NOTE: Move this into its own schema-backend variant. This is where
         # the benefits of separating the schema spec from the backend
         # implementation comes in.

+@pytest.mark.parametrize(

+    [1, 1.0, "foo", ["a", "b"], {"a": 1}, (1, 2), None, int],

+def test_dataframe_schema_validate_non_dataframe_raises_typeerror(
+    invalid_input,
+) -> None:
+    """Passing a non-dataframe object to ``validate`` should raise an
+    informative ``TypeError`` rather than an opaque ``BackendNotFoundError``.
+
+    See https://github.com/unionai-oss/pandera/issues/467. This mirrors the
+    ``is_field`` guard already present in ``SeriesSchema.validate``.
+    """
+    schema = DataFrameSchema({"a": Column(float)})
+    with pytest.raises(TypeError, match="expected pd.DataFrame"):

+
+

problem_statement.title: validate function should throw a more informative error for non-dataframe arguments
problem_statement.body:
**Describe the bug**
Input type is not checked to be DataFrame and throws an obscure error, e.g.
`AttributeError: 'int' object has no attribute 'copy'`

- [ x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.
- [x ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the latest version of pandas.
- [ ] (optional) I have confirmed this bug exists on the master branch of pandas.

#### Code Sample, a copy-pastable example

```python
import pandera as pa
pa.DataFrameSchema({'a': pa.Column(float)}).validate(int)

```

#### Expected behavior
Should probably throw a SchemaError or an error indicating wrong argument type

#### Versions
Pandera 0.6.3
Pandas 1.2.4

diff --git a/graphistry/tests/compute/gfql/test_crash_family_1882_1879.py b/graphistry/tests/compute/gfql/test_crash_family_1882_1879.py
new file mode 100644
index 0000000000..0babea4c03
--- /dev/null
+++ b/graphistry/tests/compute/gfql/test_crash_family_1882_1879.py
@@ -0,0 +1,203 @@
+"""Crash-family pins: #1882 (+#1913 finding-4) and #1879's pandas half.
+
+Every case reproduces a verified-live crash at master ``e6625ed28`` with a hand-computed
+oracle, plus the both-sides pins that lock the behavior that already worked:
+
+* #1882 -- PUBLIC ``filter_nodes_by_dict`` / ``filter_edges_by_dict`` / ``filter_by_dict``
+  on polars frames raised ``AttributeError: 'DataFrame' object has no attribute 'assign'``
+  (``filter_by_dict.py`` built the mask with pandas idioms after the resolver routed
+  POLARS). Fixed by dispatching to the existing native ``filter_by_dict_polars``; a
+  polars-in graph must come back polars (no silent engine swap).
+* #1913 finding-4 -- same family: ``prune_self_edges`` on polars edges hit polars'
+  column-selecting boolean ``__getitem__`` (raw ``ValueError``; silently selects COLUMNS
+  when the row count equals the column count). Now polars-native, with pandas'
+  ``NaN != x -> keep`` null-endpoint semantics.
+* #1879 pandas half -- Cypher/chain on a nodes-only graph (edges NEVER bound) died with a
+  bare ``TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not subscriptable`` (``ast.py`` slicing
+  ``g._edges[:0]``), with or without a policy attached (the policy toggle was inert
+  because BOTH paths crashed). Now a node-only pattern is served (it needs no edges) and
+  an edge pattern declines with a typed GFQLSchemaError; polars keeps its typed decline,
+  whose advice recommends engines that must actually serve (pinned live here).
+* empty-but-BOUND edges kept working throughout -- pinned on both engines so the
+  nodes-only fix can never regress it.
+"""
+import pandas as pd
+import pytest
+
+import graphistry
+from graphistry.compute.ast import e_forward, n
+from graphistry.compute.exceptions import GFQLSchemaError
+from graphistry.compute.filter_by_dict import filter_by_dict
+
+try:
+    import polars as pl
+    HAS_POLARS = True
+except ImportError:
+    HAS_POLARS = False
+
+polars_only = pytest.mark.skipif(not HAS_POLARS, reason="polars not installed")
+
+ENGINES = ["pandas", pytest.param("polars", marks=polars_only)]
+
+
+def _frame(engine, df):
+    return pl.from_pandas(df) if engine == "polars" else df
+
+
+def _pd(df):
+    return df.to_pandas() if hasattr(df, "to_pandas") else df
+
+
+def _attr_graph(engine):
+    """0(a) -x-> 1(b) -y-> 2(a)"""
+    ndf = pd.DataFrame({"id": [0, 1, 2], "kind": ["a", "b", "a"]})
+    edf = pd.DataFrame({"s": [0, 1], "d": [1, 2], "rel": ["x", "y"]})
+    return graphistry.nodes(_frame(engine, ndf), "id").edges(_frame(engine, edf), "s", "d")
+
+
+def _nodes_only(engine):
+    ndf = pd.DataFrame({"id": [0, 1, 2], "label__Person": [True, True, False], "v": [10, 20, 30]})
+    return graphistry.nodes(_frame(engine, ndf), "id")
+
+
+# --------------------------------------------------------------------- #1882 helpers
+class TestFilterByDictPolars:
+    """#1882: the three public surfaces serve polars frames, polars-in => polars-out."""
+
+    @polars_only
+    def test_filter_nodes_by_dict_polars(self):
+        out = _attr_graph("polars").filter_nodes_by_dict({"kind": "a"})
+        assert isinstance(out._nodes, pl.DataFrame)  # no silent engine swap
+        assert sorted(_pd(out._nodes)["id"].tolist()) == [0, 2]
+
+    @polars_only
+    def test_filter_edges_by_dict_polars(self):
+        out = _attr_graph("polars").filter_edges_by_dict({"rel": "x"})
+        assert isinstance(out._edges, pl.DataFrame)
+        assert _pd(out._edges)[["s", "d"]].values.tolist() == [[0, 1]]
+
+    @polars_only
+    def test_filter_by_dict_bare_polars(self):
+        df = pl.DataFrame({"id": [0, 1, 2], "kind": ["a", "b", "a"]})
+        out = filter_by_dict(df, {"kind": "a"})
+        assert isinstance(out, pl.DataFrame)
+        assert sorted(out["id"].to_list()) == [0, 2]
+
+    @polars_only
+    @pytest.mark.parametrize("filter_dict", [
+        {"kind": "a"},
+        {"kind": ["a", "b", None]},  # membership 3VL: a null cell is never a member
+        {"id": 2},
+    ])
+    def test_polars_matches_pandas_oracle(self, filter_dict):
+        ndf = pd.DataFrame({"id": [0, 1, 2, 3], "kind": ["a", "b", None, "a"]})
+        expect = filter_by_dict(ndf, filter_dict)["id"].tolist()
+        got = filter_by_dict(pl.from_pandas(ndf), filter_dict)["id"].to_list()
+        assert got == expect
+
+    def test_filter_nodes_by_dict_pandas_unchanged(self):
+        out = _attr_graph("pandas").filter_nodes_by_dict({"kind": "a"})
+        assert isinstance(out._nodes, pd.DataFrame)
+        assert sorted(out._nodes["id"].tolist()) == [0, 2]
+
+
+class TestPruneSelfEdges:
+    """#1913 finding-4: prune_self_edges is engine-dispatched, identical row semantics."""
+
+    #: (0,0) self -> drop; (1,2) keep; (2,2) self -> drop; (None,None) keep (pandas NaN != NaN)
+    _EDF = pd.DataFrame({"s": [0.0, 1.0, 2.0, None], "d": [0.0, 2.0, 2.0, None]})
+
+    @pytest.mark.parametrize("engine", ENGINES)
+    def test_prune_self_edges(self, engine):
+        g = graphistry.nodes(_frame(engine, pd.DataFrame({"id": [0, 1, 2]})), "id") \
+            .edges(_frame(engine, self._EDF), "s", "d")
+        out = g.prune_self_edges()
+        got = _pd(out._edges)
+        assert got[["s", "d"]].values.tolist()[0] == [1.0, 2.0]
+        assert len(got) == 2 and got[["s", "d"]].isna().all(axis=1).iloc[1]
+        if engine == "polars":
+            assert isinstance(out._edges, pl.DataFrame)  # no silent engine swap
+
+
+# --------------------------------------------------------------------- #1879 pandas half
+NODES_ONLY_QUERIES = [
+    ("plain", "MATCH (a) RETURN a.id AS id ORDER BY id", [0, 1, 2]),
+    ("label", "MATCH (a:Person) RETURN a.id AS id ORDER BY id", [0, 1]),
+    ("where", "MATCH (a) WHERE a.v > 15 RETURN a.id AS id ORDER BY id", [1, 2]),
+    ("agg", "MATCH (a) RETURN count(*) AS c", None),
+]
+
+
+class TestNodesOnlyCypherPandas:
+    """#1879: pandas serves node-only patterns on a graph whose edges were NEVER bound."""
+
+    @pytest.mark.parametrize("_name,query,expect", NODES_ONLY_QUERIES)
+    def test_nodes_only_serves(self, _name, query, expect):
+        res = _nodes_only("pandas").gfql(query, engine="pandas")
+        if expect is None:
+            assert res._nodes["c"].tolist() == [3]
+        else:
+            assert res._nodes["id"].tolist() == expect
+
+    @pytest.mark.parametrize("_name,query,expect", NODES_ONLY_QUERIES)
+    def test_policy_does_not_toggle_answers(self, _name, query, expect):
+        """#1879: attaching a policy must not change the answer (it used to flip paths)."""
+        calls = []
+        res = _nodes_only("pandas").gfql(
+            query, engine="pandas", policy={"preload": lambda ctx: calls.append(ctx["hook"])})
+        assert calls == ["preload"]  # the hook actually fired
+        baseline = _nodes_only("pandas").gfql(query, engine="pandas")
+        pd.testing.assert_frame_equal(
+            res._nodes.reset_index(drop=True), baseline._nodes.reset_index(drop=True))
+
+    def test_chain_node_only_serves_and_result_stays_nodes_only(self):
+        out = _nodes_only("pandas").chain([n({"id": 0})])
+        assert out._nodes["id"].tolist() == [0]
+        assert out._edges is None  # result mirrors the nodes-only input
+
+    def test_chain_with_policy_serves_and_result_stays_nodes_only(self):
+        """A policy forces the non-fast chain path -- the path that crashed at ast.py:265 --
+        and the served result must still drop the internally synthesized empty edges."""
+        out = _nodes_only("pandas").gfql(
+            [n({"id": 0})], engine="pandas", policy={"preload": lambda ctx: None})
+        assert out._nodes["id"].tolist() == [0]
+        assert out._edges is None  # result mirrors the nodes-only input
+
+    def test_edge_pattern_declines_typed_cypher(self):
+        with pytest.raises(GFQLSchemaError, match="no edges"):
+            _nodes_only("pandas").gfql("MATCH (a)-[r]->(b) RETURN a.id AS id", engine="pandas")
+
+    def test_edge_op_declines_typed_chain(self):
+        with pytest.raises(GFQLSchemaError, match="no edges"):
+            _nodes_only("pandas").chain([n(), e_forward(), n()])
+
+
+class TestNodesOnlyPolarsDecline:
+    """#1879 polars side: still a typed decline, and its advice must name WORKING engines."""
+
+    @polars_only
+    def test_polars_declines_typed_with_live_advice(self):
+        with pytest.raises(NotImplementedError) as exc:
+            _nodes_only("polars").gfql("MATCH (a) RETURN a.id AS id ORDER BY id", engine="polars")
+        advice = str(exc.value)
+        assert "pandas" in advice
+        # the advice is only valid because the recommended engine now serves -- run it
+        res = _nodes_only("pandas").gfql("MATCH (a) RETURN a.id AS id ORDER BY id", engine="pandas")
+        assert res._nodes["id"].tolist() == [0, 1, 2]
+
+
+class TestEmptyBoundEdgesStillServe:
+    """Both-sides pin: empty-but-BOUND edges worked before the fix and must keep working."""
+
+    @pytest.mark.parametrize("engine", ENGINES)
+    @pytest.mark.parametrize("_name,query,expect", NODES_ONLY_QUERIES)
+    def test_empty_bound_edges(self, engine, _name, query, expect):
+        g = _nodes_only(engine).edges(
+            _frame(engine, pd.DataFrame({"s": pd.Series([], dtype="int64"),
+                                         "d": pd.Series([], dtype="int64")})), "s", "d")
+        res = g.gfql(query, engine=engine)
+        got = _pd(res._nodes)
+        if expect is None:
+            assert got["c"].tolist() == [3]
+        else:
+            assert got["id"].tolist() == expect

Amplification round-001 (agent-03): `filter_nodes_by_dict`/`filter_by_dict` on polars frames raise `AttributeError: 'assign'` — the resolver routes POLARS while `filter_mask_by_dict` remains pandas-idiom. Same class as the resolve_input_engine migrations in #1873/#1878: either migrate the surface or route it through the polars predicate path. Also from the same sweep: `seeded_typed_hop` fast path declines on ANY lazy frame (values correct, sub-ms path silently lost — chain_fast_paths.py:391), and `get_degrees` on nodes-only diverges (polars bare assert vs pandas typed message).

problem_statement.title: Advertise supported output formats (available_formats) over the HTTP API
problem_statement.body:
### Summary

Expose the set of output formats a served Tesseract currently accepts (i.e. `tesseract_core.runtime.file_interactions.available_formats()`) over the HTTP API, so a client can discover at runtime whether an experimental format such as `json+cuda_ipc` is available before requesting it.

Today `available_formats()` already computes the answer server-side — `json+cuda_ipc` is included only when `enable_experimental_cuda_ipc` is set — but nothing surfaces it to clients. It is not in the OpenAPI schema and there is no endpoint that returns it.

### Why is this needed?

Downstream libraries (`tesseract-jax`, `tesseract-torch`) can exchange GPU arrays with a served Tesseract via the `json+cuda_ipc` output format, which avoids a host round-trip. Whether that works depends entirely on whether the server was started with `enable_experimental_cuda_ipc=True` — a fact the client cannot currently observe.

Because there is no capability signal, both libraries gate CUDA IPC behind a manual `cuda_ipc=True` argument the user must pass, which is really the user hand-asserting "I know this server opted in." If the assertion is wrong, the request fails (see the companion bug report about the 500). With the capability advertised, the client could enable the fast path automatically when — and only when — the server supports it, and fall back to the host round-trip otherwise. That removes the footgun and lets both libraries drop the manual flag for a transparent UX.

A schema/OpenAPI field is preferable to a dedicated endpoint: clients already fetch `openapi_schema` on connect, so no extra round-trip is needed.

### Usage example

Client-side detection, e.g. in `tesseract-jax` / `tesseract-torch`:

```python
formats = tesseract.supported_output_formats  # newly advertised, from available_formats()
use_cuda_ipc = "json+cuda_ipc" in formats and array.is_cuda
# enable the on-device path automatically, no manual opt-in needed
```

Rough shape of the advertised value:

```json
{"supported_output_formats": ["json", "json+base64", "json+binref", "json+cuda_ipc"]}
```

problem_statement.title: serve: out-of-range --port leaks a raw OverflowError traceback instead of an actionable error
problem_statement.body:
## Friction point (dogfood, release 0.12.16)

A new user who typos the port past 65535 gets a raw Python traceback instead of the friendly, actionable message we already emit for other port problems.

### Repro
```
$ rapid-mlx serve qwen3.5-4b-4bit --port 99999
...
  File "vllm_mlx/cli.py", line 323, in _port_preflight_or_die
    _sock.bind((probe_host, port))
OverflowError: bind(): port must be 0-65535.
```
Same for `--port 70000` (any value > 65535).

### Root cause
`_port_preflight_or_die` (`vllm_mlx/cli.py` ~L320-336) wraps `socket.bind()` in `except OSError`, which correctly turns a busy port into a clean message:
```
  Error: Port 8155 is already in use on 127.0.0.1.
  Try a different port: rapid-mlx serve <model> --port 8156
```
But an out-of-range port makes `bind()` raise **OverflowError** (not an `OSError` subclass), so it escapes the handler and prints a cryptic traceback.

### Expected
Validate the port range (0–65535) up front — or widen the preflight to also catch `OverflowError`/`ValueError` — and print the same style of actionable message, e.g.:
```
  Error: --port 99999 is out of range. Ports must be 0-65535.
```

### Notes
- Not a release blocker; cosmetic/UX. Filed from the 0.12.16 dogfood pass.
- `--port 0` is legitimately valid (OS picks an ephemeral port) and should keep working.
- Preflight ordering is correct — it runs before `load_model`, so this fails fast without wasting a model load. Only the error *presentation* is the problem.

_Reported by an AI agent (Claude) during release dogfood._

problem_statement.title: A bytes-valued Resource attribute breaks every OTLP encoder
problem_statement.body:
### Describe your environment

**Labels:** bug, sdk, exporter, data-loss
**Affected packages:** `opentelemetry-sdk`
**Found on:** `main` @ `0a5d76b6`
**Environment:** CPython 3.12


### What happened?

`Resource.__hash__` is implemented as `hash(json.dumps(attributes, sort_keys=True))`. `types.AnyValue` now includes `bytes`, which `json.dumps` refuses, so hashing a Resource that carries any bytes attribute raises `TypeError`.

Every OTLP encoder uses the Resource as a dictionary key to group telemetry, so the failure lands squarely in the export path for all three signals.

### Steps to Reproduce


```python
from opentelemetry.sdk.resources import Resource
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace import TracerProvider
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace.export import SimpleSpanProcessor
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace.export.in_memory_span_exporter import InMemorySpanExporter
from opentelemetry.exporter.otlp.proto.common.trace_encoder import encode_spans

resource = Resource.create({"service.name": "svc", "build.id": b"\x01\x02\x03"})

exporter = InMemorySpanExporter()
provider = TracerProvider(resource=resource)
provider.add_span_processor(SimpleSpanProcessor(exporter))
with provider.get_tracer(__name__).start_as_current_span("span"):
    pass

encode_spans(exporter.get_finished_spans())
```


### Expected Result

The Resource hashes, serialises and exports normally. `bytes` is a valid attribute value type and encodes to the OTLP `bytes_value` field.

### Actual Result


```
TypeError: Object of type bytes is not JSON serializable

# the same failure from three independent directions
hash(resource)        TypeError: Object of type bytes is not JSON serializable
resource.to_json()    TypeError: Object of type bytes is not JSON serializable
{resource: 1}         TypeError: Object of type bytes is not JSON serializable

metrics encoder       TypeError: Object of type bytes is not JSON serializable
logs encoder          TypeError: Object of type bytes is not JSON serializable

# with BatchSpanProcessor the TypeError is swallowed by the processor
spans successfully exported: 0 out of 5
```


### Additional context


Complete telemetry loss for any service that puts binary data in a resource attribute - a build fingerprint, a checksum, a compact instance identifier.

Severity comes from where it surfaces. `BatchProcessor._export` wraps the exporter call in a broad `except Exception`, so with the standard `BatchSpanProcessor` this is not a crash but a permanent, silent 100% export failure with only a log line per batch. Nothing else misbehaves, which makes it easy to misread as a collector problem.

Note the asymmetry that makes this surprising: `bytes` works correctly as a *span* attribute. Only Resource is affected.


### Would you like to implement a fix?

Yes

### Tip

<sub>[React](https://github.blog/news-insights/product-news/add-reactions-to-pull-requests-issues-and-comments/) with 👍 to help prioritize this issue. Please use comments to provide useful context, avoiding `+1` or `me too`, to help us triage it. Learn more [here](https://opentelemetry.io/community/end-user/issue-participation/).</sub>

problem_statement.title: GET /health returns 500 for the whole life of an image-gen or video-gen serve
problem_statement.body:
`GET /health` returns **500** for the whole lifetime of an image-gen or video-gen serve, and every probe writes a full traceback to the log.

## Repro

Built `main` at `f3a39da2` (`apps/rapid-mac/scripts/build.sh`) and served an image alias from the bundled sidecar:

```
"Rapid-MLX Desktop.app/Contents/Resources/rapid-mlx/bin/rapid-mlx" serve flux2-klein-4b --port 8077
curl -i http://127.0.0.1:8077/health
```

```
INFO:     127.0.0.1:56756 - "GET /health HTTP/1.1" 500 Internal Server Error
ERROR:rapid_mlx.exception_handlers:Unhandled exception on GET /health:
    'ImageEngine' object has no attribute 'get_stats'
  File "vllm_mlx/routes/health.py", line 80, in health
AttributeError: 'ImageEngine' object has no attribute 'get_stats'
```

A poll loop at 1 Hz produced **36,578 log lines in 10 minutes** — the traceback is re-printed on every probe, so an ordinary monitoring cadence turns the serve log into a traceback firehose and buries anything else in it.

## Cause

`vllm_mlx/routes/health.py:80` calls the engine unconditionally:

```python
engine_stats = cfg.engine.get_stats() if cfg.engine else {}
```

The guard only covers `cfg.engine is None`. `ImageEngine` (`vllm_mlx/runtime/image_lane.py:49`) is duck-typed on `is_image_gen` / `_loaded` and defines no `get_stats`; neither does `VideoEngine` (`vllm_mlx/runtime/video_lane.py:133`). Only `BatchedEngine` has one. So both generative-media lanes fail here.

The next line has the same shape and would fail identically once line 80 is fixed:

```python
"model_type": "mllm" if (cfg.engine and cfg.engine.is_mllm) else "llm",
```

## Blast radius

* `/healthz` is **fine** — that is what `ServerManager.swift` polls, which is why the desktop Images tab still works and why this was invisible until now.
* `/health` is the documented human-readable view. Anything that health-checks the server that way — `curl`, a container `HEALTHCHECK`, a reverse proxy, Prometheus blackbox, a CI wait loop — sees an image serve as permanently broken.
* Found because a verification harness polled `/health` and hung for 10 minutes on a server that was in fact fully up and rendering images.

## Suggested fix

Make the call capability-checked rather than presence-checked, e.g. `getattr(cfg.engine, "get_stats", None)` with an `{}` fallback, and the same for `is_mllm`. A regression test that serves an `image-gen` alias and asserts `GET /health == 200` would pin both lanes; the current tests only exercise the text lane, so the lane that lacks the attribute is exactly the lane nothing checks.

+    def to_dict(self) -> dict[str, Any]:
+        """Return a dictionary containing the Response's data.

+        into a :class:`~scrapy.http.Response` object.

problem_statement.title: Response.to_dict()
problem_statement.body:
I found myself wanting to have a quick overview about some requests/responses, so the first thing that came to mind was trying `dict(response)`, followed by `response.as_dict()`. It didn't work ;)

Unless I miss some other built-in way to do this, I think it'd be nice to have a method that returns a dict of all the "static data" of a response or request object; e.g. `r.status`, `r.url`, `r.encoding`, `r.flags`, `r.headers`, `r.meta`, `r.body` (, `r.request`) -- instead of needing to list them all, phew.

`r.body` could potentially something big, maybe a `.to_dict()` method should probably accept a parameter to exclude some key(s), instead of filtering them out again later in a list comp or such.

Also, the simplest way to turn a response into an item could then be

``` py
def parse(self, response):
    item = dict(response)
    # or
    item = response.to_dict()
    return item.update(some_other_stuff)
```

problem_statement.title: `--config-override` parses numeric-looking values as numbers, rejecting python_version=3.12
problem_statement.body:
### Description

`--config-override build_config.python_version=3.12` fails validation because the value `3.12` is parsed as a float, but `python_version` is a string field. The user has to know to quote the value (`python_version="3.12"`), and the error doesn't point at that fix. `--config-override` should coerce the value to the target field's declared type (or emit an actionable message naming the quoting fix).

### Steps to reproduce

```bash
tesseract init --name demo
tesseract build . --config-override 'build_config.python_version=3.12' --generate-only
```

### Logs

```bash
ValidationError: 1 validation error for TesseractBuildConfig
python_version
  Input should be a valid string [type=string_type, input_value=3.12, input_type=float]
    For further information visit https://errors.pydantic.dev/2.13/v/string_type
```

### OS

Mac

### Tesseract version

1.10.0

problem_statement.title: state.db title sync: de-dup on title collision instead of leaving the 2nd session blank (follow-up to #6892)
problem_statement.body:
### Summary

Follow-up from #6892 (sync auto-generated session titles to `state.db`). When two WebUI sessions generate the **same** auto-title, hermes-agent's `state.db` enforces a uniqueness rule on `sessions.title`, so the second sync raises `ValueError` — which `sync_session_title` swallows (broad `except Exception: logger.debug(...)`). The result: the second session is left blank in `hermes sessions list`, the exact symptom #6892 set out to fix, just in the collision case.

This is **pre-existing behavior of the uniqueness rule, not a regression introduced by #6892** — #6892's Codex gate explicitly classified it as a non-blocking follow-up, so it shipped without this. Filing so it isn't lost.

### Root cause

`api/state_sync.py` `sync_session_title()`:
```python
db.ensure_session(session_id=session_id, source='webui')
db.set_auto_title_if_empty(session_id, title)   # raises ValueError if `title` already in use by another session
```
`set_auto_title_if_empty` → `set_auto_title` → `_set_session_title`, whose uniqueness check raises `ValueError(f"Title '{title}' is already in use by session {conflict_id}")` for a non-lineage conflict. `sync_session_title`'s broad `except` swallows it at debug level, leaving the row untitled.

### Fix shape

In `sync_session_title`, catch the collision specifically and retry with a de-duplicated title rather than giving up:
```python
try:
    db.set_auto_title_if_empty(session_id, title)
except ValueError:
    # Title already used by another session — derive a unique variant and retry.
    alt = db.get_next_title_in_lineage(title)   # or equivalent de-dup helper
    if alt:
        db.set_auto_title_if_empty(session_id, alt)
```
(Confirm the exact de-dup helper name on `SessionDB`; `get_next_title_in_lineage` was suggested by the gate — verify it exists and returns a unique candidate, else add a minimal numeric-suffix de-dup.)

### Test

Add a regression test: two sessions generate the identical auto-title; assert BOTH end up with non-null, distinct titles in `state.db` (the second gets the de-duplicated variant), and neither is left blank.

### Scope / priority

Low-severity polish — only bites when two sessions independently produce a byte-identical LLM title, and only affects the CLI/TUI `sessions list` label (the WebUI sidecar title is unaffected). Good first-issue-ish backend task.

problem_statement.title: Stabilize Prometheus Exporter: Resource Attributes
problem_statement.body:
As part of the [initiative](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-specification/issues/4805) to stabilize the Prometheus Exporter spec, the Python SDK's Prometheus Exporter should introduce support for [Resource Attributes as Metric Attributes](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-specification/blob/main/specification/metrics/sdk_exporters/prometheus.md#resource-attributes-as-metric-attributes) configuration to align with the spec.

The current implementation status is documented in https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-specification/issues/4987#issuecomment-4223457917.

problem_statement.title: DOCX textboxes are silently dropped and the result differs run to run: id() of transient lxml proxies used as node identity
problem_statement.body:
### Bug

`MsWordDocumentBackend` silently drops textboxes from DOCX files. The **same file parsed twice in the same process yields different documents**, and the loss is silent: `ConversionStatus.SUCCESS`, no warnings, no errors.

On a 200-textbox document, **4–14 of the 200 textboxes survive**. How many, and which ones, changes from run to run.

### Root cause

`processed_textbox_elements` stores `id(element)` — an integer — and holds **no reference** to the element itself:

```python
# docling/backend/msword_backend.py
element_id = id(element)
if element_id not in self.processed_textbox_elements:
    ...
    if textbox_elements:
        self.processed_textbox_elements.append(element_id)
        for tb_element in textbox_elements:
            self.processed_textbox_elements.append(id(tb_element))
        tbc = self._handle_textbox_content(textbox_elements, doc)
```

lxml element proxies are created on demand and freed as soon as the last reference goes away. Because the list keeps only the integer, each proxy is freed right after its iteration, and CPython hands the **same address** to the proxy of a *different* node later on. The reused address is already in `processed_textbox_elements`, so the guard reads it as "already processed" and the textbox is skipped entirely.

The list is instance-scoped and grows through the whole document, so the collision probability grows with document length.

`_collect_textbox_paragraphs` has the same pattern (`processed_paragraphs` as a list of ids, `container_paragraphs` keyed by `id(...)`), so it is exposed to the same failure once execution reaches it.

### Reproduction

Self-contained, no external fixture — builds a 4.4 KB DOCX with 200 DrawingML textboxes, each carrying a unique string:

```python
import io, zipfile
from docling.datamodel.base_models import DocumentStream
from docling.document_converter import DocumentConverter

N = 200
OPC = "http://schemas.openxmlformats.org"
VND = "application/vnd.openxmlformats"

def textbox(i):
    return (
        "<w:p><w:r><w:drawing>"
        '<wp:inline distT="0" distB="0" distL="0" distR="0">'
        '<wp:extent cx="2000000" cy="500000"/>'
        f'<wp:docPr id="{1000+i}" name="TextBox {i}"/>'
        f'<a:graphic xmlns:a="{OPC}/drawingml/2006/main">'
        '<a:graphicData uri="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/word/2010/wordprocessingShape">'
        '<wps:wsp xmlns:wps="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/word/2010/wordprocessingShape">'
        '<wps:cNvSpPr txBox="1"/>'
        '<wps:spPr><a:xfrm><a:off x="0" y="0"/><a:ext cx="2000000" cy="500000"/></a:xfrm>'
        '<a:prstGeom prst="rect"><a:avLst/></a:prstGeom></wps:spPr>'
        f"<wps:txbx><w:txbxContent><w:p><w:r><w:t>CALLOUT-{i:04d}</w:t></w:r></w:p></w:txbxContent></wps:txbx>"
        "<wps:bodyPr/></wps:wsp></a:graphicData></a:graphic>"
        "</wp:inline></w:drawing></w:r></w:p>"
    )

document = (
    '<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8" standalone="yes"?>'
    f'<w:document xmlns:w="{OPC}/wordprocessingml/2006/main"'
    f' xmlns:wp="{OPC}/drawingml/2006/wordprocessingDrawing"'
    f' xmlns:a="{OPC}/drawingml/2006/main"'
    ' xmlns:wps="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/word/2010/wordprocessingShape"'
    ' xmlns:v="urn:schemas-microsoft-com:vml"'
    ' xmlns:w10="urn:schemas-microsoft-com:office:word"'
    f' xmlns:mc="{OPC}/markup-compatibility/2006">'
    "<w:body><w:p><w:r><w:t>start</w:t></w:r></w:p>"
    + "".join(textbox(i) for i in range(N))
    + "<w:sectPr/></w:body></w:document>"
)

buf = io.BytesIO()
with zipfile.ZipFile(buf, "w", zipfile.ZIP_DEFLATED) as z:
    z.writestr("[Content_Types].xml",
        '<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8" standalone="yes"?>'
        f'<Types xmlns="{OPC}/package/2006/content-types">'
        f'<Default Extension="rels" ContentType="{VND}-package.relationships+xml"/>'
        '<Default Extension="xml" ContentType="application/xml"/>'
        '<Override PartName="/word/document.xml"'
        f' ContentType="{VND}-officedocument.wordprocessingml.document.main+xml"/></Types>')
    z.writestr("_rels/.rels",
        '<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8" standalone="yes"?>'
        f'<Relationships xmlns="{OPC}/package/2006/relationships">'
        f'<Relationship Id="rId1" Type="{OPC}/officeDocument/2006/relationships/officeDocument"'
        ' Target="word/document.xml"/></Relationships>')
    z.writestr("word/_rels/document.xml.rels",
        '<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8" standalone="yes"?>'
        f'<Relationships xmlns="{OPC}/package/2006/relationships"/>')
    z.writestr("word/document.xml", document)
data = buf.getvalue()

converter = DocumentConverter()
for run in range(5):
    result = converter.convert(DocumentStream(name="callouts.docx", stream=io.BytesIO(data)))
    found = {t.text for t in result.document.texts if t.text.startswith("CALLOUT-")}
    print(f"run {run}: status={result.status.value}  textboxes={len(found)}/{N}")
```

Output (docling 2.114.0, Python 3.12.14, lxml 6.1.1, Linux x86_64):

```
run 0: status=success  textboxes=4/200
run 1: status=success  textboxes=4/200
run 2: status=success  textboxes=4/200
run 3: status=success  textboxes=14/200
run 4: status=success  textboxes=5/200
```

Expected: `200/200` on every run.

### Impact on real documents

Measured on a corpus of technical manuals (36 DOCX files): **9 of 36 produce a different document on every parse.** Examples, parsing the same bytes repeatedly in one process:

| file | text items across 5 runs | with the workaround below |
|---|---|---|
| A (18 MB, 34 pictures) | 3762, 3785, 3771, 3785, 3762 | 3813 every time |
| B (8 MB, 34 pictures) | 340, 355, 348, 333, 334 | 359 every time |

Note that the stable value is the **maximum** — every unpatched run loses content. What disappears are illustration captions and callouts: single-line strings like "Coupling", "Flywheel housing", "Step 1: align and install the drive end of the coupling". For a retrieval/RAG pipeline this is the worst possible loss shape — the document indexes successfully, reports success, and is missing random pieces.

### Not the cause (ruled out by measurement)

* **Threads** — `num_threads=1` still gives 4 different outputs out of 4.
* **`PYTHONHASHSEED`** — the divergence happens *within a single process*, so hash randomization cannot explain it.
* **Accumulated backend state** — no monotonic drift; values move in both directions (353, 355, 341, 340, 359, 351).
* **`document_timeout`** — unset in the reproduction, status is `success`, and text is both lost *and* gained between runs, which truncation cannot produce.

### Suggested fix

Give the backend a real identity for the nodes instead of a transient address. Any of:

1. Hold references to the elements alongside their ids (smallest change, no behaviour difference);
2. Key the bookkeeping on the elements themselves rather than `id(...)` — lxml elements are hashable, and a set of elements keeps them alive by construction;
3. Materialize and retain the body's proxies once per conversion, so every `id()` in the backend is unique and stable for the lifetime of the document.

Verified locally that (3) fixes it: `200/200` on five consecutive runs, and the two real documents above become deterministic at their maximum values. Conversion time is unchanged; peak RSS grows by the size of the retained proxies and is released with the backend.

Happy to open a PR if maintainers indicate which of the three shapes they prefer.

### Versions

`docling` 2.114.0 · `docling-core` 2.91.0 · `lxml` 6.1.1 · Python 3.12.14 · Linux x86_64

problem_statement.title: Enable override default type of selector to use on xpath method
problem_statement.body:
## Summary

When calls `response.xpath` scrapy automatically chooses the "best parsing rules" but looking from the code of **parsel** it always try to parse using `html` parse even with xml documents. I would like that user could pass the type on method call, like: `response.xpath("xpath", type='xml')`

## Motivation

I have a response that **Content-Type** is `application/xhtml+xml;charset=iso-8859-1`, but body itself is a xml document, but scrapy consider `html` the best parsing rule type, because when i try to parse `CDATA` a get empty values.

## Describe alternatives you've considered

I using `seletor = Selector(text=response.text, type='xml')` to parse my data.

## Additional context

Here a proof-of-concept that i made:

```python
from parsel import Selector

xml_doc = """
<?xml version='1.0' encoding='iso-8859-1'?>
<rows>
    <page>1</page>
    <total>1</total>
    <records>1</records>
    <row id="1">
        <cell><![CDATA[Scrapy]]></cell>
        <cell><![CDATA[https://scrapy.org/]]></cell>
        <cell><![CDATA[Python]]></cell>
    </row>
</rows>
"""

seletor = Selector(text=xml_doc)

print(seletor.xpath("//cell[1]/text()").get())  # None

seletor = Selector(text=xml_doc, type='xml')

print(seletor.xpath("//cell[1]/text()").get())  # Scrapy
```

problem_statement.title: MarkdownHeaderSplitter loses the leading header when a secondary split runs on an unsplit document
problem_statement.body:
**Describe the bug**

When `MarkdownHeaderSplitter` is configured with a `secondary_split` and `keep_headers=False`, the document's leading header line can be dropped from the output entirely — it appears neither in any chunk's content nor in any chunk's metadata.

`_apply_secondary_splitting` strips a leading header from each chunk:

https://github.com/deepset-ai/haystack/blob/main/haystack/components/preprocessors/markdown_header_splitter.py#L238-L244

```python
if not self.keep_headers:  # skip header extraction if keep_headers
    # extract header information
    header_match = re.match(self._header_pattern, doc.content)
    if header_match:
        content_for_splitting = doc.content[header_match.end() :]
```

For chunks produced by an actual header split this is a no-op: their content begins right after the header line (it starts with `\n`), so `re.match` never fires. The strip therefore only takes effect on the two fallback paths of `_split_text_by_markdown_headers`, which return the whole document as a single chunk with **empty** meta:

- "no headers found" (line ~146)
- "only headers with no content" (line ~208)

On those paths the header line is cut from the content, and because the meta has no `header` key to hold it, the text is simply lost. Note also that the strip matches any level 1–6 via `self._header_pattern`, ignoring `header_split_levels`.

**Expected behavior**

The header text should survive somewhere in the output — either in the chunk content or in the `header` metadata. Splitting a document should not silently discard part of it.

**To Reproduce**

Case 1 — the document's only header is at a level excluded from `header_split_levels`:

```python
from haystack import Document
from haystack.components.preprocessors import MarkdownHeaderSplitter

s = MarkdownHeaderSplitter(
    keep_headers=False, header_split_levels=[2], secondary_split="word", split_length=5
)
out = s.run(documents=[Document(content="# Title\nsome content here")])["documents"]
for d in out:
    print(repr(d.content), d.meta)
```

Actual:
```
'\nsome content here' {'source_id': '...', 'page_number': 1, 'split_id': 0, 'split_idx_start': 0}
```
`Title` is in neither the content nor the meta.

Expected: `'# Title\nsome content here'` (the document has no level-2 header, so it is returned unsplit and should be returned intact).

Case 2 — a document consisting only of headers:

```python
s = MarkdownHeaderSplitter(keep_headers=False, secondary_split="word", split_length=5)
out = s.run(documents=[Document(content="# Alpha\n# Beta")])["documents"]
for d in out:
    print(repr(d.content), d.meta)
```

Actual:
```
'\n# Beta' {'source_id': '...', 'page_number': 1, 'split_id': 0}
```
`# Alpha` is gone.

Expected: `'# Alpha\n# Beta'` — this path explicitly logs "returning original document", so the original document should come back unchanged.

**Additional context**

Chunks that really did come from a header split are unaffected and still behave correctly (header in `meta["header"]`, not in the content). The issue is limited to the unsplit-document fallbacks, where there is no metadata to preserve the header in.

This looks distinct from the previously fixed header-loss issues in this component (#11920 content before an embedded header, #12064 trailing header with no body, #11042 `parent_headers`), which all concern the header-split paths rather than the fallback returns.

**FAQ Check**
- [x] Have you had a look at [our new FAQ page](https://docs.haystack.deepset.ai/docs/faq)?

**System:**
- OS: macOS (Darwin 25.3.0)
- Haystack version: 3.2.0rc0 (reproduced on `main` @ 15ec337)

problem_statement.body:
## QwenPaw Version

2.2

## Description

任务执行中时我通过对话框新发消息触发了409报错。新发的消息不是应该放到消息队列即可吗，为什么要触发报错？



## Environment

- **QwenPaw version:** [2.2]
- **OS:** [Windows 11]


## Steps to Reproduce

1.执行一个任务
2.执行中时通过对话框提交文件
3.触发409报错

## Actual vs Expected

+def _abort_unhandled_multiprocessing_child(args: Sequence[str]) -> None:
+    """Stop a frozen multiprocessing child that escaped its runtime hook.

+    PyInstaller's multiprocessing runtime hook consumes this private flag and
+    dispatches ``spawn_main()`` before the application entry point runs.  If
+    the flag reaches this function, the packaged executable is missing or did

problem_statement.title: [Bug] macOS StdIO MCP spawn child re-enters backend_guard and kills the active backend
problem_statement.body:
## Environment

- QwenPaw Desktop: 2.2.0-beta.6
- OS: macOS 26.4.1, Apple Silicon / arm64
- Installation: packaged macOS Desktop App
- Trigger: invoking a StdIO MCP tool
- Observed with: `@tokenhub-cash/mcp` / `tokenhub-tools`

## Symptoms

When a StdIO MCP tool is invoked during an active conversation:

- The current conversation is interrupted and may disappear from the UI.
- The Console workbench becomes stuck or unresponsive.
- Feishu long connections repeatedly disconnect and reconnect.
- The backend restarts every 2–5 minutes.
- `desktop.log` repeatedly reports that it is terminating an “orphaned” backend, although that PID is the active backend currently serving requests.

Captured example:

```text
== qwenpaw tauri sidecar 2026-09-02T09:09:53.070910 ==
argv=['.../qwenpaw-backend',
      '--multiprocessing-fork',
      'tracker_fd=87',
      'pipe_handle=89']

2026-09-02 09:09:53 | INFO |
qwenpaw/tauri/backend_guard.py:97 |
Terminating orphaned QwenPaw backend pid 51111

2026-09-02 09:09:58 | WARNING |
qwenpaw/tauri/backend_guard.py:103 |
Orphaned backend pid 51111 did not exit; killing it

QWENPAW_BACKEND_READY {"port":49427}
```

The same pattern was observed repeatedly in the rotated and current desktop logs.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Install or enable a StdIO MCP server.
2. Start QwenPaw Desktop.
3. Start a conversation.
4. Invoke any tool exposed by the StdIO MCP server.
5. Observe the backend process and `desktop.log`.

For example:

```bash
ps -axo pid,ppid,command | grep qwenpaw-backend
grep -E \
  'multiprocessing-fork|Terminating orphaned|Orphaned backend|QWENPAW_BACKEND_READY' \
  ~/.qwenpaw/desktop.log
```

## Actual behavior

The multiprocessing child re-enters the desktop backend entry point and calls:

```python
reconcile_singleton_backend(WORKING_DIR)
```

It reads the shared `desktop_backend.pid`, sees the PID of the active parent backend, identifies it as a QwenPaw backend, and sends SIGTERM followed by SIGKILL. The child then writes its own PID to the same PID file and may start another backend, producing a self-killing restart loop.

## Expected behavior

Only the top-level desktop sidecar should participate in single-backend reconciliation.

Multiprocessing spawn/fork helper processes must:

- not call `reconcile_singleton_backend`;
- not overwrite `desktop_backend.pid`;
- not bind the desktop backend port;
- continue only with their multiprocessing child bootstrap.

## Source-level evidence

In `v2.2.0-beta.6`:

- `_run_backend_server()` unconditionally calls the singleton guard:
  https://github.com/agentscope-ai/QwenPaw/blob/v2.2.0-beta.6/src/qwenpaw/tauri/entry.py#L296-L300

- The module entry point unconditionally calls `main()`:
  https://github.com/agentscope-ai/QwenPaw/blob/v2.2.0-beta.6/src/qwenpaw/tauri/entry.py#L393-L395

- The guard terminates any recorded PID whose command line contains `qwenpaw-backend`:
  https://github.com/agentscope-ai/QwenPaw/blob/v2.2.0-beta.6/src/qwenpaw/tauri/backend_guard.py#L76-L107

The spawned process has the characteristic command line:

```text
qwenpaw-backend --multiprocessing-fork tracker_fd=N pipe_handle=M
```

On the bundled macOS Python runtime, `multiprocessing.freeze_support()` does not dispatch to the multiprocessing child bootstrap on macOS, so the child reaches the normal entry path.

## Suggested fix

Guard the singleton reconciliation so it runs only for the top-level desktop sidecar.

For example, detect the multiprocessing child before backend startup using the multiprocessing spawn marker or an explicit sidecar-role environment variable:

```python
if not is_multiprocessing_child():
    reconcile_singleton_backend(WORKING_DIR)
```

A role/environment check supplied only by the Tauri sidecar would be preferable to relying solely on a command-line substring.

## Regression tests requested

1. Unit test that a process with `--multiprocessing-fork` does not terminate the PID recorded in `desktop_backend.pid`.
2. Unit test that multiprocessing children do not rewrite `desktop_backend.pid`.
3. Integration test that invoking a StdIO MCP tool keeps the original backend PID and port alive.
4. Regression test that normal desktop relaunch still cleans up a genuinely orphaned backend.

## Related change

The singleton guard was introduced by PR #5570 while fixing the orphaned-backend problem reported in #5550:

- https://github.com/agentscope-ai/QwenPaw/issues/5550
- https://github.com/agentscope-ai/QwenPaw/pull/5570

That fix handles orphaned top-level backends, but the current implementation does not distinguish them from multiprocessing child processes.

problem_statement.title: FOM costs are missing from reported system cost
problem_statement.body:
### Version Checks (indicate both or one)

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the lastest [release](https://github.com/pypsa/pypsa/releases) of PyPSA.

- [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the current [`master`](https://github.com/pypsa/pypsa/tree/master) branch of PyPSA.


### Issue Description

Some time ago a new cost category - fixed operations and maintenance (FOM) - was introduced to PyPSA, together with a corresponding attribute - `fom_cost`.

While I believe FOM costs are properly taken into account in the definition of the objective function, they seem not to be included in the output of `network.statistics.system_cost` method. Also, the output dataframe of `network.statistics` does not contain a column for FOM costs. This might lead to an incomplete reporting of system costs in any quantitative analysis based on the PyPSA framework.

### Reproducible Example

```python
import pypsa
from pypsa.costs import annuity

n = pypsa.Network()

n.add("Bus", "bus")
n.add("Load", "load", bus="bus", p_set=1)

overnight_cost = 1000
lifetime = 10
discount_rate = 0

n.add(
    "Generator",
    "generator",
    bus="bus",
    p_nom_extendable=True,
    marginal_cost=1,
    fom_cost=10,
    capital_cost=annuity(discount_rate, lifetime) * overnight_cost,
)

+    async for event in handler.on_subscribe_to_task(
+        SubscribeToTaskRequest(id=task_id), alice
+    ):
+        received = event
+        break
+    assert received is not None
+    assert getattr(received, 'id', None) == task_id
+
+    agent.release.set()
+    await handler.aclose()
+
+
+@pytest.mark.timeout(10)
+@pytest.mark.asyncio
+async def test_on_cancel_of_parked_task_is_owner_scoped():
+    """Issue #1159 x #1170: a non-owner cancel of another user's PARKED
+    (input-required) live task must be rejected and must NOT write a terminal
+    CANCELED state. This is the exact cross-tenant regression the #1170 fix
+    (cancel writes a terminal state) would otherwise expose on the un-guarded
+    cached-active path."""
+    agent = _ParkThenHangAgent()
+    store = InMemoryTaskStore()
+    handler = DefaultRequestHandlerV2(
+        agent_executor=agent,
+        task_store=store,
+        agent_card=create_default_agent_card(),
+    )
+    alice = _ctx('alice')
+    bob = _ctx('bob')
+
+    task_id = await _start_live_task(handler, alice, 'park')
+    await asyncio.wait_for(agent.parked.wait(), timeout=5)
+    assert await handler._active_task_registry.get(task_id) is not None
+
+    # update_status enqueues the input-required transition; wait until it is
+    # persisted to the store before the cross-tenant cancel so the assertions
+    # below do not race the event pipeline.
+    alice_view = None
+    for _ in range(500):
+        alice_view = await store.get(task_id, alice)
+        if (
+            alice_view is not None
+            and alice_view.status.state == TaskState.TASK_STATE_INPUT_REQUIRED
+        ):
+            break
+        await asyncio.sleep(0.01)
+    assert alice_view is not None
+    assert alice_view.status.state == TaskState.TASK_STATE_INPUT_REQUIRED
+
+    # Bob (non-owner) is rejected...
+    with pytest.raises(TaskNotFoundError):
+        await handler.on_cancel_task(CancelTaskRequest(id=task_id), bob)
+
+    # ...and Alice's task is untouched: still input-required, not CANCELED.
+    alice_view = await store.get(task_id, alice)
+    assert alice_view is not None
+    assert alice_view.status.state == TaskState.TASK_STATE_INPUT_REQUIRED
+
+    agent.release.set()
+    await handler.aclose()

problem_statement.title: [Bug]: SubscribeToTask and CancelTask bypass owner-aware TaskStore for live tasks
problem_statement.body:
### What happened?

`DefaultRequestHandlerV2.on_subscribe_to_task` and `on_cancel_task` resolve the task through `ActiveTaskRegistry` by `task_id` alone. `get_or_create()` returns the cached `ActiveTask` before the owner-aware `TaskStore` is consulted, so a caller other than the task owner can subscribe to and cancel another user's live task.

Owner isolation itself works: `GetTask` and `SendMessage` consult `task_store.get(task_id, context)` first and correctly raise `TaskNotFoundError`. Only the two registry-backed paths skip it, so behaviour is inconsistent across request paths. This narrows the task-authorization half of #786, which predates owner-aware stores and `resolve_user_scope`.

Practical exploitability is low: `task_id` defaults to `uuid4()`, so it cannot be guessed or enumerated — the caller must already know the id.

**Expected:** `SubscribeToTask` / `CancelTask` for a task outside the caller's partition raise `TaskNotFoundError`, the same response as for a nonexistent task.

**Actual:** the call succeeds. The subscriber receives the owner's `Task` and event stream; `CancelTask` cancels the task and invokes `AgentExecutor.cancel()`.

**Affected:** a2a-sdk 1.1.2 (latest) and current `main`.

**Root cause**

- `active_task_registry.py:52-53` — `get_or_create()` returns `self._active_tasks[task_id]` with no owner check; `call_context` is not consulted on that path.
- `default_request_handler_v2.py:169` (`on_cancel_task`) and `:398` (`on_subscribe_to_task`) call `get_or_create()` without a prior `task_store.get(task_id, context)`. `_setup_active_task` does perform it (`:203`), which is why `SendMessage` is unaffected.

Preconditions: the task must still be live (present in `ActiveTaskRegistry`) and the caller must know its `task_id`. Tasks that are no longer active are isolated correctly.

**Side effect:** `ActiveTask.cancel()` assigns the caller's context to `TaskManager._call_context` (`active_task.py:718`), so the cancelled task is additionally persisted into the caller's store partition.

**Reproduction** — Python 3.13, `pip install a2a-sdk==1.1.2` (no extras):

```python
"""Minimal reproduction: owner-isolation bypass for live tasks in a2a-sdk 1.1.2.

`SubscribeToTask` and `CancelTask` resolve the task through `ActiveTaskRegistry`
by `task_id` alone. The registry returns the cached `ActiveTask` before the
owner-aware `TaskStore` is ever consulted, so any authenticated caller can read
another user's in-flight task stream and cancel that task.

`SendMessage` is not affected: `_setup_active_task` performs an owner-aware
`task_store.get()` first.

Run: python repro_owner_isolation.py
"""

import asyncio
import logging

from a2a.auth.user import User
from a2a.server.agent_execution import AgentExecutor, RequestContext
from a2a.server.context import ServerCallContext
from a2a.server.events import EventQueue
from a2a.server.request_handlers import DefaultRequestHandlerV2
from a2a.server.tasks import InMemoryTaskStore, TaskUpdater
from a2a.types.a2a_pb2 import (
    AgentCapabilities,
    AgentCard,
    CancelTaskRequest,
    GetTaskRequest,
    Message,
    Part,
    Role,
    SendMessageConfiguration,
    SendMessageRequest,
    SubscribeToTaskRequest,
    Task,
    TaskState,
    TaskStatus,
)


# Unrelated teardown noise from the event queue would otherwise mix into the output.
logging.getLogger('a2a').setLevel(logging.ERROR)


class NamedUser(User):
    """Authenticated user whose name is the owner key of the default resolver."""

    def __init__(self, name: str) -> None:
        self._name = name

    @property
    def is_authenticated(self) -> bool:
        return True

    @property
    def user_name(self) -> str:
        return self._name


class LongRunningAgent(AgentExecutor):
    """Agent that stays in `working` state so the task remains live."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.working = asyncio.Event()
        self.cancel_called = asyncio.Event()

    async def execute(
        self, context: RequestContext, event_queue: EventQueue
    ) -> None:
        await event_queue.enqueue_event(
            Task(
                id=context.task_id,
                context_id=context.context_id,
                status=TaskStatus(state=TaskState.TASK_STATE_SUBMITTED),
            )
        )
        updater = TaskUpdater(event_queue, context.task_id, context.context_id)
        await updater.start_work()
        self.working.set()
        await asyncio.sleep(3600)

    async def cancel(
        self, context: RequestContext, event_queue: EventQueue
    ) -> None:
        self.cancel_called.set()
        updater = TaskUpdater(event_queue, context.task_id, context.context_id)
        await updater.cancel()


def user_message(text: str) -> Message:
    return Message(
        message_id=f'msg-{text}',
        role=Role.ROLE_USER,
        parts=[Part(text=text)],
    )


async def main() -> None:
    agent = LongRunningAgent()
    store = InMemoryTaskStore()
    handler = DefaultRequestHandlerV2(
        agent_executor=agent,
        task_store=store,
        agent_card=AgentCard(capabilities=AgentCapabilities(streaming=True)),
    )

    alice = ServerCallContext(user=NamedUser('alice'))
    bob = ServerCallContext(user=NamedUser('bob'))

    # Alice starts a long-running task; the producer keeps running in the
    # background after the HTTP response, so the task stays in the registry.
    alice_task = await handler.on_message_send(
        SendMessageRequest(
            message=user_message('alice-work'),
            configuration=SendMessageConfiguration(return_immediately=True),
        ),
        alice,
    )
    task_id = alice_task.id
    await asyncio.wait_for(agent.working.wait(), timeout=5)
    print(f"Alice's live task: {task_id} state={TaskState.Name(alice_task.status.state)}")

    # Control: every path that consults the owner-aware store first is isolated.
    print('\n[control] store.get() as Bob ->', await store.get(task_id, bob))
    try:
        await handler.on_get_task(GetTaskRequest(id=task_id), bob)
        print('[control] GetTask as Bob -> returned a task (unexpected)')
    except Exception as exc:  # noqa: BLE001
        print(f'[control] GetTask as Bob -> {type(exc).__name__} (isolated)')
    try:
        await handler.on_message_send(
            SendMessageRequest(
                message=Message(
                    message_id='bob-followup',
                    role=Role.ROLE_USER,
                    parts=[Part(text='hijack')],
                    task_id=task_id,
                ),
                configuration=SendMessageConfiguration(return_immediately=True),
            ),
            bob,
        )
        print('[control] SendMessage on Alice\'s task as Bob -> accepted (unexpected)')
    except Exception as exc:  # noqa: BLE001
        print(
            f"[control] SendMessage on Alice's task as Bob -> "
            f'{type(exc).__name__} (isolated)'
        )

    # Bug 1: Bob subscribes to Alice's live task and receives her task state.
    stream = handler.on_subscribe_to_task(SubscribeToTaskRequest(id=task_id), bob)
    first_event = await asyncio.wait_for(anext(stream), timeout=5)
    print(
        f'\n[BUG 1] SubscribeToTask as Bob -> {type(first_event).__name__} '
        f'id={getattr(first_event, "id", None)} '
        f'(Alice\'s task: {getattr(first_event, "id", None) == task_id})'
    )
    await stream.aclose()

    # Bug 2: Bob cancels Alice's live task.
    cancelled = await handler.on_cancel_task(CancelTaskRequest(id=task_id), bob)
    print(
        f'[BUG 2] CancelTask as Bob -> state='
        f'{TaskState.Name(cancelled.status.state)} '
        f'agent.cancel() called={agent.cancel_called.is_set()}'
    )

    # Side effect: ActiveTask.cancel() overwrites TaskManager._call_context with
    # the caller's context (active_task.py:718), so the cancelled task is also
    # persisted into Bob's partition — Bob now owns a copy of Alice's task.
    print(
        '\n[side effect] store.get() as Bob   ->',
        (await store.get(task_id, bob)) is not None,
    )
    print(
        '[side effect] store.get() as Alice ->',
        (await store.get(task_id, alice)) is not None,
    )

    await handler.aclose()


if __name__ == '__main__':
    asyncio.run(main())
```

The three control checks in the script confirm the owner-aware store isolates users correctly; only the two registry-backed paths bypass it.

**Suggested fix:** consult the owner-aware store before returning a cached `ActiveTask` — either in the two handler methods or inside `get_or_create()` — and raise `TaskNotFoundError` when the task is not in the caller's partition, so existence is not leaked. Optionally, leave `TaskManager._call_context` untouched in `ActiveTask.cancel()`.

### Relevant log output

```shell
Alice's live task: afff69f4-eef4-499f-8c99-e1cc4eb45644 state=TASK_STATE_SUBMITTED

[control] store.get() as Bob -> None
[control] GetTask as Bob -> TaskNotFoundError (isolated)
[control] SendMessage on Alice's task as Bob -> TaskNotFoundError (isolated)

[BUG 1] SubscribeToTask as Bob -> Task id=afff69f4-eef4-499f-8c99-e1cc4eb45644 (Alice's task: True)
[BUG 2] CancelTask as Bob -> state=TASK_STATE_CANCELED agent.cancel() called=True

[side effect] store.get() as Bob   -> True
[side effect] store.get() as Alice -> True
```

- [X] I agree to follow this project's Code of Conduct

Building an image using pyinfra returns:

```
[@podman/docker.io/fedora:44] podman build complete, image ID: 3b9bc6d8d5fc

Using podman (5.8.4):

```
❯ podman images --format "table {{.ID}} {{.Id}}" | head -n 2

0d05fac3b9bc  0d05fac3b9bc6d8d5fc7b323a35a23daf0ab61fc38685de569ce69f6feb7fbe6
```

The returned image id from pyinfra is starting 7 chars in into the full-length image id, I'm guessing this is the culprit:

```
https://github.com/pyinfra-dev/pyinfra/blob/3.x/src/pyinfra/connectors/docker.py#L179
```

Unsure whether this is specifically podman or also a docker connector problem.

problem_statement.title: sum() over a dimension crashes when a sibling dimension is empty
problem_statement.body:
I found this edge case while working on lpspec. I think its better handled here than in lpspecs linopy lane

> [!NOTE]
> The following content was generated by AI, on behalf of a user of linopy.

Summing an expression over one dimension raises inside the term reshape when *another* dimension of the expression has size 0 — even though summing over the empty dimension itself works, and the result (an expression with no terms) is well-defined.

```python
import linopy, pandas as pd

m = linopy.Model()
x = m.add_variables(
    coords=[pd.RangeIndex(4, name='t'), pd.Index([], name='cycle'), pd.Index(['a', 'b'], name='line')],
    name='x',
)
x.sum('cycle').sizes   # Frozen({'t': 4, 'line': 2}) — fine
x.sum('line')          # ValueError: cannot reshape array of size 0 into shape (4,0,newaxis)
```

Traceback ends in `expressions.py`, `BaseExpression._sum` (`variables.py:1243 → expressions.py:1633 → expressions.py:2141`). Reproduced on `0.9.1.post1.dev3+g09c34dd9d` (master).

Where it bites: a PyPSA-style model whose cycle basis is empty (no meshed network) — `sum(..., 'line')` of a term still carrying the empty `cycle` dimension. Expected: the same result as `LinearExpression.from_constant(m, xr.zeros_like(...))` over the kept coordinates, i.e. `{'t': 4, 'cycle': 0}` with zero terms — which is what `x.sum('cycle')` already returns for the mirror case. Presumably the stacking reshape needs the term count taken from the summed dimension rather than inferred with `-1`, which fails once the array has zero elements.

problem_statement.title: [DynamoDB] Query and Scan do not enforce Select semantics
problem_statement.body:
Moto does not fully enforce DynamoDB's `Select` semantics for `Query` and `Scan`. This allows invalid requests to succeed and makes `Scan` with `Select="COUNT"` include `Items`.

This is present in the latest Moto release, `5.2.2`, and on the current `master` branch at 7dc0838503a3da50ac83980dc82c07572bb5212a.

The following code creates a table with a `KEYS_ONLY` GSI and demonstrates both behaviors:

```python
import boto3
from botocore.exceptions import ClientError
from moto import mock_aws


@mock_aws
def reproduce():
    client = boto3.client("dynamodb", region_name="us-east-1")

    client.create_table(
        TableName="select-repro",
        BillingMode="PAY_PER_REQUEST",
        AttributeDefinitions=[
            {"AttributeName": "pk", "AttributeType": "S"},
            {"AttributeName": "gsi_pk", "AttributeType": "S"},
        ],
        KeySchema=[{"AttributeName": "pk", "KeyType": "HASH"}],
        GlobalSecondaryIndexes=[
            {
                "IndexName": "test_gsi",
                "KeySchema": [{"AttributeName": "gsi_pk", "KeyType": "HASH"}],
                "Projection": {"ProjectionType": "KEYS_ONLY"},
            }
        ],
    )

    try:
        client.query(
            TableName="select-repro",
            IndexName="test_gsi",
            Select="ALL_ATTRIBUTES",
            KeyConditionExpression="gsi_pk = :value",
            ExpressionAttributeValues={":value": {"S": "group-1"}},
        )
    except ClientError as exc:
        print(exc.response["Error"]["Code"])
    else:
        print("Query accepted")

    response = client.scan(
        TableName="select-repro",
        Select="COUNT",
    )
    print("Items" in response)


reproduce()
```

**Expected Result**

The query should raise a `ValidationException` because `ALL_ATTRIBUTES` is not supported on a GSI whose projection type is not `ALL`.

The scan response should contain `Count` and `ScannedCount`, but not `Items`.

**Actual**

Moto accepts the query and prints:

```text
Query accepted
```

Moto also includes `Items` in the scan response, so the second value printed is:

```text
True
```

problem_statement.title: [FEATURE] Support MJCF slider-crank actuator transmission
problem_statement.body:
## Description

`ModelBuilder.add_mjcf()` does not import actuators using `cranksite`, `slidersite`, and `cranklength`. Such actuators are omitted even though Newton already stores a two-element actuator transmission target, exposes `actuator_cranklength`, and defines `TrnType.SLIDERCRANK`.

## Expected behavior

Resolve both sites, store them in `actuator_trnid`, preserve the positive crank length and all ordinary actuator parameters, then export the actuator through MjSpec as `mjTRN_SLIDERCRANK`.

## Validation

Use a minimal slider-crank mechanism and compare the compiled transmission type, crank length, actuator length, and actuator moment against native MuJoCo at a nonzero joint pose. Missing sites and nonpositive crank lengths should produce clear errors.

problem_statement.title: add_segmentation_to_nwbfile with default metadata refuses an extractor that has ROIs but no traces
problem_statement.body:
`add_segmentation_to_nwbfile` accepts an extractor with ROIs and no traces when the caller passes metadata that names no `RoiResponses` block (there is a test for that, `test_no_roi_responses_no_traces`). It refuses the same extractor when the caller passes no metadata at all:

```python
from pynwb.testing.mock.file import mock_NWBFile
from roiextractors.testing import generate_dummy_segmentation_extractor
from neuroconv.tools.roiextractors import add_segmentation_to_nwbfile

segmentation = generate_dummy_segmentation_extractor(
    num_rois=3, has_raw_signal=False, has_dff_signal=False, has_deconvolved_signal=False, has_neuropil_signal=False
)
add_segmentation_to_nwbfile(segmentation_extractor=segmentation, nwbfile=mock_NWBFile())
# ValueError: RoiResponses metadata was provided but the segmentation extractor has no trace data.
```

With `metadata=None` the function fills in `_get_ophys_metadata_placeholders()`, and that template carries a `RoiResponses` entry under `default_metadata_key`. `_add_roi_response_traces_to_nwbfile` then sees the key present and raises the "metadata was provided" error, although nobody provided anything. A few lines lower the same function already knows the difference and computes `user_provided_roi_responses_metadata`, which excludes the placeholder key; the raise just runs before that and uses the wider test. The `_segmentation_extractor_has_data` check at the entry point deliberately admits a masks-only extractor, so this is the one path where it is then rejected anyway.

The raise should apply only to metadata the caller wrote.

problem_statement.title: Postgres: CAST(x AS "char") is parsed as CHAR, so the one-byte "char" type becomes bpchar
problem_statement.body:
- Read dialect: `postgres`
- Write dialect: `postgres`
- Still reproduces on `main` at `45158c35c`

`CAST(x AS "char")` is parsed as `CHAR`, so PostgreSQL's one-byte `"char"` becomes `bpchar` — a different type that answers the same cast with a different value.

```
input:    SELECT CAST(65 AS "char")     -- PostgreSQL: A
emitted:  SELECT CAST(65 AS CHAR)       -- PostgreSQL: 6
```

This is narrower than "quoted type names should not be resolved". Resolving them is deliberate and tested — `tests/dialects/test_postgres.py:977` asserts `1::"int"` becomes `CAST(1 AS INT)`. `"char"` is the one PostgreSQL type name where quoting changes *which type is named*, so it is the case that normalization cannot cover.

**Fully reproducible code snippet**

```python
import sqlglot

print(sqlglot.parse_one('SELECT CAST(a AS "char") FROM t', read="postgres").sql(dialect="postgres"))
# SELECT CAST(a AS CHAR) FROM t
```

The tokenizer keeps the two apart; the resolution happens in the parser:

```python
from sqlglot.dialects.postgres import Postgres

tok = Postgres().tokenizer_class()
print([(t.token_type.name, t.text) for t in tok.tokenize('"char"')])   # [('IDENTIFIER', 'char')]
print([(t.token_type.name, t.text) for t in tok.tokenize('char')])     # [('CHAR', 'char')]
```

**On PostgreSQL 17.10**

`"char"` is a one-byte internal type; unquoted `char` is `bpchar`. Neither cast raises, so the substitution is silent.

| statement | result |
|---|---|
| `SELECT CAST(65 AS "char")` | `A` |
| `SELECT CAST(65 AS CHAR)` — emitted | `6` |
| `SELECT pg_typeof(CAST(65 AS "char"))` | `"char"` |
| `SELECT pg_typeof(CAST(65 AS CHAR))` | `character` |
| `SELECT typname, typlen FROM pg_type WHERE typname IN ('char','bpchar')` | `char` → `1`, `bpchar` → `-1` |

**Why `"char"` is special rather than arbitrary**

Quoting suppresses keyword aliasing, so a quoted type name resolves against `pg_type.typname` literally and case-sensitively:

| written | result |
|---|---|
| `CAST(1 AS "char")` | `"char"` — the one-byte type |
| `CAST(1 AS "text")` | `text` |
| `CAST(1 AS "int4")` | `integer` |
| `CAST(1 AS "bpchar")` | `character` |
| `CAST(1 AS "int")` | `ERROR: type "int" does not exist` |
| `CAST(1 AS "integer")` | `ERROR: type "integer" does not exist` |
| `CAST(65 AS "CHAR")` | `ERROR: type "CHAR" does not exist` |

`int` and `integer` are grammar keywords aliasing `int4`; neither is a `typname`, so their quoted spellings do not resolve. Only names actually in `pg_type` work — and `char` is one, denoting the one-byte type rather than `bpchar`.

**Where it happens**

`Parser._parse_types` (`sqlglot/parser.py:6489`) re-tokenizes the identifier's *name*, which has already had its quotes stripped, and matches the result against `TYPE_TOKENS`:

```python
identifier = allow_identifiers and self._parse_id_var(any_token=False, tokens=(TokenType.VAR,))
if isinstance(identifier, exp.Identifier):
    try:
        tokens = self.dialect.tokenize(identifier.name)   # "char" -> char -> TokenType.CHAR
    except TokenError:
        tokens = None

    if tokens and (type_token := tokens[0].token_type) in self.TYPE_TOKENS:
        ...
    elif self.dialect.SUPPORTS_USER_DEFINED_TYPES:
        this = self._parse_user_defined_type(identifier)
```

`identifier.args["quoted"]` is available and not consulted, so a quoted name takes the same path as an unquoted one. For every type name but `"char"` that is the intended normalization.

**A possible fix**

Disabling the normalization wholesale breaks `test_postgres.py::test_postgres`, `test_redshift.py::test_cast` and `test_clickhouse.py::test_clickhouse`, which assert it. A dialect-declared exception list keeps those and fixes this one:

```python
# sqlglot/parser.py, on Parser
QUOTED_TYPES_DISTINCT_FROM_KEYWORD: t.ClassVar[set] = set()

# in _parse_types
if (
    identifier.name not in self.QUOTED_TYPES_DISTINCT_FROM_KEYWORD
    or not identifier.args.get("quoted")
) and tokens and (type_token := tokens[0].token_type) in self.TYPE_TOKENS:
    ...

# sqlglot/parsers/postgres.py, on PostgresParser
QUOTED_TYPES_DISTINCT_FROM_KEYWORD: t.ClassVar[set] = {"char"}
```

The quoted name then falls through to `_parse_user_defined_type`, which already round-trips it verbatim. On `main` at `45158c35c` this preserves `CAST(1 AS "char")`, still normalizes `CAST(1 AS "int")` to `CAST(1 AS INT)`, leaves unquoted spellings and other dialects unchanged, and `tests/test_parser.py` and `tests/dialects/` pass — 843 tests, 11545 subtests — with one pre-existing environment failure (`TestDialect::test_lazy_load`, which shells out to a `python` executable) that fails identically without the change.

**Official Documentation**

- PostgreSQL [Special Character Types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/datatype-character.html) — `"char"` is one byte; `character(n)`/`bpchar` is blank-padded.
- PostgreSQL [Identifiers and Key Words](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-syntax-lexical.html#SQL-SYNTAX-IDENTIFIERS) — a quoted identifier is never a key word.

---

*Investigated with LLM assistance. The reproductions, the patched test-suite run, and the PostgreSQL 17.10 results were run against `main` at `45158c35c`.*

problem_statement.title: AsciiDoc backend loads local and remote images without explicit opt-in
problem_statement.body:
## Description

This issue has been spotted while reviewing #4118. 

The AsciiDoc backend unconditionally reads image files from the local filesystem
when converting a document that references them. It does so with no user-facing
opt-in flag and no path-validation, in contrast to every other Docling backend
that handles external resources (Markdown, HTML, OpenDocument).

## Background

Every other declarative backend (Markdown, HTML, OpenDocument) routes image
loading through `ImageResourceLoader`, which requires the caller to set
`enable_local_fetch=True` or `enable_remote_fetch=True` explicitly. This ensures
that:

- local filesystem access is never triggered unless the caller consciously allows
  it;
- remote fetches are blocked by default and subject to SSRF guards
  (`validate_url_safety`) when enabled;
- path traversal outside the document's directory is rejected.

The AsciiDoc backend bypasses all of these controls. A document with a crafted
image path (`image::../../sensitive.png[]`) can cause Docling to silently open
arbitrary files on the local filesystem whenever the backend processes that file,
without the calling application having opted in to local resource fetching.

## Additional quality issue

Beyond the security gap, the original code always produced an `ImageRef` object
populated with fabricated data:

- image dimensions defaulted to a hardcoded 128×128 sentinel fallback (or were
  read from the AsciiDoc attribute string, which is optional and unvalidated);
- DPI was hardcoded to 70 regardless of the actual image;
- the URI was constructed by naive string concatenation (`"file://" + path`)
  with no normalization, escaping, or traversal check.

This means the `ImageRef` attached to every `PictureItem` in an AsciiDoc
document contained metadata that did not reflect the image on disk.

## Expected behaviour

The AsciiDoc backend should follow the same pattern as the Markdown and HTML
backends:

- Images should not be loaded unless `fetch_images=True` is set in
  `AsciiDocBackendOptions`.
- Local file access should additionally require `enable_local_fetch=True`.
- Remote URL fetching should additionally require `enable_remote_fetch=True`.
- Path resolution and all safety checks should be delegated to
  `ImageResourceLoader`, the shared utility already used by the other backends.
- When images are loaded, metadata (dimensions, DPI) should come from the decoded
  image file, not from hardcoded constants or unvalidated document attributes.

problem_statement.title: Cache the resource label limit during server event validation
problem_statement.body:
### Problem

Server-side Resource validation reads the resource-label limit from the current settings context for every Resource object. Events often contain multiple resources, so row deserialization repeats this lookup many times.

Profiling a backlogged trigger worker attributed roughly one-third of its CPU to this path. Memoizing the limit made event deserialization about 2x faster, removing most of that repeated settings CPU.

### Proposed change

Resolve server.events.maximum_labels_per_resource lazily once per process and reuse it in validation. Preserve validation behavior and cover repeated validation with a regression test.

+import asyncio
+from collections.abc import Iterator
+from contextlib import contextmanager
+from typing import Any
+
+from ...element import Element
+
+
+class CancelableWaitElement(Element):
+    """Cancel tasks awaiting an interaction with this element when it is deleted.
+
+    Unlike ``Dialog``, which resolves pending awaits with ``None`` on deletion, elements using this mixin
+    cancel the awaiting task: their awaits have no "didn't happen" return channel,
+    so resuming them would be indistinguishable from the awaited interaction actually occurring.
+    """
+
+    def __init__(self, **kwargs: Any) -> None:
+        # NOTE: assigned before super().__init__ which registers the element,
+        # so _handle_delete finds the dict even if a subclass constructor fails halfway
+        self._waiting_tasks: dict[asyncio.Task, asyncio.Event] = {}
+        super().__init__(**kwargs)
+
+    @contextmanager
+    def _cancel_when_deleted(self, event: asyncio.Event) -> Iterator[None]:
+        """Cancel the current task if this element is deleted before ``event`` is set.
+
+        A deleted element can never fire the awaited interaction,
+        so the task is cancelled rather than resolved to keep the code after the ``await`` from running.
+        """
+        if self.is_deleted:
+            # raise directly instead of task.cancel() so a caller catching the CancelledError keeps a clean task,
+            # just like when the deletion happens during the wait
+            raise asyncio.CancelledError
+        task = asyncio.current_task()
+        assert task is not None
+        self._waiting_tasks[task] = event
+        try:
+            yield
+        finally:
+            self._waiting_tasks.pop(task, None)
+
+    def _handle_delete(self) -> None:
+        for task, event in self._waiting_tasks.items():
+            if not task.done() and not event.is_set():  # an interaction that was already processed wins over the deletion
+                task.cancel()
+        self._waiting_tasks.clear()
+        super()._handle_delete()
