problem_statement.title: button.clicked() never returns after Client.delete() and strands one task per abandoned page load (1.2 GB over 150k loads)
problem_statement.body:
*Filed by Claude Code on @evnchn's behalf.* ### First Check - [x] I added a very descriptive title here. - [x] This is not a security issue (those should be reported via the [security advisory](https://github.com/zauberzeug/nicegui/security/advisories/new) instead). - [x] This is not a Q&A. I am sure something is wrong with NiceGUI or its documentation. - [x] I used the GitHub search to find a similar [issue](https://github.com/zauberzeug/nicegui/issues) and came up empty. ### Example Code ```python import asyncio from nicegui import Client, app, background_tasks, ui @ui.page('/') def index() -> None: button = ui.button('go') async def waiter() -> None: await button.clicked() # never returns once the client is deleted background_tasks.create(waiter(), name='waiter') @app.on_startup async def monitor() -> None: while True: await asyncio.sleep(5) Client.prune_instances(client_age_threshold=1) parked = [t for t in asyncio.all_tasks() if t.get_name() == 'waiter'] print(f'>>> live clients: {len(Client.instances):>5} | parked waiters: {len(parked):>6}', flush=True) ui.run(reload=False) ``` Drive it with HTTP-only page loads — no browser, no websocket: ```bash for i in $(seq 1 4000); do curl -s -o /dev/null http://localhost:8080/ & done; wait ``` ### Description **TL;DR:** `await button.clicked()` never returns and never gets cancelled when its client is deleted, so every abandoned page load permanently strands one task. `Client.delete()` ends with `self._connected.set() # for terminating connected() waits`, which wakes the `await self.client.connected()` inside `clicked()` into a **success** return — so it proceeds to `await event.wait()` for a click that can no longer arrive. Measured: 150,000 HTTP-only page loads leave 148,545 parked tasks and grow RSS by **1,215 MB**, with no reclamation. Same root cause as #6226 — `connected()` reporting success on a deleted client — but the symptom is an unbounded task leak rather than a raise, so it is filed separately. Sibling of #6230, found in the same sweep. **Expected** `parked waiters` returns to 0 as the clients are pruned, the way `live clients` does. **Actual** `parked waiters` equals the cumulative number of page loads and never decreases: ``` >>> live clients: 192 | parked waiters: 192 >>> live clients: 519 | parked waiters: 3079 >>> live clients: 0 | parked waiters: 4000 <- first 4000 loads done >>> live clients: 623 | parked waiters: 5360 >>> live clients: 0 | parked waiters: 8000 <- second 4000 done >>> live clients: 0 | parked waiters: 12000 <- third 4000 done ``` `live clients` does return to 0, so the `Client` objects themselves are released correctly. It is only the stranded tasks — and everything they hold, including the `ui.button` element — that accumulate. **Mechanism** `Button.clicked()` (`nicegui/elements/button.py` lines 62-67) registers a one-shot event, awaits `self.client.connected()`, then awaits that event. `Client.delete()` (`nicegui/client.py` line 472) sets `_connected`, which releases the `connected()` wait as a normal return rather than an error, and nothing afterwards observes that the client is gone. The second await has no timeout, no cancellation and no deletion hook, so the task parks for the lifetime of the process. `background_tasks.create` keeps a strong reference in its module-level `running_tasks` set until the task completes, so a parked task is never garbage collected. Three other methods have the same `await self.client.connected()` followed by `await self._initialized_event.wait()` shape and appear to share the defect, though I only measured the button: - `ui.scene.initialized()` — `nicegui/elements/scene/scene.py` line 187 - `ui.scene_view.initialized()` — `nicegui/elements/scene/scene_view.py` line 79 - `ui.leaflet.initialized()` — `nicegui/elements/leaflet/leaflet.py` line 105 ### NiceGUI Version 3.15.0 ### Python Version 3.14.2 ### Browser Other ### Operating System macOS ### Additional Context
Growth to 1.2 GB — the measured run 30 rounds of 5,000 HTTP-only page loads on released 3.15.0 / Python 3.14.2 / macOS 26 arm64. RSS is current resident size read from `ps -o rss=`, not `ru_maxrss` (which is a high-water mark and cannot show reclamation). A `gc.collect()` ran before every sample, so nothing here is waiting on the cycle collector. | parked waiters | RSS above baseline | |---:|---:| | 160 | 10.9 MB | | 3,382 | 173.1 MB | | 6,430 | 254.6 MB | | 64,747 | 658.6 MB | | 96,523 | 854.1 MB | | 140,435 | 1,163.5 MB | | 148,545 | **1,215.4 MB** | Steady-state marginal cost is about 6.9 KB per stranded task. The curve is linear with no plateau, and `live clients` returned to 0 at the end of the run while the 148,545 waiters remained.
Why the leak needs `background_tasks.create` to be visible Worth stating because it changes what a reader will see if they vary the repro. If the waiter is started with a plain `asyncio.create_task` and nothing holds the returned task, the stranded task forms a reference cycle — task holds coroutine holds the `asyncio.Event` whose `_waiters` holds the task's future — that is unreachable from outside, and the cycle collector reclaims it. The count then returns to 0 and the leak looks like it does not exist. It is a silent destruction of a pending task rather than correct cleanup, but it does not accumulate memory. `background_tasks.create` is the documented way to start background work in NiceGUI, and it keeps a strong reference in `running_tasks` until completion. Since the task never completes, that reference is permanent, and the leak is real and unbounded. I initially measured this the first way and briefly concluded there was no leak. Correcting it is what produced the numbers above.
What is not claimed - Only `Button.clicked()` was measured. The three `initialized()` methods are listed on the basis of matching source shape, not a run. - The measurement uses HTTP-only clients pruned by `prune_instances`, which is the cheapest way to create and destroy many clients. A client that connects and later disconnects reaches the same `await event.wait()` park by inspection, but I did not measure that path, since it needs a real browser per cycle. - `client_age_threshold=1` only shortens the wait. NiceGUI already runs `app.timer(10, Client.prune_instances)` with a 60 s default, so the same accumulation happens on the stock schedule, just more slowly.
Provenance Found while sweeping for other instances of the shape reported in #6226. An adversarial review pass by Codex, a different model lineage, independently flagged the same four call sites from the source before any of this was measured.

+    Flatten labels and drop the -1 sentinels.

problem_statement.title: `remove_variables` deletes unrelated constraints: `-1` means "masked" in a variable but "empty term slot" in a constraint
problem_statement.body:
### Version Checks (indicate both or one)

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the lastest [release](https://github.com/pypsa/linopy/releases) of Linopy.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the current [`master`](https://github.com/pypsa/linopy/tree/master) branch of Linopy.


### Issue Description

## Summary

Since 0.8, `Model.remove_variables(name)` deletes every constraint for which `Constraint.has_variable(variable)` is true. That test is

```python
# linopy/constraints.py
def has_variable(self, variable: variables.Variable) -> bool:
    return bool(self.data["vars"].isin(variable.labels.values.ravel()).any())
```

`-1` appears on both sides of that comparison with two unrelated meanings:

- in `variable.labels`, `-1` marks an entry masked out by `mask=`;
- in `constraint.data["vars"]`, `-1` marks an unused term slot in the padded  `_term` dimension.

So **any masked variable tests as "used by" any constraint that has a padded term slot**, and removing the former silently deletes the latter. Models that use `mask=` at all are affected, and the more masking there is, the more constraints are destroyed.

The failure is quiet: the model still builds, it has simply lost constraints, so it typically goes on to solve unbounded or to a wrong optimum. The emitted `UserWarning` names constraints that genuinely have nothing to do with the removed variable, which makes it read like a false alarm rather than a symptom.

### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd
import xarray as xr
import linopy
from linopy import Model

print("linopy", linopy.__version__)

idx = pd.Index([0, 1, 2], name="i")
m = Model()

a = m.add_variables(
    name="a", lower=0, coords=[idx],
    mask=xr.DataArray([True, False, True], coords=[idx]),
)
b = m.add_variables(
    name="b", lower=0, coords=[idx],
    mask=xr.DataArray([True, True, False], coords=[idx]),
)

m.add_constraints(b >= 1, name="only_b")

print("a labels   :", a.labels.values)                                  # [ 0 -1  2]
print("b labels   :", b.labels.values)                                  # [ 3  4 -1]
print("only_b vars:", m.constraints["only_b"].data["vars"].values.ravel())  # [ 3  4 -1]

m.remove_variables("a")
print("only_b still in model:", "only_b" in m.constraints)
```

### Expected Behavior

`only_b` should survive: it does not use `a`. More generally, `has_variable` should ignore the `-1` sentinel on both sides.


## Suggested fix

Restrict the membership test to real labels:

```python
def has_variable(self, variable: variables.Variable) -> bool:
    labels = variable.labels.values.ravel()
    labels = labels[labels >= 0]
    used = self.data["vars"]
    return bool(used.where(used >= 0).isin(labels).any())
```

(or filter `used` to `>= 0` first — the point is that neither side should let `-1` match `-1`.)


### Installed Versions

<details>
- linopy 0.7.0 (correct), 0.8.0 and 0.9.0 (both affected)
- Python 3.13, xarray 2025.12.0, pandas 2.x
</details>

problem_statement.title: [FEATURE] Support MJCF jointinparent actuator transmission
problem_statement.body:
## Description

`ModelBuilder.add_mjcf()` does not recognize the common actuator target attribute `jointinparent`. The actuator is silently omitted, even though `SolverMuJoCo.TrnType.JOINT_IN_PARENT` and the final MuJoCo enum mapping already exist.

## Why this matters

For ball and free joints, `jointinparent` expresses the actuator gear in the parent frame. It is not equivalent to an ordinary `joint` transmission once the joint rotates. Dropping or downgrading it changes generalized actuator moments.

## Proposed behavior

- Resolve `jointinparent` through the same named-joint/DOF mapping as `joint`.
- Preserve `JOINT_IN_PARENT` as a distinct transmission type and direct-control actuator.
- Export it as `mjTRN_JOINTINPARENT`.
- Compare the resulting actuator moment against native MuJoCo at a rotated ball-joint pose.

problem_statement.title: dep-logic 0.7.0 drops Python 3.9 support, breaking env_spec.py for 3.9 target interpreters
problem_statement.body:
### Describe the bug

`dep-logic` 0.7.0 (released 2026-08-10) dropped Python 3.9 support: `Requires-Python` went from `>=3.9` to `>=3.10`, and `specifiers/base.py` changed `UnparsedVersion = t.Union[Version, str]` to the bare-runtime `UnparsedVersion = Version | str`, which raises `TypeError` on import under Python <3.10.

PDM's own dependency constraint on `dep-logic` has stayed `dep-logic>=0.5` with no upper bound across at least 2.27.0, 2.28.0, and 2.28.1, so any fresh resolve of PDM's own environment now pulls in 0.7.x.

That breaks `pdm.models.in_process.env_spec`, which PDM executes *with the target project's interpreter* (not PDM's own) to introspect that environment. If the target/project interpreter is Python 3.9 (a perfectly normal thing for PDM to be managing — PDM itself only needs a modern interpreter to *run*, not to manage older targets), the script crashes trying to import `dep_logic`:

```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File ".../pdm/models/in_process/env_spec.py", line 25, in <module>
    print(json.dumps(get_current_env_spec(), indent=2))
  File ".../pdm/models/in_process/env_spec.py", line 11, in get_current_env_spec
    from dep_logic.tags import Platform
  File ".../dep_logic/tags/__init__.py", line 2, in <module>
    from .tags import (
  File ".../dep_logic/tags/tags.py", line 9, in <module>
    from dep_logic.specifiers.range import RangeSpecifier
  File ".../dep_logic/specifiers/__init__.py", line 11, in <module>
    from dep_logic.specifiers.arbitrary import ArbitrarySpecifier
  File ".../dep_logic/specifiers/arbitrary.py", line 8, in <module>
    from dep_logic.specifiers.base import BaseSpecifier, UnparsedVersion, VersionSpecifier
  File ".../dep_logic/specifiers/base.py", line 9, in <module>
    UnparsedVersion = Version | str
TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for |: 'type' and 'type'
```

This makes every PDM command that calls `get_current_env_spec()` (see "To reproduce") unusable for any project whose target interpreter is below 3.10, the moment PDM's own environment happens to resolve `dep-logic` fresh (e.g. after a PDM reinstall/upgrade). It's the same class of problem as #3657 (hishel 1.0.0) — an unpinned upper bound on a 0.x dependency let a breaking release through untested.

### To reproduce

1. Have a project whose configured interpreter (`pdm use`) is Python 3.9.x.
2. Ensure PDM's own environment resolves `dep-logic>=0.7` (e.g. `pip install --user -U pdm` today, or any fresh install of PDM 2.27.0/2.28.0/2.28.1 — the constraint is unbounded on all three).
3. Run `pdm info --env` in that project (also reproduces on `pdm install`, `pdm lock`, `pdm publish` — anything that calls `get_current_env_spec()`).

Observed — same traceback as above, wrapped in PDM's subprocess error:

```
$ pdm info --env
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
  File "<pdm-site-packages>/dep_logic/specifiers/base.py", line 9, in <module>
    UnparsedVersion = Version | str
TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for |: 'type' and 'type'
[CalledProcessError]: Command '['<project>/.venv/bin/python', '-EsS', '<pdm-site-packages>/pdm/models/in_process/env_spec.py', '<system-site-packages>', '<pdm-site-packages>']' returned non-zero exit status 1.
```

### Expected Behavior

PDM should keep working against Python 3.9 target environments regardless of which `dep-logic` release its own environment happens to resolve — either by capping the `dep-logic` version bound (e.g. `dep-logic>=0.5,<0.7`) or by not relying on a dependency with a higher `Requires-Python` floor inside a script that's deliberately executed under the *target* project's interpreter.

### Environment Information

```
PDM version: 2.28.1
dep-logic (in PDM's own environment): 0.7.1
PDM's own interpreter: CPython 3.14
Target project interpreter (.venv, via `pdm use`): CPython 3.9.25
Platform: Linux x86_64
```

`pdm info --env` itself is what crashes (see above), so its normal JSON output isn't available — the fields above come from `pdm info` (which still works) plus the resolved `dep-logic` version.

### Verbose Command Output

Same traceback as above; also reproduces identically on `pdm install`, `pdm lock`, and `pdm publish --skip-existing` (all call into `get_current_env_spec()` on the target interpreter).

### Additional Context

- `dep-logic` version history around the break:
  | Version | Released | `Requires-Python` | `UnparsedVersion` |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | 0.6.0 | 2026-05-19 | `>=3.9` | `t.Union[Version, str]` |
  | 0.7.0 | 2026-08-10 | `>=3.10` | `Version \| str` |
  | 0.7.1 | 2026-08-10 | `>=3.10` | `Version \| str` |
- The 0.7.0 changelog entry ("Update dependencies and improve type hints across the codebase", https://github.com/pdm-project/dep-logic/pull/21) doesn't mention the `Requires-Python` bump or that it's a breaking change for consumers on 3.9.
- `pdm`'s own `Requires-Python: >=3.10` is fine for running the CLI itself, but (as noted above) doesn't protect `env_spec.py`, since that script runs under the target interpreter, not PDM's.

### Are you willing to submit a PR to fix this bug?

- [ ] Yes, I would like to submit a PR.

problem_statement.title: DESIGN_MATRIX: literal  `NONE`, `NaN` or `Null` are treated as an empty cell
problem_statement.body:
### What happened? (You can include a screenshot if it helps explain)

A `DefaultValues` sheet whose value column contains the literal string `NONE`, `NaN` or `Null` (capitalization does not matter) are rejected as if the cell were blank. An error message like this will be created:

```
ert.config._design_matrix_validator - WARNING - DESIGN_MATRIX validation of DESIGN2PARAMS
would have failed with: Error reading design matrix designmatrix.xlsx
(DesignSheet01 DefaultValues): Default sheet contains empty cells ['Row 15, column 1']
```

Note that that the error message also pointed to the wrong row. Ert either uses 0-based indexing for rows or strips away the first row. In the `designmatrix.xlsx` I received, the offending line was in row 16 while Ert reported the issue to be in line 16.

This behavior was introduced by cd916ddcfd4203563f740ae6b4dd33c5063343d6 via https://github.com/equinor/ert/pull/11108 where `pandas` was replaced by `polars` for reading the design matrix. This should be mean the behavior is part of Ert since 14.5.0.
During the migration, a stricter than before check for the **design sheet** https://github.com/equinor/ert/blob/864db9ed93043881f59b6845780add6c41d97fdf/src/ert/config/design_matrix.py#L314
and the **default sheet** 
https://github.com/equinor/ert/blob/864db9ed93043881f59b6845780add6c41d97fdf/src/ert/config/design_matrix.py#L471 were introduced. Pandas was accepting certain capitalisations of the rejected names, e.g. it accepted `NONE`, but rejected `None`. 


### What did you expect to happen?

The user expected that `NONE` was accepted. If it should not be rejected and the behavior is intended, a more helpful error message and correct line number could have been helpful. 

I could not find any documentation listing disallowed values.

### Steps to reproduce

Can be used via the 
```python
# pip install xlsxwriter
import xlsxwriter
from ert.config.design_matrix import DesignMatrix

XLSX = "design_matrix_none.xlsx"

wb = xlsxwriter.Workbook(XLSX)

design = wb.add_worksheet("DesignSheet01")
design.write_row(0, 0, ["REAL", "PARAM_A"])
design.write_row(1, 0, [0, 1])
design.write_row(2, 0, [1, 2])

defaults = wb.add_worksheet("DefaultValues")
defaults.write_string(0, 0, "WELL_STRATEGY")
defaults.write_string(0, 1, "NONE")   # or NaN, or Null. Capitalization does not matter
wb.close()

DesignMatrix(XLSX, "DesignSheet01", "DefaultValues")
```


### Environment where bug has been observed

- [ ] Equinor Komodo (specify version)
- [ ] Python virtualenv (specify Python version)
- [x] MacOS
- [x] RHEL8
- [ ] RHEL9
- [x] Local queue
- [ ] LSF queue
- [ ] Slurm queue
- [ ] OpenPBS queue

+def _load_host_keys_file(host_keys: HostKeys, filename: str) -> None:
+    """
+    Load a single known_hosts file, skipping any line paramiko cannot parse.
+
+    ``HostKeys.load`` only ignores lines that raise ``SSHException``, so a line
+    it fails on for any other reason (``@cert-authority``/``@revoked`` markers,
+    a truncated key) aborts the whole file and drops every valid key in it. That
+    makes pyinfra treat known hosts as unknown and append them again (issue
+    #1339). See: https://github.com/paramiko/paramiko/pull/1990
+    """

+        for lineno, line in enumerate(f, 1):
+            line = line.strip()
+            if not line or line.startswith("#"):
+                continue
+
+            try:
+                entry = HostKeyEntry.from_line(line, lineno)
+            # Broad by necessity: paramiko raises a bare ``Exception`` subclass
+            # (``InvalidHostKey``) for undecodable key data.
+            except Exception as e:

+                continue
+
+            if entry is None:
+                continue
+
+            for hostname in entry.hostnames:
+                host_keys.add(hostname, entry.key.get_name(), entry.key)
+

problem_statement.title: Duplicate entries in known_hosts
problem_statement.body:
## Describe the bug

Pyinfra creates duplicate entries in `~/.ssh/known_hosts` when unable to connect.

## To Reproduce

```
$ cat ~/.ssh/known_hosts
@cert-authority *.internal.example.com ssh-ed25519 <key> <comment>

$ pyinfra $host exec -- echo "hello world"
--> Loading config...
```

problem_statement.title: `Agent` loops to `max_agent_steps` when a reasoning model returns no text because it hits `max_output_tokens`
problem_statement.body:
## Describe the bug

Under the default `exit_conditions=["text"]`, a reply that is empty because the model spent its whole `max_output_tokens` budget on reasoning does not exit the loop. The `Agent` keeps calling the LLM until `max_agent_steps`, and when the budget is systematically too small for the task every retry truncates identically, so all of those calls are wasted.

### Details
An assistant reply can be empty for two different reasons, and the `"text"` exit currently treats them the same:

| Reply is empty because | 2.29.0 | After #11665 | Desired |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| a malformed tool call was discarded | exits | retries | retries |
| generation hit `max_output_tokens` | exits | **retries until `max_agent_steps`** | exits |

#11665 fixed the first row, which was its intent. But the condition it introduced is `bool(last.text)`, so it changed the second row too.

### Expected behavior

The "Desired" column above: exit when the reply is empty because it was truncated, and keep #11665's recovery loop for every other empty reply.

## Reproduce
### What we observed

Measured against the real OpenAI API, `gpt-5.6-terra`, `OpenAIResponsesChatGenerator` (streaming), haystack 2.31.0.

With a reasoning budget well below what the task's reasoning pass needs (`max_output_tokens=256`, `reasoning={"effort": "high"}`, on a hard combinatorics prompt), the truncation is deterministic rather than a coin flip:

```
trial 1: text=EMPTY  output_tokens=256 reasoning_tokens=256  status='incomplete' reason='max_output_tokens'
trial 2: text=EMPTY  output_tokens=256 reasoning_tokens=256  status='incomplete' reason='max_output_tokens'
trial 3: text=EMPTY  output_tokens=256 reasoning_tokens=256  status='incomplete' reason='max_output_tokens'
trial 4: text=EMPTY  output_tokens=256 reasoning_tokens=256  status='incomplete' reason='max_output_tokens'
=> zero-text on 4/4 attempts
```

Wrapping the same generator in an `Agent` with `max_agent_steps=5`, one tool, and the default `exit_conditions=["text"]`:

```
assistant replies (= real API calls): 5
  [0] user      'Let S be the set of all 12-digit positive integers whos...'
  [1] assistant EMPTY
  [2] assistant EMPTY
  [3] assistant EMPTY
  [4] assistant EMPTY
  [5] assistant EMPTY

reasoning tokens burned across the run: 1280
Agent reached maximum agent steps of 5, stopping.
```

This becomes worse when `max_agent_steps` is higher. For example, `max_agent_steps` is 100 by default.

### Reduced reproduction, no API key

```python
from typing import Any

from haystack import component
from haystack.components.agents import Agent
from haystack.dataclasses import ChatMessage
from haystack.tools import Tool

llm_calls = 0


@component
class TruncatedGenerator:
    """Mimics a reply that hit `max_output_tokens` during reasoning: no text, no tool calls."""

    @component.output_types(replies=list[ChatMessage])
    def run(self, messages: list[ChatMessage], tools: Any = None, **kwargs: Any) -> dict:
        global llm_calls
        llm_calls += 1
        return {
            "replies": [
                ChatMessage.from_assistant(
                    "",
                    meta={"status": "incomplete", "incomplete_details": {"reason": "max_output_tokens"}},
                )
            ]
        }


def noop(x: str) -> str:
    """A tool, so that a ToolInvoker is configured."""
    return x


tool = Tool(
    name="noop",
    description="noop",
    function=noop,
    parameters={"type": "object", "properties": {"x": {"type": "string"}}, "required": ["x"]},
)

agent = Agent(
    chat_generator=TruncatedGenerator(),
    tools=[tool],
    exit_conditions=["text"],   # the default
    max_agent_steps=15,
)
agent.warm_up()
agent.run(messages=[ChatMessage.from_user("Write a very long essay.")])

print(f"LLM calls: {llm_calls}   (expected 1, got {llm_calls})")
```

On 2.31.0 this prints `LLM calls: 15`. On 2.29.0 and earlier it prints `LLM calls: 1` (verified by running the same script against 2.29.0).

## Possible fix

### 1. Retry on the discarded tool call itself, not on empty text.

The condition #11665 wanted to retry on is "haystack discarded a malformed tool call". Every generator already detects exactly that and logs a warning, then drops the fact:

| Generator | Discard site (2.31.0) |
| --- | --- |
| `OpenAIChatGenerator` | `chat/openai.py:634` |
| `OpenAIResponsesChatGenerator` | `chat/openai_responses.py:611`, `:825` |
| shared streaming path | `generators/utils.py:134` |
| `HuggingFaceAPIChatGenerator` | `chat/hugging_face_api.py:77` |
| `HuggingFaceLocalChatGenerator` | `chat/hugging_face_local.py:85` |

If that were recorded on the message instead of only logged, the Agent could retry on it directly rather than inferring it from `bool(last.text)`. That is more precise, and it keeps provider knowledge out of `agent.py`: each generator sets the flag at its own discard site, and the Agent reads one haystack-owned field.

It also means the Agent never needs to know about truncation. A truncated reply simply would not set the flag, so it exits by default. The same goes for other empty-text replies that are currently retried by mistake, such as a reasoning-only reply or a content-filter stop.

### 2. If keeping the empty-text condition, exclude truncation explicitly.
On OpenAI, the only provider we tested, the signal is:

| OpenAI API | Generator | Truncation signal on the message |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Responses | `OpenAIResponsesChatGenerator` | `meta["incomplete_details"]["reason"] == "max_output_tokens"` |
| Chat Completions | `OpenAIChatGenerator` | `meta["finish_reason"] == "length"` |

This is localized to `agent.py` but needs provider-specific knowledge there, or a normalized `finish_reason == "length"` that generators populate consistently. Other providers report truncation differently.

The check is inline in `run` (`haystack/components/agents/agent.py:869`) and `run_async` (`:1113`) on 2.31.0, and extracted into `_is_text_exit` (`:201-211`) on 3.0.0.

**FAQ Check**

- [x] Have you had a look at [our new FAQ page](https://docs.haystack.deepset.ai/docs/faq)?

**System:**
- OS: Linux
- Haystack version: 2.31.0

problem_statement.title: Large-session fuzzy duplicate matching remains quadratic by row count
problem_statement.body:
## Problem

`api.models._matching_visible_duplicate()` first checks exact visible-key identity, then falls back to scanning every existing key of the same role for substring / normalized fuzzy matches.

Current `master` already skips fuzzy work when either individual payload exceeds 200 KB, but the fallback remains quadratic when a transcript has thousands of ordinary-sized rows:

```text
for each candidate row:
    for each existing row of the same role:
        substring and normalized-content comparisons
```

A production-shaped compression sidecar that exposed this class contains 5,287 messages. Even with modest per-message content, the fallback can perform millions of comparisons while holding the Python GIL and delaying unrelated WebUI health/session endpoints.

This is independent of resident-cache byte budgeting (#6651), concurrent sidecar parsing (#7123), and compression-lineage pagination (#5776).

## Reproduction

Current `master` builds the fuzzy lookup for a non-exact candidate against 1,001 visible keys. A deterministic regression replaces the lookup builder with a sentinel and observes that the sentinel is reached.

## Expected behavior

- Exact visible-key equality remains authoritative at every transcript size.
- For normal/small transcripts, substring and normalized fuzzy recovery remain unchanged.
- Above a conservative visible-key threshold, non-exact candidates skip the O(n) fallback so end-to-end reconciliation cannot become O(n²).
- The threshold boundary is covered explicitly.

## Trade-off

A large transcript may retain an occasional near-duplicate whose visible key is not exactly equal. This is preferable to making the whole WebUI unresponsive. Exact duplicates continue to collapse, and the existing 200 KB per-message guard already establishes the same exact-only policy for a different large-input axis.

## Acceptance evidence

The regression must fail on current `master`, then pass with:

```text
1,001 keys + exact candidate: exact match returned
1,001 keys + fuzzy-only candidate: None, fuzzy lookup not built
1,000 keys + fuzzy-only candidate: existing fuzzy behavior preserved
small set + fuzzy-only candidate: existing fuzzy behavior preserved
```

## Non-goals

- No change to visible-key construction.
- No change to exact deduplication.
- No storage, API, or UI contract change.
- A future indexed fuzzy matcher could safely raise/remove the threshold without changing this issue's bounded-work requirement.

problem_statement.title: Correcting or deleting a drawer never invalidates its closets, and no verb can rebuild them
problem_statement.body:
Closets are derived from a source file at mine time and are only ever rebuilt by re-mining that file. No drawer-mutation path touches them. So a drawer that is corrected in place keeps a closet that quotes the pre-correction text, indefinitely, and there is no way to fix it short of re-mining a file that may no longer exist.

This bites hardest on retraction: the one case where the old text is not merely stale but actively harmful, because it reads as a live instruction.

## Why it happens

Closets are built from the **file content**, not from the stored drawers:

- `build_closet_lines(source_file, drawer_ids, content, wing, room)` — `mempalace/palace.py:133`, called at `mempalace/miner.py:632` with the mined file's `content`.
- They are replaced only by `purge_file_closets` + `upsert_closet_lines` (`mempalace/palace.py:191` and `:204`), keyed on `source_file`. Every caller is a mine/ingest path: `miner.py:647-648`, `closet_llm.py:283-284`, `diary_ingest.py:181-182`.

Neither drawer-mutation tool goes near the closets collection:

- `tool_update_drawer` — `mempalace/mcp_server.py:798`. Rewrites the drawer document and metadata via `col.update(...)`. No closet call.
- `tool_delete_drawer` — `mempalace/mcp_server.py:694`. Deletes the drawer. No closet call.

The only `closet` references in `mcp_server.py` are the KG's `source_closet` provenance field (`:883`, `:900`, `:904`, `:1271`), which is unrelated.

Writing to Chroma directly has the same result, for the same reason.

## Reproduction

```
1. Mine a file whose text contains a queued instruction.
   -> drawer_<wing>_<room>_<id>   "TODO next session: <instruction>"
   -> closet_<wing>_<room>_<id>_01 contains a topic line quoting it

2. The task gets done. Retract the drawer in place:
   mempalace_update_drawer(drawer_id, content="[RETRACTED - COMPLETE. DO NOT ACT ON THIS.] ...")

3. Search for the instruction.
   The drawer is corrected. The closet still quotes the withdrawn text verbatim.
```

Step 3 has no remedy in the CLI: `init | mine | search | compress | wake-up | status | doctor | repair`. Re-mining is the only rebuild path, and it needs the original `source_file` — which for a drawer filed from a session handoff, a scratch path, or any synthetic source no longer exists.

## Impact

In `search_memories`, a stale closet is not inert. Per `mempalace/searcher.py:342-363`, closets contribute a **rank boost keyed by `source_file`** plus a `cdoc[:200]` **preview string** lifted straight from the closet document. So the withdrawn text can both promote its own source's drawers and be shown verbatim in the result preview.

It is worse for anything that mirrors the closets collection as first-class searchable documents rather than as a ranking signal. I hit this building a BigQuery mirror: after correctly retracting a drawer and propagating the correction, a semantic search for the withdrawn instruction returned the **stale closet as the single highest-ranked result**, at 0.797 similarity — well above the corrected drawer. The retraction was complete and correct at the drawer layer and completely undone one layer up.

## Secondary: pointers outlive their drawers

Closet topic lines embed `→drawer_id_a,drawer_id_b` references. `tool_delete_drawer` removes the drawer without touching them, so those pointers dangle with nothing to detect or repair it. Low severity today — `_extract_drawer_ids_from_closet` (`searcher.py:146`) is defined but has no callers, so nothing currently resolves them — but it is the same root cause and will matter as soon as something does.

## Possible directions

Roughly in order of cost:

1. **Invalidate on mutation.** Have `tool_update_drawer` / `tool_delete_drawer` mark the affected `source_file`'s closets stale, and have search skip or de-boost stale closets. Cheap, and it makes the failure fail safe rather than silently.
2. **A rebuild verb.** `mempalace compress --rebuild <source_file|wing/room>` that regenerates closets from the **stored drawers** instead of the source file. This also closes the "source file is gone" hole, which no re-mine can.
3. **Propagate the retraction.** On update, re-derive just the affected topic lines from the new drawer text. Most correct, most work, and needs a defined story for line-to-drawer attribution.

(1) plus (2) would have been enough here: the retraction would have been visible to the closet layer, and there would have been a way to act on it.

Related in kind, though a different mutation: #1938 (wing-name migration re-keys drawers but leaves hallways/tunnels on the old wing). Same shape — a mutation path that leaves a derived layer pointing at the old world.

problem_statement.title: Windows stdio MCP: mempalace_mine returns OSError 22 when fd capture fallback is needed
problem_statement.body:
## Reproduction

MemPalace 3.6.0 on Windows, launched as a long-lived MCP stdio server. Calling `mempalace_mine` with an existing directory (including `dry_run=true, limit=1`) returns immediately:

```json
{"success":false,"error":"mine failed: [Errno 22] Invalid argument","error_class":"OSError"}
```

The equivalent CLI reaches the expected peer-writer guard because the live MCP owns the palace lease. A normal console-process probe of `_capture_fd_stdout` succeeds, so the defect is specific to a hosted stdio stream.

## Root cause

`_capture_fd_stdout` documents Python-level fallback when fd-level stdio is unavailable, but only `os.dup(1)` is guarded. These operations can still raise `OSError` and bypass the fallback:

- `sys.stdout.flush()` / `sys.stderr.flush()`
- the initial `os.dup2(tmp.fileno(), 1)`
- restoration via `os.dup2(saved_fd, 1)`

The tests exercise only the successful fd path. MCP requires stdout to remain exclusively JSON-RPC, so restoration must remain fail-closed.

## Executable specification

### Resolved caller matrix

| Site | Effective cwd/path | Runtime/version/platform | Permissions/trust | Configuration precedence | Input existence |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| MCP stdio `mempalace_mine` | Absolute existing project directory | MemPalace 3.6.0 / Python tool environment / Windows | Same-user local MCP process; palace writer lease | Explicit tool args, then loaded MemPalace config | Existing directory required |
| CLI `mempalace mine` control | Same absolute directory | Same MemPalace/Python/Windows | Same user; correctly rejected while MCP lease is held | CLI args, then config | Existing directory required |
| Unit-level `_capture_fd_stdout` | Temporary process/file | Supported Python platforms | Process-local fds | Function contract | Callback exists |

### State/failure matrix

| State | Immutable ownership | Preflight | Mutation order | Mixed state | Atomicity | Concurrency | Idempotency | Recovery | Fail-closed |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| fd capture available | MCP owns protocol stdout | flush + duplicate fd | save, redirect, run, restore, close | Python and C output captured | restore in finally | one synchronous tool call | each call restores fd | saved fd restores stdout | yes |
| fd redirect unavailable before callback | MCP still owns protocol stdout | redirect attempt fails | close saved fd, run once under Python capture | C-level output cannot be captured | no fd mutation retained | unchanged | retry is safe | Python-only fallback | yes; protocol fd was never redirected |
| restoration fails after callback starts | MCP protocol stdout is at risk | saved fd exists | restoration attempted before return | fd state is unsafe | cannot claim successful capture | unchanged | no retry inside call | surface hard failure | yes; never silently continue |

### Acceptance-to-proof map

| Criterion or invariant | Positive proof | Negative or mutation proof | Command |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Declared fallback executes callback once when initial fd redirect is unavailable | focused test returns callback result and Python output | monkeypatched initial `os.dup2` raises `OSError(22)`; current 3.6.0 fails | `pytest -q tests/test_mcp_mine.py -k fd_redirect_unavailable` |
| Successful fd path still captures Python/C stdout | existing capture test | direct fd write must not leak | `pytest -q tests/test_mcp_mine.py -k stdout_captured_not_leaked_to_fd` |
| Restoration failure does not silently report success | focused test raises/surfaces the restore error | monkeypatched second `os.dup2` fails | `pytest -q tests/test_mcp_mine.py -k restore_failure` |
| MCP framing stays clean | existing subprocess stdio tests | any non-JSON stdout fails | `pytest -q tests/test_mcp_stdio_protection.py` |

## Plan

1. Add the two focused failure-path tests and observe the initial-redirect test fail on 3.6.0.
2. Make setup transactional: guard flush/save/initial redirect; close any saved fd and use Python-only capture only if stdout was never redirected.
3. Keep restoration errors fail-closed after the callback starts.
4. Run focused mine/stdout tests, then the affected MCP test files.

problem_statement.title: [Bug]: PDF backend culls visible `hexbin` cells after path collection optimization
problem_statement.body: ### Bug summary Matplotlib 3.11.0 introduced PDF backend culling for path collections to avoid very large PDFs when many colored `scatter` markers are outside the visible canvas (https://github.com/matplotlib/matplotlib/pull/30746). This works for `scatter`, but it incorrectly clips `hexbin` output when the `hexbin` offsets include negative coordinates. ### Code for reproduction ```Python import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import numpy as np rng = np.random.default_rng(19680801) x = rng.normal(size=10_000) y = rng.normal(size=10_000) fig, ax = plt.subplots() ax.hexbin(x, y, gridsize=25, edgecolors="none") fig.savefig("hexbin.png") fig.savefig("hexbin.pdf") ``` ### Actual outcome The above code produces [hexbin.pdf](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/29671979/hexbin.pdf). Converting it to PNG with `magick` shows: ### Expected outcome The above happens only for the PDF backend. For the PNG format, it is rendered as expected as below. ### Additional information The key difference from `scatter` is how the collections are transformed. For `scatter`, the collection offsets transformed by `offset_transform` are the actual marker centers in canvas/display coordinates, and the marker path is centered around that offset. Therefore, checking whether the offset plus marker extent intersects the PDF canvas is valid. For `hexbin`, the collection is built from one reusable hexagon path plus many offsets, but the offsets are transformed with `AffineDeltaTransform(self.transData)`. That transform intentionally removes the translation component from `transData`, so the transformed offsets are displacement vectors, not full canvas-space marker centers. The missing translation is carried by the transformed prototype path. The PDF backend culling logic treated those displacement offsets as if they were absolute canvas positions, so visible hexagons with negative offsets were skipped. This makes the PDF output lose part of the `hexbin` plot, while raster backends such as Agg/PNG render correctly. This issue can be fixed, with keeping the PR #30746 optimization, but by culling using the final translated path bounds rather than assuming the transformed offset alone is the marker center. This preserves the `scatter` PDF size optimization while correctly handling `hexbin` and any other path collection whose offset transform is not an absolute canvas-position transform. ### Operating system macOS Sequoia 15.6 ### Matplotlib Version 3.11.0 ### Matplotlib Backend PDF ### Python version 3.13 ### Jupyter version _No response_ ### Installation None

problem_statement.title: config_context silently accepts a string validation_depth and disables all depth gating
problem_statement.body:
### Summary

`config_context(validation_depth=...)` is type-hinted `ValidationDepth | None`, but a plain string is stored **un-coerced** — and since `ValidationDepth` is not a str-Enum, every `@validate_scope` comparison (`config.validation_depth == ValidationDepth.X`) is silently `False`. Result: **all depth gating, both scopes, all backends, becomes a no-op** with no error or warning.

The env-var path *does* coerce (`config.py`: `validation_depth = ValidationDepth(validation_depth)` for `PANDERA_VALIDATION_DEPTH`), so the two configuration paths behave inconsistently for the same value.

Found via the xarray backend: a supposedly structural `"SCHEMA_ONLY"` validation of a lazily-backed Dataset materialized the data (remote chunk fetches on zarr-backed stores), because the properly-`@validate_scope(scope=ValidationScope.DATA)`-decorated `check_nullable` was never skipped.

### MRE (dask used only as a materialization counter)

```python
import dask
import dask.array as da
import numpy as np
import xarray as xr
import pandera.xarray as pa
from pandera.config import ValidationDepth, config_context

loads = {"n": 0}
def _load():
    loads["n"] += 1
    return np.zeros((4, 5))

def make_ds():
    arr = da.from_delayed(dask.delayed(_load)(), shape=(4, 5), dtype=float)
    return xr.Dataset({"DBZH": (("azimuth", "range"), arr)})

schema = pa.DatasetSchema(
    data_vars={"DBZH": pa.DataVar(dtype=np.float64, dims=("azimuth", "range"))}
)

with config_context(validation_depth="SCHEMA_ONLY"):        # string
    schema.validate(make_ds())
print(loads["n"])   # 1  — data computed; depth gating silently disabled

loads["n"] = 0
with config_context(validation_depth=ValidationDepth.SCHEMA_ONLY):  # enum
    schema.validate(make_ds())
print(loads["n"])   # 0  — gating works as designed
```

Confirming the stored value: inside the string context, `get_config_context().validation_depth` is `'SCHEMA_ONLY'` (a `str`) and `== ValidationDepth.SCHEMA_ONLY` is `False`.

### Suggested fix

Coerce in `config_context` (and anywhere else user-supplied): `validation_depth = ValidationDepth(validation_depth)` — raising `ValueError` on unknown values — mirroring the existing env-var handling. Alternatively make `ValidationDepth` a `(str, Enum)` so string comparisons hold. Either way, an invalid value should fail loudly instead of silently disabling gating.

### Related minor quirk (can split out if preferred)

For a lazy `DataTreeSchema` failure, `str(SchemaErrors)` renders as `{}` — the individual reports are only reachable via `.schema_errors`, which makes CI logs opaque.

### Environment

pandera 0.32.1, xarray 2026.7.0, python 3.12 (linux)

problem_statement.title: SqlCatalog table operations should filter on `iceberg_type`
problem_statement.body:
### Feature Request / Improvement

In #3263, the `iceberg_type` column was added to the SQLCatalog and filters it in `list_tables`, but the other table operations (i.e. load_table, drop_table, rename_table, commit_table) don't check it yet. That means a view row written by iceberg java or iceberg-rust can bleed in pythons SQLCatalog table operations.

Java's V1 catalog applies `WHERE (iceberg_type = 'TABLE' OR iceberg_type IS NULL)` everywhere ([JdbcUtil.java#L168](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/blob/main/core/src/main/java/org/apache/iceberg/jdbc/JdbcUtil.java#L168)). We should do the same.

Probably worth extracting a small helper since the predicate would now appear in ~5+ places.

Repro steps:

```python
catalog = SqlCatalog("test", uri="sqlite:///...", warehouse="...")
catalog.create_namespace("ns")

# bypass and sim java/rust writing a view row
with catalog.engine.connect() as conn:
    conn.execute(text(
        "INSERT INTO iceberg_tables VALUES "
        "('test', 'ns', 'a_view', 's3://fake/m.json', NULL, 'VIEW')"
    ))
    conn.commit()

catalog.drop_table(("ns", "a_view"))  # Silently deletes the view row :/
```

problem_statement.title: `overwrite().delete_data_file()` fails with non-identity partition transforms (`BucketTransform`) due to manifest-pruning predicate reconstruction (regression vs 0.11.1)
problem_statement.body:
### Apache Iceberg version

main (development)

### Please describe the bug 🐞

Found when running 0.12RC

## Summary

`delete_data_file()` in the overwrite snapshot path crashes when the table partition spec uses a non-identity transform (for example, `BucketTransform` on a `string` source column).

Observed error:
```text
TypeError: Cannot convert LongLiteral into string
```

This appears to be introduced by commit `8a47d2bf` (["Optimization: Prune manifest in snapshot overwrite operations"](https://github.com/apache/iceberg-python/pull/3011)), which added `_SnapshotProducer._build_delete_files_partition_predicate()` and calls it from `_manifests()`.

## Affected API Pattern

This affects the lower-level transactional overwrite path:

```python
with table.transaction() as txn:
    with txn.update_snapshot().overwrite() as ov:
        ov.delete_data_file(existing_file)
```

This does **not** report through the same path as `table.delete(predicate)` / `table.overwrite(df, overwrite_filter=...)`, which operate from user-provided predicates.

## Root Cause

`_SnapshotProducer._build_delete_files_partition_predicate()` groups deleted files by `spec_id` and stores each `data_file.partition` record.

It then calls:

```python
self._transaction._build_partition_predicate(
    partition_records=partition_records,
    schema=self.schema(),
    spec=self.spec(spec_id),
)
```

`Transaction._build_partition_predicate` currently builds `EqualTo(Reference(source_column_name), stored_partition_value)` for each partition field.

That is only valid for `IdentityTransform`, where the stored partition value is the source-column domain value.

For `BucketTransform`, the stored partition value is a bucket id (integer), not the original source value (e.g. `string`). Binding then fails with:

```text
TypeError: Cannot convert LongLiteral into string
```

There is already an explicit identity-only guard in `Transaction.dynamic_partition_overwrite` before using `_build_partition_predicate`; the overwrite delete-data-file call site added in `8a47d2bf` does not have a corresponding guard.

```
    with TemporaryDirectory(prefix="pyiceberg-bucket-delete-bug-") as tmp_dir:
        warehouse = Path(tmp_dir) / "warehouse"
        warehouse.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

        identifier = (namespace, table_name)

        catalog.create_namespace(namespace)

        schema = Schema(
```

problem_statement.title: pivot_longer column_level collapses duplicate labels and loses the row index
problem_statement.body:
## Summary

When `pivot_longer` receives `column_level`, `_data_checks_pivot_longer` reconstructs the DataFrame through a dictionary keyed by labels from the selected level. This has two observable effects:

1. Repeated labels at that level are silently collapsed, so measured columns and their values can be lost.
2. The original row index is discarded, even when `ignore_index=False`.

## Minimal reproducer

```python
import pandas as pd
import janitor

columns = pd.MultiIndex.from_tuples([("x", "a"), ("x", "b")])
df = pd.DataFrame(
    [[1, 2], [3, 4]],
    columns=columns,
    index=pd.Index([10, 20], name="row"),
)

result = df.pivot_longer(column_level=0, ignore_index=False)
print(result)
```

The result contains only values from the second `x` column and has a new `RangeIndex`. Both selected columns should participate in the reshape, and the original index labels should be retained and repeated.

## Likely cause

The `column_level` branch converts the columns to a dictionary before constructing a new DataFrame. Duplicate dictionary keys overwrite earlier entries, and the constructor is not given the original index.

## Proposed scope

- Replace dictionary reconstruction with a shallow DataFrame copy followed by column reassignment.
- Add regression coverage for repeated labels at the selected level.
- Add regression coverage for `ignore_index=False` with a non-default index.
- Preserve extension-array dtypes and existing column-selection behavior.

## Performance note

On a 10,000-row by 100-column frame, shallow relabeling took about 0.014 ms versus about 1.08 ms for dictionary reconstruction while preserving shape and index.

problem_statement.body:
Specification [(3.1.4)](https://a2a-protocol.org/latest/specification/#314-list-tasks)

> When `includeArtifacts` is false (the default), the artifacts field MUST be omitted entirely from each Task object in the response. The field should not be present as an empty array or null value.

Actual behavior:
```python
from google.protobuf.json_format import MessageToDict

task = Task(
    id="task-1",
    context_id="context-1",
    status=TaskStatus(state=TaskState.TASK_STATE_WORKING),
)
task.ClearField("artifacts")

response = ListTasksResponse(tasks=[task])
data = MessageToDict(
    response,
    preserving_proto_field_name=False,
    always_print_fields_with_no_presence=True,
)

print(data["tasks"][0]["artifacts"]) 
```

problem_statement.title: YAML specification: global conversion_options override a session's own conversion_options
problem_statement.body:
In `run_conversion_from_yaml`, the options for each interface are assembled as

```python
conversion_options[key] = dict(session_conversion_options.get(key, dict()), **global_conversion_options)
```

The right-hand mapping wins in that construction, so a value in the top-level `conversion_options` block overrides the same option stated for a single session. A specification that sets `stub_test: True` globally to keep the run fast and then turns it off for one session, or that names a global `iterator_options` and refines it for one interface in one session, silently gets the global value for that session.

Metadata in the same function merges the other way: the global block, then the experiment's, then the session's, with the more specific one winning. The conversion options should follow the same order, so a session's own options override the global ones.

```yaml
conversion_options:
  stub_test: true

experiments:
  exp:
    sessions:
      - nwbfile_name: full_session
        source_data: {...}
        conversion_options:
          ap:
            stub_test: false   # currently ignored in favor of the global True
```

The specification schema and the docs say nothing about precedence, so this is a behaviour change only for a specification that states the same option at both levels, which is the case where the current result is the surprising one.

problem_statement.title: Activate `source` field on PackageSettings/VariantInfo and add `source_resolver` PBI property
problem_statement.body:
## Context

The new `SourceResolver` data model is complete in `_resolver.py` (PRs #1228, #1235), but the `source` field is still **commented out** on `PackageSettings` and `VariantInfo` in `_models.py`, and `PackageBuildInfo` has no `source_resolver` property. This is the foundation that all other wiring work depends on.

**Parent epic:** #1254 (Phase 1 — critical path, blocks all other phases)

## Problem

The new resolver config cannot be used at runtime because the `source` field isn't active on the settings models and there's no way to access it through `PackageBuildInfo`.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `source: SourceResolver | None` field is active on both `PackageSettings` and `VariantInfo`
- [ ] `SourceResolver` is importable from `fromager.packagesettings`
- [ ] `PackageBuildInfo` has a `source_resolver` property that returns variant-level `source` if set, else package-level `source`, else `None`
- [ ] Loading YAML with `source:` config produces the correct `SourceResolver` instance
- [ ] `pbi.source_resolver` returns `None` when no `source:` is configured (legacy config unchanged)
- [ ] All existing tests pass (no legacy behavior change)

## Files

- `src/fromager/packagesettings/_models.py`
- `src/fromager/packagesettings/_pbi.py`
- `src/fromager/packagesettings/__init__.py`

## Related

- #1207 — Mutual exclusivity validation (can be done as part of this or separately)
- Depends on: nothing
- Blocks: Phase 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9

problem_statement.title: Commands in flattened subapps don't fully render in generated docs
problem_statement.body:
The cyclopts [subcommand docs](https://cyclopts.readthedocs.io/en/latest/commands.html#flattening-subcommands) suggest using `app.command(sub_app, name="*")` to flatten a subapp into its parent command.

However `generate_docs` does not render the command help completely.

By contrast, using `app.update(sub_app)` (which is undocumented?) seems to achieve the same result, and _does_ render the flattened command properly.

For example:

```python
from cyclopts import App

app = App(name="app")

sub_app_update = App(name="update")
sub_app_star = App(name="star")


@sub_app_update.command()
def update(foo: int) -> None: ...


@sub_app_star.command()
def star(bar: int) -> None: ...


app.command(sub_app_star, name="*")
app.update(sub_app_update)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(app.generate_docs())
```

->

---

# app

```console
app COMMAND
```

## Table of Contents

- [`update`](#app-update)

**Commands**:

* [`star`](#app-star)
* [`update`](#app-update)

## app update

```console
app update FOO
```

**Parameters**:

* `FOO, --foo`: **[required]**

---

As you can see there is no documentation for `app star` other than the entry under `Commands`.

Also, are the two forms (otherwise) equivalent or am I missing something?

problem_statement.title: Repeating ui.timer raises "The parent slot of Timer(id=N) has been deleted" when its client is deleted while waiting in _can_start() — the _should_stop() guard is unreachable
problem_statement.body:
### First Check

- [x] I added a very descriptive title here.
- [x] This is not a security issue (those should be reported via the [security advisory](https://github.com/zauberzeug/nicegui/security/advisories/new) instead).
- [x] This is not a Q&A. I am sure something is wrong with NiceGUI or its documentation.
- [x] I used the GitHub search to find a similar [issue](https://github.com/zauberzeug/nicegui/issues) and came up empty.

### Example Code

```python
from nicegui import ui


@ui.page('/')
def page() -> None:
    ui.timer(60, lambda: None)


ui.run()
```

Then request the page over plain HTTP without ever opening the websocket (a bot, a prefetch, a user bouncing before the handshake, an HTTP-only load probe):

```bash
curl -s http://localhost:8080/ > /dev/null
```

After `Client.prune_instances` deletes the never-connected client (~60 s), the timer task wakes and — depending on a garbage-collection race — dies with:

```
  File "nicegui/background_tasks.py", line 152, in _handle_exceptions
    task.result()
  File "nicegui/timer.py", line 90, in _run_in_loop
    with self._get_context():
  File "nicegui/elements/timer.py", line 15, in _get_context
    return self.parent_slot or nullcontext()
  File "nicegui/element.py", line 150, in parent_slot
    raise RuntimeError(f'The parent slot of {name}(id={self.id}{markers}) has been deleted.')
RuntimeError: The parent slot of Timer(id=2) has been deleted.
```

Because it races the cycle collector it is intermittent per occurrence — but at fleet scale it is loud: on our staging deployment this single raise is **~49% of all captured Sentry events** (~3,400 events across two message wordings, 3.14.x: "The parent slot of the element has been deleted.").

### Description

The sequence:

1. A repeating `ui.timer` is created during page build. `_run_in_loop` suspends in `_can_start()` on `await self.client.connected()` while the websocket handshake is pending.
2. The client never connects and is deleted (`prune_instances`, or any other `Client.delete()` while the timer still waits).
3. `Client.delete()` runs `remove_all_elements()` (which cancels the timer via `_handle_delete`) and then `self._connected.set()  # for terminating connected() waits` — which wakes the parked waiter into a **success** return. `_can_start()` answers `True` for a deleted client.
4. `_run_in_loop` proceeds to `with self._get_context():`. If the cycle collector has already collected the slot tree, the `parent_slot` weakref dereferences to `None` and `element.py` raises — **one line before** `while not self._should_stop():`, the guard built for exactly this case (`self.is_deleted` is already `True` at this point and would exit cleanly).

So the timer is already properly canceled and deleted; it just touches the dead slot before it is allowed to notice. No application frame appears in the stack, and no user ever sees anything — but every occurrence goes through `app.handle_exception` at ERROR level, which is costly for anyone forwarding logs to a paid error tracker.

**Suggested fix:** check `self._should_stop()` before entering `self._get_context()` in `_run_in_loop` (and equivalently `self.active and not self._should_stop()` before the context in `_run_once`). At the failure point `_deleted` is `True`, so the hoisted check exits cleanly, and `Timer._cleanup` is already guarded by `if not self._deleted:` so the finally-path stays safe.

A complementary (or alternative) fix would be for `_can_start()` to return `False` when the wake came from `Client.delete()` rather than a real connection — e.g. re-checking `self.client.id in Client.instances` / `self.is_deleted` after `connected()` returns — since `connected()` currently reports success on a deleted client.

### NiceGUI Version

3.15.0 (same raise with the older message wording on 3.14.x)

### Python Version

3.14.6

### Browser

Not applicable (server-side; triggered by HTTP-only page loads)

### Operating System

Linux (Docker)

### Additional Context

The two suspension points and the GC dependency make this hard to reproduce deterministically in a unit test — the raise only happens when the cycle collector runs between the `connected()` wake-up and the timer task's resumption — but the code path above is fully deterministic once the weakref is dead.

problem_statement.title: Bug: NATS subscribers declared with `filter_subjects` render an empty AsyncAPI address
problem_statement.body:
**Describe the bug**

A NATS JetStream pull subscriber can be declared without a `subject`, addressing the stream through `filter_subjects` instead. Such a subscriber works at runtime — including Path parameters, since each filter subject is compiled as an address — but its address never reaches the AsyncAPI schema. The channel renders with an empty subject and a degenerate name.

**How to reproduce**

```python
import json

from nats.js.api import ConsumerConfig

from faststream.nats import JStream, NatsBroker, PullSub
from faststream.specification import AsyncAPI

broker = NatsBroker()


@broker.subscriber(
    stream=JStream("st"),
    pull_sub=PullSub(),
    durable="d",
    config=ConsumerConfig(filter_subjects=["logs.{level}"]),
)
async def handle() -> None: ...


schema = json.loads(AsyncAPI(broker, schema_version="3.0.0").to_specification().to_json())
print(json.dumps(schema["channels"], indent=1))
```

**Observed behavior**

```json
{
 ":Handle": {
  "address": ":Handle",
  "servers": [{"$ref": "#/servers/development"}],
  "messages": {"SubscribeMessage": {"$ref": "#/components/messages/:Handle:SubscribeMessage"}},
  "bindings": {"nats": {"subject": "", "bindingVersion": "custom"}}
 }
}
```

**Expected behavior**

The subject(s) the consumer actually filters on should appear in the channel — as the address and in the NATS channel binding — and the channel name should be derived from them rather than collapsing to `:Handle`.

**Root cause**

`NatsSubscriberSpecificationConfig` carries only `subject` and `queue` (`faststream/nats/subscriber/config.py`), so the specification layer has no knowledge of `filter_subjects` at all. `NatsSubscriberSpecification.subject` reads `self.config.subject`, which is empty here.

The usecase layer does know: `filter_addresses` builds one `Address` per filter subject (`faststream/nats/subscriber/usecases/basic.py`) and `subscription_addresses` yields them, which is why the subscriber works. `_resolved_subject_string` already joins them, but is used only for log context.

**Additional context**

This is not specific to address templates — `filter_subjects=["logs.info"]` renders an empty address too. It was found while scoping #2357 (AsyncAPI render for pattern cases), and is deliberately kept out of it: #2357 is about *which* string a template renders as, this is about an address not being rendered at all.

The two do interact, though, and whoever picks this up should read #2357 first. #2357 adds channel `parameters` derived from the address. Different filter subjects can carry different `{param}` sets, which cannot be described by a single channel — so the natural shape here is one channel per filter subject, the same shape `KafkaSubscriberSpecification` already uses for its topics.

+            self.context.add_message({"role": "user", "content": f"Message {i}"})
+        await summarizer.process_frame(LLMFullResponseStartFrame())
+        self.assertIsNotNone(request_frame)
+
+        # Summarize messages 1..3, keeping the last two. The context becomes
+        # [system, summary, Message 3, Message 4].
+        await summarizer.process_frame(
+            LLMContextSummaryResultFrame(
+                request_id=request_frame.request_id,
+                summary="Summary.",
+                last_summarized_index=3,
+            )
+        )
+        self.assertEqual(len(self.context.messages), 4)

+        # Two kept messages plus two new ones is below the threshold of five.
+        for i in range(2):
+            self.context.add_message({"role": "user", "content": f"New message {i}"})
+        self.assertFalse(await self._check_trigger(summarizer))
+
+        # The fifth conversation message since the summary triggers again.
+        self.context.add_message({"role": "user", "content": "New message 2"})
+        self.assertTrue(await self._check_trigger(summarizer))
+
+        await summarizer.cleanup()

+    async def test_message_count_resets_when_context_replaced(self):
+        """Replacing the context after a summary drops the summary from the count."""
+        config = LLMAutoContextSummarizationConfig(
+            max_context_tokens=100000,

+        )

+        summarizer = LLMContextSummarizer(context=self.context, config=config)
+        await summarizer.setup(frame_processor_setup(self.task_manager))
+
+        request_frame = None

+        async def on_request_summarization(summarizer, frame):
+            nonlocal request_frame

problem_statement.title: LLMContextSummarizer: messages_since_summary never resets and counts the injected summary message
problem_statement.body:
## Problem

In `LLMContextSummarizer._should_summarize()` (`src/pipecat/processors/aggregators/llm_context_summarizer.py:232` on current main), the message-count trigger uses:

```python
messages_since_summary = len(self._context.messages) - 1
```

The `-1` is a static stand-in for "subtract the system message", not a real since-last-summary counter. Nothing in the class stores a marker of when the last summary was applied, so:

- The counter never resets after a summarization. `max_unsummarized_messages` effectively means "total context length minus one", not "messages since the last summary".
- After `_apply_summary()` the context is `[system?] + [summary] + recent`, so the injected summary message is counted as a conversation message. With a system prompt and `min_messages_after_summary=4`, the count reads 5 right after a summary even though only 4 conversation messages remain.
- When `messages[0]` is not a system message, the pre-first-summary count is under by one instead.

## Suggested fix

Track real state: record the message count (or index) when a summary is applied in `_apply_summary()`, reset it there, and compute messages-since-summary against that marker. Exclude the preserved system message and the injected summary message from the count.

## Context

Found while fixing the related token-trigger bug (system prompt counted toward `max_context_tokens`); that fix is intentionally kept separate. See the linked PR.

problem_statement.title: [PERF] Build pivot_longer reorder indexer with one NumPy allocation
problem_statement.body:
## Summary

`_build_indexer_reorder_contents` currently constructs `np.arange(length * reps)`, reshapes it, and ravels in Fortran order. Because the final ravel requires a reordered copy, the helper temporarily holds roughly twice the output allocation.

A mathematically equivalent NumPy formulation can construct the row-by-column offsets directly:

```python
rows = np.arange(length)[:, None]
columns = np.arange(reps) * length
indexer = np.add(rows, columns).ravel()
```

This keeps the implementation in NumPy, preserves the current positional contract, and substantially lowers peak temporary memory.

## Measurements

Same-process medians on pandas 3.0.5 / NumPy 2.3.5:

| Shape | Current | One-allocation formulation | Current peak | New peak |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `length=100_000`, `reps=20` (2M output) | 1.49 ms | 1.49 ms | 30.52 MiB | 16.15 MiB |
| `length=1_000`, `reps=1_000` (1M output) | 1.09 ms | 0.63 ms | 15.26 MiB | 7.77 MiB |
| `length=1_000_000`, `reps=8` (8M output) | 10.53 ms | 8.11 ms | 122.07 MiB | 68.79 MiB |

The generated arrays were element-for-element equivalent.

## Scope

- Replace only `_build_indexer_reorder_contents`.
- Add focused helper equivalence tests for zero/small sizes and both row-heavy and column-heavy shapes.
- Confirm public `pivot_longer` behavior for extension arrays with `sort_by_appearance=True`.
- Measure end-to-end runtime and peak memory on many-row and many-column workloads.
- Preserve `np.intp`-compatible indexing and overflow/error behavior.

## Acceptance criteria

- Exact positional equivalence with the current helper.
- No ordering or dtype regression across nullable integer, string, categorical, datetime, and timezone-aware extension arrays.
- Peak helper allocation materially decreases for large outputs.
- No meaningful runtime regression for small or representative workloads.
- Complete pivot tests pass under supported pandas environments.

## Dependencies

Land after #1636 / PR #1643 so its allocation changes remain independently reviewable. This NumPy baseline should precede any Rust experiment in pyjanitor-devs/janitor-rs#18.

problem_statement.body:
## Description

`has_measurements()`, `remove_measurements()`, `has_barriers()` and `remove_barriers()` fall back to `self._statements` when the module has not been unrolled. That list can still contain `for` / `while` / `switch` bodies, and the statement walker does not descend into them — so an occurrence inside a loop or switch is invisible.

## Reproduction

```python
from pyqasm import loads

src = """OPENQASM 3.0;
include "stdgates.inc";
qubit[2] q;
bit[2] c;
for int i in [0:1] { c[i] = measure q[i]; barrier q; }
"""

m = loads(src)
print(m.has_measurements(), m.has_barriers())   # False False  <- wrong
m.remove_measurements()                          # no-op

m2 = loads(src)
m2.unroll()
print(m2.has_measurements(), m2.has_barriers())  # True True
```

## Scope

Pre-existing — `main` behaves identically, and #345 strictly improves matters by closing the same gap for `box` and `if` on the unrolled path. Filed because #345's walker is the natural home for the remainder, and it would be easy to read that PR as having closed the class of bug entirely.

Note this only affects the **non-unrolled** path. `for`, `while` and `switch` are fully unrolled by `unroll()` and do not reach `_unrolled_ast` with their bodies intact, so `Box` and `BranchingStatement` really are the only two containers the unrolled walk has to handle.

## Suggested fix

Either extend `iter_quantum_statements` to descend into loop and switch bodies for the non-unrolled path, or document on those four methods that they are only meaningful after `unroll()`.

Found in review of #345 (L3).

problem_statement.title: `_traverse_union` corrupts the scope graph when a set-operation operand isn't a Query, causing infinite recursion in `qualify()` (reproducible with valid SQL: VALUES on redshift/mysql/bigquery)
problem_statement.body:
**Before you file an issue**
- Read dialect: none required for the first repro; `redshift` / `mysql` / `bigquery` (second repro, explicit below)
- Write dialect: n/a (crashes before generating output)
- Reproduces on current `main` (`bac1a897b`, 2026-08-25, `v30.17.0-72-gbac1a897b`)

**Summary**

`_traverse_union` (`sqlglot/optimizer/scope.py`) builds a `Scope` for each set-operation operand by consuming `_traverse_scope()`'s generator in a loop. When an operand isn't one of the node types `_traverse_scope` knows how to build a scope for (not a `Select`, `SetOperation`, `Subquery`, `Table`, `UDTF`, `DDL`, or `DML`), `_traverse_scope` logs a warning and returns without yielding anything — but the calling loop doesn't check for that, and proceeds to use its loop variable unconditionally. That corrupts the `Scope` graph into a **self-referential** structure instead of raising, and `Scope.external_columns` then recurses into the cycle unboundedly:

- On pure Python this raises `RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded`.
- On the compiled `sqlglot[c]` build, by the same mechanism reported in #7732, the same unbounded recursion is expected to run in mypyc-compiled frames that don't reliably honor Python's recursion check and crash the process (`SIGSEGV`) instead of raising. I did not reproduce that half myself (no `sqlglot[c]` build in my environment) — flagging it as expected-but-unverified, not confirmed.

This is **not limited to malformed SQL**. A lenient parse of truncated/malformed input can produce a non-Query operand, but so can ordinary, valid SQL on three dialects, via how they parse a bare `VALUES (...)`.

**Fully reproducible code snippets**

1) Malformed/truncated SQL (a parse fragment leaving a bare `Column` where a `Query` was expected):

```python
import sqlglot
from sqlglot.optimizer.qualify import qualify

qualify(sqlglot.parse_one("a UNION SELECT 1"))
# RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded
```

2) Valid SQL — `VALUES (1) UNION ALL SELECT 1` is the exact example already used in `_traverse_union`'s own source comment ("Access the args directly instead of the left/right properties, because set operation operands aren't guaranteed to be Query nodes, e.g. in VALUES (1) UNION ALL SELECT 1"). Most dialects parse a bare `VALUES (...)` into a synthetic `Select`, which works fine. Three dialects instead parse it as `exp.Anonymous`, which hits this bug:

```python
import sqlglot
from sqlglot.optimizer.qualify import qualify

for dialect in ("redshift", "mysql", "bigquery"):
    qualify(sqlglot.parse_one("VALUES (1) UNION ALL SELECT 1", dialect=dialect), dialect=dialect)
    # RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded
```

| dialect | `VALUES (1)` parses to | `qualify()` |
|---|---|---|
| `redshift` | `exp.Anonymous` | **RecursionError** |
| `mysql` | `exp.Anonymous` | **RecursionError** |
| `bigquery` | `exp.Anonymous` | **RecursionError** |
| *(none / generic)* | `exp.Select` | OK |
| `postgres` | `exp.Select` | OK |
| `snowflake` | `exp.Select` | OK |
| `duckdb` | `exp.Select` | OK |

**Root cause**

`_traverse_union`'s per-operand loop (`sqlglot/optimizer/scope.py`, currently around line 800):

```python
def _traverse_union(scope: Scope) -> Iterator[Scope]:
    ...
    while expression_stack:
        ...
        for scope in _traverse_scope(new_scope):
            yield scope

        if prev_scope:
            union_scope_stack.pop()
            union_scope.union_scopes = [prev_scope, scope]
            ...
```

`scope` here is both the loop variable **and** the function's own parameter (`def _traverse_union(scope: Scope) -> Iterator[Scope]:`). If `_traverse_scope(new_scope)` yields nothing (the "Cannot traverse scope" warning path), the `for` loop runs zero iterations, and `scope` is left bound to whatever it held *before* the loop — on the first operand processed, that's the union's own outer scope, since nothing has reassigned it yet.

That makes `prev_scope = scope` (the `else` branch, taken on the first operand) bind `prev_scope` to the union's *own* scope rather than a real operand scope. When the second (valid) operand is then processed, `union_scope.union_scopes = [prev_scope, scope]` runs with `union_scope` being that same outer scope, so this line becomes self-referential — confirmed directly:

```python
>>> from sqlglot.optimizer.scope import traverse_scope
>>> root = traverse_scope(sqlglot.parse_one("a UNION SELECT 1"))[-1]
>>> root.union_scopes[0] is root
True
```

`Scope.external_columns` (`scope.py`, ~line 474) recurses through `union_scopes` and only memoizes its result *after* the recursive call returns:

```python
if self._external_columns is None:
    if isinstance(self.expression, exp.SetOperation):
        left, right = self.union_scopes
        self._external_columns = left.external_columns + right.external_columns  # assigned AFTER both calls return
```

so `self._external_columns` stays `None` throughout the descent, and the `left is self` cycle recurses without ever reaching the memo guard.

**Related issues**

This is the same downstream mechanism (self-referential `union_scopes` -> unbounded `external_columns` recursion) as #8195, reached through a different malformed-operand shape. I confirmed this directly by hand-constructing #8195's exact `Alias`-wrapped-`Subquery` operand tree and running it through `traverse_scope`/`external_columns` on current `main`: it hits the identical warning (`Cannot traverse scope ... with type 'Alias'`), the identical self-reference (`union_scopes[0] is root`), and the identical `RecursionError`. #8195 was closed by a parser-level fix (a570cf8a) that stops BigQuery from mis-parsing `FULL` as an alias in that one specific construct — which prevents that particular malformed tree from being built, but doesn't touch `_traverse_union` itself, so the general failure mode is still reachable through any other route to a non-Query operand, including the two above.

(#7732 is a different bug, in `resolver.py`'s column-type resolution for `LATERAL FLATTEN`/`UNNEST`, unrelated to this one beyond sharing the same "RecursionError in pure Python, expected SIGSEGV in `sqlglot[c]`" failure shape.)

**Fix**

I have a fix ready: give the loop its own variable, and raise `OptimizeError` immediately if `_traverse_scope` yields nothing for an operand instead of proceeding with a corrupted graph. `_traverse_ctes` in the same file already handles the equivalent situation correctly (initializes `child_scope: Scope | None = None` before its loop and checks `if child_scope:` after) — a good existing reference for the pattern. Full test suite passes locally (1239 passed, 19363 subtests) with a new regression test covering both cases above. Will link the PR here once it's up.
