+"""#1310: a qualified-only (shadowed) module generic's instantiation
+discovery had no effect-operation registry at all, unlike the unshadowed
+discovery walk #1207 already fixed.
+
+``_monomorphize_shadowed_module_generics`` seeds a shadowed generic's
+instances from ``ast.ModuleCall`` sites inside a module's own bodies via
+``_collect_shadowed_qualified_calls`` (codegen) and the mirroring
+``walk_seed`` closure (the verifier's ``_collect_shadowed_qualified_instances``,
+#732).  Neither ever installed the ``handle[State<T>]`` op-result registry
+``Monomorphizer._collect_calls`` merges in for the unshadowed path, so an
+argument like ``get(())`` fell through to the phantom-type-variable ``Bool``
+default. The WASM call-site rewrite (``CallsMixin._resolve_generic_call``),
+which runs with the real handler context during actual codegen, still named
+the correct clone (``mod$mlib5$idg$Int``), so discovery silently emitted a
+clone nothing calls, the real one was never registered, and the caller
+(``outer``, then ``main``) was dropped with E602/E620 on check-green,
+verify-clean source.
+
+Four cells:
+
+* the issue's own repro, a private module generic instantiated from an
+  effect-operation result, pinned end to end (no E602/E620, the checker's
+  own clone name in the WAT, and the runtime value);
+* a nested-distinct-state variant (mirroring
+  ``test_mono_effect_op_naming_1207.py``'s ``_NESTED_DISTINCT_STATE``) through
+  the SAME shadowed path, so a fix that merely stops defaulting to ``Bool``
+  without preserving merge-not-replace semantics for nested handlers is
+  still caught: it would name the inner call from the OUTER cell and sum to
+  the wrong value, and it now also asserts the outer cell's ``$Nat`` clone is
+  ABSENT, matching the first cell's shape (a WAT scan that only checked for
+  ``$Int`` would still pass a discovery walk emitting BOTH clones); and
+* the #732 differential (two cells, non-nested and nested), asserting
+  codegen's ``_emitted_instances`` and the verifier's ``_instances`` name the
+  IDENTICAL instantiation for the effect-op-result argument.
+
+The differential does NOT reuse cells 1/2's fixtures, and this is measured,
+not a style choice: ``idg``/``idg2`` are called BARE from inside their OWN
+declaring module, and the verifier's ``ContractVerifier._collect_instantiations``
+reroutes exactly that call shape to a mangled bare ``FnCall`` (name
+``mod$mlib5$idg``) via the pre-existing, #1310-unrelated
+``_reroute_to_module_qualified`` machinery (#1000/#1029) BEFORE
+``_collect_shadowed_qualified_instances``'s ``walk_seed`` ever sees it, so
+``walk_seed``'s own ``ast.ModuleCall`` match, and the ``HandleExpr`` merge
+guarding it, never fire for cells 1/2's call shape.  Reverting the merge only
+from ``walk_seed`` while keeping cells 1/2's fixtures leaves BOTH
+``_emitted_instances`` and ``_instances`` at ``Int`` (verified: the private
+self-reference is discovered instead through the ordinary unshadowed
+worklist over ``generic_decls["mod$mlib5$idg"]``, which already carried
+#1207's fix and was never broken), so a differential built on cells 1/2 alone
+would stay green under a verifier-only revert, silently failing to be a
+differential at all.  Codegen's ``_collect_shadowed_qualified_calls`` has no
+such reroute (it keeps the raw ``ast.ModuleCall`` until its OWN emission

+one-sided.

+    the boundary the two calls actually sit in.
+    """
+    verify_errors, result, cg_errors = build_multi_module(
+        tmp_path, {"mlib6.vera": _MLIB6, "main.vera": _MAIN6},
+    )
+    assert not cg_errors, f"codegen errors: {cg_errors}"
+    assert not verify_errors, f"verify errors: {verify_errors}"
+    names = wat_fn_names(result.wat)
+    assert "mod$mlib6$idg2$Int" in names, (
+        f"expected the inner cell's clone in the emitted WAT; got {names}"
+    )
+    assert "mod$mlib6$idg2$Nat" not in names, (
+        "the outer handler's State<Nat> leaked into the inner call's "
+        f"discovery instead of the inner State<Int> cell; emitted: {names}"
+    )
+    assert module_value(result) == ("ok", 7)
+
+
+def _discovered_sets(
+    module_path: tuple[str, ...], module_src: str, main_src: str,
+) -> tuple[
+    set[tuple[str, tuple[str, ...]]], set[tuple[str, tuple[str, ...]]],
+]:
+    """``(codegen_emitted, verifier_discovered)`` for *main_src* against one
+    imported module.
+
+    This is the #732 cross-component differential (see
+    ``tests/test_monomorphize_differential.py``) applied to the shadowed
+    path this fix touches: codegen's ``_emitted_instances`` is fed by
+    ``_collect_shadowed_qualified_calls``'s ``instances`` dict, and the
+    verifier's ``_instances`` is fed by ``_collect_shadowed_qualified_instances``'s
+    ``walk_seed`` closure and its ``seed`` set, for a call shape where both
+    discovery walks actually reach their own ``HandleExpr``-merge arm (see
+    the module docstring: this is NOT true of cells 1/2's fixtures).
+    Reverting either arm alone makes ONE side keep defaulting the effect-op
+    argument to the phantom ``Bool`` type variable while the other now
+    infers ``Int``, so the two recorded sets stop agreeing. The doctrine is
+    that the verifier must statically check exactly the set codegen emits,
+    and only this equality pins that for the shadowed, effect-op-result
+    path.
+    """
+    mod = resolved_module(module_path, module_src)
+    with tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(
+        mode="w", suffix=".vera", delete=False, encoding="utf-8",
+    ) as f:
+        f.write(main_src)
+        f.flush()
+        main_path = f.name
+    try:
+        program = transform(parse_file(main_path))
+        gen = CodeGenerator(
+            source=main_src, file=main_path, resolved_modules=[mod],
+        )
+        gen.compile_program(program)  # type: ignore[arg-type]
+        codegen_set = getattr(gen, "_emitted_instances", set())
+        verifier = ContractVerifier(
+            source=main_src, file=main_path, resolved_modules=[mod],
+        )
+        verifier.register_program(program)  # type: ignore[arg-type]
+        verifier_set = {
+            (n, ct) for n, cts in verifier._instances.items() for ct in cts
+        }
+    finally:
+        os.unlink(main_path)
+    return codegen_set, verifier_set
+
+
+def test_shadowed_generic_effect_op_discovery_differential() -> None:
+    """External qualified call: codegen and the verifier must discover the
+    identical ``mod$mlib7$idg3`` instantiation from ``mlib7::idg3(get(()))``.
+
+    ``idg3`` is PUBLIC in ``mlib7`` but shadowed at the importer by a
+    same-named private local declaration, so the call must be qualified,
+    exactly the shape ``walk_seed``'s ``ast.ModuleCall`` match (and the
+    ``HandleExpr`` merge guarding it) exists for.  Deleting the merge from
+    only one of the two discovery walks turns this red: codegen would keep
+    emitting ``mod$mlib7$idg3$Int`` while the verifier fell back to
+    ``mod$mlib7$idg3$Bool`` (or vice versa), so the sets would disagree even
+    though each one, read alone, looks self-consistent.  Measured directly
+    (not just asserted): reverting codegen's merge alone yields
+    ``{('mod$mlib7$idg3', ('Bool',))}`` vs the verifier's unchanged
+    ``{('mod$mlib7$idg3', ('Int',))}``; reverting the verifier's merge alone
+    yields the mirror image.  Both were executed against this exact fixture
+    before this test was written.
+    """
+    codegen_set, verifier_set = _discovered_sets(("mlib7",), _MLIB7, _MAIN7)
+    assert ("mod$mlib7$idg3", ("Int",)) in codegen_set, (
+        f"codegen must emit the shadowed generic's clone at Int, "
+        f"got {sorted(codegen_set)}"
+    )
+    assert ("mod$mlib7$idg3", ("Bool",)) not in codegen_set, (
+        f"codegen fell through to the phantom Bool default, "
+        f"got {sorted(codegen_set)}"
+    )
+    assert verifier_set == codegen_set, (
+        f"verifier ({sorted(verifier_set)}) must discover exactly codegen's "
+        f"emitted set ({sorted(codegen_set)}) for the effect-op-result "
+        f"argument of a shadowed generic; a one-sided fix desyncs this"
+    )
+
+
+def test_shadowed_generic_effect_op_discovery_differential_nested() -> None:
+    """The nested-distinct-state variant of the external-qualified-call
+    differential, same equality.
+
+    ``idg4`` is called via ``mlib8::idg4(get(()))`` from the INNER
+    ``handle[State<Int>]`` body, nested inside an OUTER
+    ``handle[State<Nat>]`` in the IMPORTER's own code: the merge-not-replace
+    scoping must still land both sides on ``mod$mlib8$idg4$Int``, never
+    ``$Nat`` (the outer cell leaking in) nor a desync between the two
+    discovery walks.  Measured directly: reverting codegen's merge alone
+    yields ``{('mod$mlib8$idg4', ('Bool',))}`` vs the verifier's unchanged
+    ``{('mod$mlib8$idg4', ('Int',))}``; reverting the verifier's merge alone
+    yields the mirror image.  Both executed against this exact fixture
+    before this test was written.
+    """
+    codegen_set, verifier_set = _discovered_sets(("mlib8",), _MLIB8, _MAIN8)
+    assert ("mod$mlib8$idg4", ("Int",)) in codegen_set, (
+        f"codegen must emit the inner cell's clone at Int, "
+        f"got {sorted(codegen_set)}"
+    )
+    assert ("mod$mlib8$idg4", ("Nat",)) not in codegen_set, (
+        f"the outer handler's Nat leaked into discovery, "
+        f"got {sorted(codegen_set)}"
+    )
+    assert verifier_set == codegen_set, (
+        f"verifier ({sorted(verifier_set)}) must discover exactly codegen's "
+        f"emitted set ({sorted(codegen_set)}) for the nested handler "
+        f"variant; a one-sided fix desyncs this"
+    )

+def _request_max_length(limit: int) -> AfterValidator:
+    """
+    Length check applied to request data only.
+
+    Django does not enforce TextField.max_length at the model or database
+    level (it is only reflected in form widgets), so stored values may
+    legally exceed it.  A hard pydantic constraint would make response
+    serialization fail with a 500 for such rows (see #1692).  Instead we
+    validate incoming payloads (on par with Django forms and DRF) and skip
+    the check when serializing responses.
+    """
+
+    def check(value: Any, info: core_schema.ValidationInfo) -> Any:
+        context = info.context
+        if context and "response_status" in context:
+            return value  # serializing a response - skip
+        if value is not None and len(value) > limit:
+            raise PydanticKnownError("string_too_long", {"max_length": limit})
+        return value
+
+    return AfterValidator(check)
+

problem_statement.title: [BUG] If a TextField has a max_length, it should not be used for validation
problem_statement.body:
**Describe the bug**

Consider this `description` field:

```
    description = models.TextField(
        verbose_name="description", blank=True, max_length=2048
    )
```

According to the [docs](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/6.0/ref/models/fields/#django.db.models.TextField
), this max_length does not place a restraint on the database: 

> If you specify a max_length attribute, it will be reflected in the [Textarea](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/6.0/ref/forms/widgets/#django.forms.Textarea) widget of the auto-generated form field. However it is not enforced at the model or database level. Use a [CharField](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/6.0/ref/models/fields/#django.db.models.CharField) for that.

Now when we query the API for an object with a description longer than 2048, we get:

```
E       pydantic_core._pydantic_core.ValidationError: 1 validation error for NinjaResponseSchema
E       response.description_en
E         String should have at most 2048 characters [type=string_too_long, input_value='012345678901234567890123...78901234567890123456789', input_type=str]
E           For further information visit https://errors.pydantic.dev/2.12/v/string_too_long
```

Note that in the example above, the field is called `description_en`. This is because we use https://github.com/deschler/django-modeltranslation. I don't think that that matters: It's still a TextField. But it might matter, so i mention it here. 

**Versions:**

 - Python version: 3.13
 - Django version: 5.2.12
 - Django-Ninja version: 1.5.3
 - Pydantic version: 2.12.5

problem_statement.title: aiohttp integration corrupts SigV4-signed propagation headers, breaking aiobotocore S3 calls (since 2.69.0)
problem_statement.body:
### How do you use Sentry?

Sentry Saas (sentry.io)

### Version

2.69.0

### Steps to Reproduce

Since 2.69.0, S3 calls made through aiobotocore fail with `SignatureDoesNotMatch` whenever a Sentry transaction is active. Synchronous boto3 is not affected.

aiobotocore sends botocore's already-signed requests through aiohttp. #7050 made the Boto3 integration add `sentry-trace` and `baggage` at `before-sign`, so both are named in `SignedHeaders`. The aiohttp client integration then rewrites them after signing, appending to `baggage`:

```python
if key == BAGGAGE_HEADER_NAME and params.headers.get(BAGGAGE_HEADER_NAME):
    params.headers[key] += "," + value
```

The sent value no longer matches the signed value, so the request is rejected.

`stdlib` already skips propagation headers named in `SignedHeaders`, which is why sync boto3 is fine. The aiohttp path never got the same guard.

Reproduction against any S3-compatible endpoint:

```python
import asyncio, sentry_sdk
import aiobotocore.session as abcs

async def main():
    sentry_sdk.init(dsn="<dsn>", traces_sample_rate=1.0)
    session = abcs.get_session()
    async with session.create_client(
        "s3", region_name="auto", endpoint_url="<endpoint>",
        aws_access_key_id="<key>", aws_secret_access_key="<secret>",
    ) as client:
        with sentry_sdk.start_transaction(op="t", name="r2"):
            await client.list_objects_v2(Bucket="<bucket>", MaxKeys=1)

asyncio.run(main())
```

### Expected Result

The request is sent with the headers botocore signed, and succeeds.

### Actual Result

```
botocore.exceptions.ClientError: An error occurred (SignatureDoesNotMatch) when calling the
ListObjectsV2 operation: The request signature we calculated does not match the signature you
provided. Check your secret access key and signing method.
```

Isolation, against a real Cloudflare R2 bucket, with credentials, botocore 1.43.75 and aiobotocore 3.9.1 held constant:

```
aiobotocore, all default integrations       SignatureDoesNotMatch
aiobotocore, AioHttpIntegration disabled    OK
aiobotocore, Boto3Integration disabled      OK
synchronous boto3, all integrations         OK
```

By SDK version, same setup:

```
2.63.0  OK
2.66.0  OK
2.67.0  OK
2.68.0  OK
2.69.0  SignatureDoesNotMatch
```

To rule out the endpoint being strict about what may be signed: with no SDK involved, botocore signing `baggage`, `sentry-trace`, an arbitrary `x-koodle-test` or `x-amz-meta-*` is accepted every time. The problem is only that the header changes after signing.

Two notes for anyone hitting this. Calls fail only inside a transaction, so anything running outside one keeps working and it presents as intermittent. And the workarounds are `trace_propagation_targets` set to exclude the endpoint, or pinning `sentry-sdk<2.69.0`.

Fix in #7427.

problem_statement.title: toml postargs: passed as str not list from cli
problem_statement.body:
Say you have something like this..

```toml
commands = [[
    "pylint",
    "--",
    { replace = "posargs", default = ["tests"], extend = true }
]]
```

If you try to run: 
   `tox -- tests src` 
it will throw an error like: 
    `ERROR: file or directory not found: tests src` 
and the pytest command looks like 
    `testenv: commands[0]> pytest -- 'tests src'`
it's treating 'tests src' as a single argument.

(tox 4.60.1, python 3.14)

I would expect it to pass the values as separate arguments

`testenv: commands[0]> pytest -- 'tests' 'src'`

problem_statement.title: Import scripts with the same name more than once (and sys.path growing)
problem_statement.body:
While debugging some odd behaviour in one of my tests, I realised that while running tests `sys.path` keeps on growing - each time a script is executed, a path is added, but never removed (not to mention we also add empty paths ... over and over :)  ).

I am wondering if it's worth avoiding this (i.e. keeping a copy of `sys.path` before calling `load_script`, then resetting it after execution of the script).

I also looked at removing the script symbol (`del trans_func` after calling it).

None of this is expected to have a real issue for an application, since they will call PSyclone only once with one script (even Fab uses subprocesses, i.e. you always get a clean `sys.path`).

The growing `sys.path` could in theory affect parallel testing (e.g. if we have one test expecting NOT to find a script of a given name, but accidentally a previous test adds a path that has a script with that name) - which is what I though was happening in my case:

I had three tests, each providing a script with the same name but slightly different behaviour. Each individual test worked, but when I executed them all (in parallel or not), some of them would fail. Reason of course is that the first executed script imported the script, and all further imports are fulfilled from the (Python internal) cached copy - no matter if we do a `del trans_func` (which removes the symbol, but NOT the cached import), and/or clean up `sys.path`. Fix for me was easy, just use three different names.

So, summary, we have thing with testing that we have to be careful about (different tests using the same script name), but can't fix it (there seems to be no way to affect the imported cache, unless we try using `reimport`??). 

The clean up (sys.path and removing the symbol) feels nice, but doesn't do anything. TBH, it feels like we should (at least) fix sys.path ;) But that's just me being ... peculiar about this :)  I am happy if we agree to just close this issue, but equally happy to clean up sys.path (and/or the symbol, but that makes probably even less sense ;) ). I will try to add a sentence or two to the docs as part of my script args PR otherwise.

problem_statement.title: Excessive information_schema queries from constraint-existence checks on models with primary_key set but contract not enforced
problem_statement.body:
### Describe the bug

For models that declare a model-level `primary_key` property but do **not** have `contract.enforced: true` and do **not** have an explicit `constraints:` block, dbt-databricks still runs a full "does this constraint already exist?" lookup against `information_schema` on every run, for every such model.

This generates 2 queries per model with a `primary_key` set (against `information_schema.key_column_usage` and `information_schema.table_constraints`), plus an additional query against `information_schema.referential_constraints` for any foreign keys. No constraint is actually being applied or enforced for these models — the checks appear to run purely because the property is set.

In one project we investigated: 255 of 303 models (84%) have `primary_key` set, with `contract.enforced: false` and no `constraints` block anywhere in the project, yet every run issues the constraint-existence check for all 255 of them. In a warehouse shared across many projects, this pattern (where present) contributes disproportionately to `information_schema` query volume — enough, in our case, to help trip Unity Catalog's per-metastore rate limit (`RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED.UC_INFORMATION_SCHEMA_PER_METASTORE_DB_RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED`) and fail otherwise-unrelated jobs sharing that metastore. (We checked a second project in the same account with no `primary_key` usage at all, confirming this is tied to modeling convention/project, not something universal — but it's still a real cost wherever the convention is used.)

### Steps To Reproduce

1. Create a model with a model-level `primary_key` property set, but do not enable `contract.enforced` and do not define an explicit `constraints:` block, e.g.:
```yaml
models:
  - name: my_model
    primary_key: [id]
    columns:
      - name: id
```
2. Run `dbt build` (or `dbt run`) with debug logging (`--debug`) against a Databricks/Unity Catalog target.
3. Observe in the debug log that dbt-databricks issues a query similar to:
```sql
SELECT kcu.constraint_name, kcu.column_name
FROM `<catalog>`.information_schema.key_column_usage kcu
WHERE kcu.table_catalog = '...'
  AND kcu.table_schema = '...'
  AND kcu.table_name = 'my_model'
  AND kcu.constraint_name = (
    SELECT constraint_name
    FROM `<catalog>`.information_schema.table_constraints
    WHERE table_catalog = '...'
      AND table_schema = '...'
      AND table_name = 'my_model'
      AND constraint_type = 'PRIMARY KEY'
  )
ORDER BY kcu.ordinal_position;
```
4. Repeat for every model with `primary_key` set — query count scales linearly with the number of such models, regardless of whether any constraint is actually meant to be applied.

### Expected behavior

Constraint-existence checks (and any subsequent DDL) should only run for models where a constraint is actually going to be applied/enforced — i.e., where `contract.enforced: true` and/or an explicit `constraints:` block is present. A model-level `primary_key` property used purely for documentation/lineage purposes should not trigger live `information_schema` verification queries against the warehouse on every run.

This looks related to #1342, which described constraints being applied without an enforced contract as a regression and was closed as fixed — but the behavior described here reproduces on `dbt-databricks==1.12.1`, suggesting either the fix didn't cover the `primary_key`-property-only case (no `constraints:` block at all), or this is a related but distinct code path.

Separately, #845 requests batching per-column constraint/comment operations into fewer queries — applying that kind of batching to the constraint-existence check described here would also directly mitigate the volume problem even if the "don't check at all when not enforced" fix isn't feasible short-term.

### System information

**The output of `dbt --version`:**
```
Plugins:
  - databricks: 1.12.1
```

Environment: dbt Cloud, Databricks/Unity Catalog target, multi-project account.

### Additional context

Observed via Databricks warehouse-side error `RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED.UC_INFORMATION_SCHEMA_PER_METASTORE_DB_RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED`, which surfaced the underlying query volume. Table/schema/catalog identifiers have been genericized here to avoid sharing customer-identifying information.

title: Derive one sort for a refined payload, wherever a term is rebuilt
issue_title: E699 Z3 sort mismatch verifying a module that rebuilds an imported Option<Nat> as Option<{refined}>
gold_patch:
diff --git a/CHANGELOG.md b/CHANGELOG.md
index 94acc19a5..2261f837d 100644
--- a/CHANGELOG.md
+++ b/CHANGELOG.md
@@ -25,6 +25,8 @@ The format is based on [Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/en/1.1.0/).
 
 ### Fixed
 
+- **One sort for a refined payload, wherever a term is rebuilt** ([#1421](https://github.com/aallan/vera/issues/1421), [#1424](https://github.com/aallan/vera/issues/1424)).  `vera verify` died with an `[E699]` internal compiler error — `Z3Exception: sort mismatch` — on programs `vera check` accepts, whenever a `match` arm rebuilt a value whose payload is a refinement: `match mk(x) { Some(@PosInt) -> Some(@PosInt.0), None -> None }`, and the cross-module spelling where an imported `Option<Nat>` is rewrapped as an `Option<{ @Int | @Int.0 > 0 }>`.  `_adt_sort_key` classified each type argument as primitive, ADT, or un-nameable, and a refinement is none of those — so it keyed `Option<?>` while every route that resolved the same payload to its base keyed `Option<Int>`.  Two Z3 sorts for one Vera type, and Z3 raises rather than returning an error when the arms meet under a `z3.If`.  A refinement now contributes its BASE through one shared helper — the rule `_vera_type_to_z3_sort` already stated, which had two implementations and no single one.  The unwrap is ONE LEVEL and a refinement over a refinement stays unmodelled by design: `_translate_refined_predicate` reads `{ @Base | P }` with a primitive base, so stripping a chain would supply a sort while its predicates stayed absent, modelling the payload as an unconstrained `Int` and reporting `violated`/**E526** on a division the chain proves safe.  Both routes therefore agree by REFUSING a chain, which keeps every current verdict; conjoining a chain's predicates is [#1434](https://github.com/aallan/vera/issues/1434).  The fix is in the derivation rather than in a catch, so there is no crash left to wrap.  Same family as [#884](https://github.com/aallan/vera/issues/884) (two Vera types colliding on one sort NAME) and [#1360](https://github.com/aallan/vera/issues/1360) (two routes deriving different sorts for a nested constructor); #1360 made the crash emit a parseable envelope, and this removes the crash.  Every affected shape now gets a real verdict: the cross-module rewrap is an honest **E505** (a `Nat` can be 0 where the refinement needs `> 0`), the same-module one is clean with a `refine_bind`/`tier3_unguarded`/E506, and a rewrap through a wrapper or out of a tuple component verifies at Tier 1.  Over all 293 examples and conformance programs no obligation, status or summary moves — no corpus program crashed at the base, so none can move.
+
 - **A disclosed fact stays disclosed across an import** ([#1399](https://github.com/aallan/vera/issues/1399)).  [#1373](https://github.com/aallan/vera/issues/1373) stopped a caller claiming a Tier-1 proof that rests on a callee's fact the run could neither prove nor guard, and stopped it *within a module*.  The same program split across two files still proved at Tier 1: an imported callee's obligations never enter the importing run's stream, and `disclosed_fn_names` derives the disclosed set BY READING that stream, so `_scrutinee_is_disclosed_call` answered False for every `lib::mk(...)` scrutinee no matter what `vera verify lib.vera` said about it.  Measured on the issue's reproducer: one file reported `use_it`'s postcondition `tier3` + **E534**, two files reported it `verified`, and the only difference was the file boundary.  The fix is a per-module disclosed **manifest** (`vera/disclosure.py`): each module's own verification emits the set `disclosed_fn_names` derives, keyed by the module's owner path, and the importer reads it through the resolved-module closure that already resolves the imported declarations.  It is derived, never declared — produced by running the module's own verification and asking the same shared derivation, so there is no second rule to drift from the in-module one and nothing for a library author to annotate.  The importer takes the NAMES only: the library's obligations stay in the library's run, so the documented accounting identity `len(obligations) == total + violated + tier3_unguarded` remains a statement about the work this run did.  Transitivity falls out of the recursion — computing module A's manifest runs A's own verification, which asks its own index about B — so a three-hop chain taints hop by hop, and a diamond's two importers of one base both demote from one computation.  Lookup covers all three places a disclosure can live: this run's own set (a local callee, and an unshadowed imported generic whose clone this run verifies), the `mod$<path>$<name>` key a shadowed or private imported generic's clone is verified under (a KEY MISMATCH that would have missed even a disclosure that did reach the stream), and the defining module's manifest — reached from a bare call through the name -> owning-module map recorded where the imported namespace is injected, so `import lib(mk);` does not escape through a change of spelling.  The manifest is content-addressed on the module's own source, its closure's sources and the solver budget, which is what makes an edit to an imported module invalidate it for the warm `VerificationSession` without a step anyone has to remember; a cell walks disclosed -> clean -> disclosed on one session with the entry's own text untouched, and goes red when the module-source component is dropped from the cache key.  Cost lands only where the question is asked: a module is verified for its manifest lazily, on the first call whose declared-type facts a match arm actually reads, so importing without matching on an imported call pays nothing.  A module is verified against the closure `vera verify <module>` would resolve for it — members, `direct` flags and ORDER alike, the last of those because several harvests over `_resolved_modules` are first-wins `setdefault`s (imported return types feeding monomorphization discovery among them), so a hand-rolled traversal that ordered a transitive-only diamond `od, oc, oe` where the resolver orders it `oc, od, oe` could select a different declaration for one name; the equality is pinned by a differential against `ModuleResolver` itself rather than against a restatement of its rule.  Manifests are computed BOTTOM-UP over the import DAG, each module verified exactly once with its dependencies' answers already cached, and both DAG walks are iterative: answering lazily and letting the answer recurse nests one whole verify pipeline per import hop, which is quadratic in the chain and bounded by the interpreter's stack rather than by the closure — a 70-module chain reported `E699` after 19 s on a program that verifies clean in 1.1 s without the manifest, and the warm session raised `RecursionError` into the LSP.  Bottom-up plus one `body_check_memo` shared across the closure's sub-checks takes a 150-module chain from `E699` to a clean verify, its peak stack from 469 frames to 56 (flat in depth), and its verification phase from 167 s to 17 s; the residual constant is one `vera verify` per consulted module, which is what R9 asks for, over registration work [#1275](https://github.com/aallan/vera/issues/1275) tracks.  A bare call is consulted only once the lexical chain `_scoped_fn_lookup` walks has been asked first, so a `where` helper sharing a name with a public import no longer demotes its parent's clean postcondition.  And the demotion says what caused it: across an import the library's `E504` belongs to the library's run, so the manifest carries the culprit's module, position and code and the `E534` cites them — the unqualified "the run reported it as neither proved nor guarded" was not true of the importing run, which reported no such thing.  Over all 291 examples and conformance programs, no program's obligation stream, status or summary moves.
 - **A burndown driven to zero can now be written down** ([#1401](https://github.com/aallan/vera/issues/1401)).  `scripts/check_doc_counts.py` reads "how many open bugs are there" from three places, and two of them had no zero state, so the condition was reachable exactly when a burndown succeeded and blocked the PR that made it succeed.  `bug_rows` recognised `KNOWN_ISSUES.md`'s empty form only when the whole `## Bugs` body equalled `No known bugs.`, but the section also carries a standing description of what the table is, so the documented form was rejected by the message that prescribed it; the marker is now read BESIDE that description — no rows, and the section's last line is the marker.  `roadmap_burndown_rows` had no empty form at all, so `*Zero open bugs, driven to zero.*` was unwritable: ROADMAP's burndown now reads as zero when its section is RETIRED (a burndown all of whose rows are closed is past, and past lives in HISTORY/CHANGELOG) and when the section is kept with its table replaced by the sibling marker `No open bugs.`.  `--check-bug-issues` agrees at zero too, passing when file and tracker are both empty and still reporting a tracker that is not — the "an empty query is a failed one" guard now qualifies on there being rows to check, the distinction being drawn where the query is made (`open_bug_issues` raises `BugQueryError` rather than returning `[]`).  None of the empty forms is a way past the gate: a table emptied WITHOUT a marker stays unreadable, a marker beside a stray row is a contradiction, a marker quoted in prose is not a claim, and both zero forms are still cross-checked against each other and against the header word.  Both tables are read by one function now, so the counts stay like for like at zero as they are at N, and each way of being unreadable gets its own sentence.
 - **`check_limitations_sync.py`'s section scan is bounded before it finds a table** ([#1405](https://github.com/aallan/vera/issues/1405)).  `extract_limitation_table_issues` broke out of a section only once a table row had been seen, so a section with no table — a `## Bugs` section driven to zero — walked past its own boundary and reported the next section's table as its contents: the whole Limitations table read as the Bugs table.  No verdict was wrong, because `main()` unions the two sets on both the presence and the `--check-states` path, but that is a property of the call sites rather than of the function, and the same scan reads the four spec-chapter limitation sections.  It now stops at the next second-level heading, the discipline its sibling `extract_section_issues` already had.

--- /dev/null
+++ b/tests/test_verifier_refined_sort_derivation.py
@@ -0,0 +1,447 @@
+"""One sort for a refined payload, wherever a term is rebuilt (#1421).
+
+`_adt_sort_key` names the Z3 sort a Vera ADT gets.  It classified each type
+argument as primitive, ADT, or un-nameable — and a REFINEMENT is none of those,
+so `Option<{ @Int | @Int.0 > 0 }>` was keyed `Option<?>` while every route that
+resolved the same payload to its base keyed `Option<Int>`.  Two Z3 sorts for one
+Vera type, and Z3 raises rather than returning an error when they meet: the
+arms of `match mk(x) { Some(@PosInt) -> Some(@PosInt.0), None -> None }` have to
+join under a `z3.If`, and the raise escaped as an `[E699]` internal compiler
+error on a program `vera check` accepts.
+
+The fix is in the derivation, not in a catch: a refinement contributes its
+BASE.  That rule is already stated in `_vera_type_to_z3_sort` — "a
+refinement's Z3 SORT is its base's sort; the predicate constrains values, not
+the carrier set, and is enforced separately" — so `Option<{ @Int | P }>` and
+`Option<Int>` are one sort and the two routes agree by construction.  What was
+missing was ONE implementation of it.
+
+The unwrap is ONE LEVEL and a chain is left unmodelled by design: the
+predicate half of that rule stops at a primitive base, so stripping a chain
+would supply a sort without the predicates and turn valid code into a false
+E526.  See `strip_refinements`.
+
+Same family as #884 (two Vera types colliding on one sort NAME) and #1360 (two
+routes deriving different sorts for a nested constructor).  #1360 made the
+crash emit a parseable envelope; this makes the sorts agree so there is no
+crash to wrap.  #1424 is the same defect reached from a single module and is
+closed by the same fix.
+
+Four shapes crash on `release/v0.2.0`; the fifth is the unrefined control,
+which never crashed and must not move.  Every cell asserts a REAL VERDICT,
+not merely the absence of the crash: a
+verifier that answered `E699` for these programs was unusable on them, and one
+that answered "no obligations" would be hiding them.
+"""
+
+from __future__ import annotations
+
+import json
+import os
+import subprocess
+import sys
+from pathlib import Path
+
+import pytest
+
+import vera
+
+_PKG_PARENT = str(Path(vera.__file__).resolve().parents[1])
+
+
+def _cli(*args: str) -> subprocess.CompletedProcess[str]:
+    env = dict(os.environ)
+    existing = env.get("PYTHONPATH", "")
+    env["PYTHONPATH"] = (
+        f"{_PKG_PARENT}{os.pathsep}{existing}" if existing else _PKG_PARENT
+    )
+    return subprocess.run(
+        [sys.executable, "-m", "vera.cli", *args],
+        capture_output=True, text=True, encoding="utf-8", check=False,
+        env=env, timeout=600,
+    )
+
+
+def _tree(tmp_path: Path, files: dict[str, str]) -> dict[str, Path]:
+    tmp_path.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
+    out: dict[str, Path] = {}
+    for name, text in files.items():
+        p = tmp_path / f"{name}.vera"
+        p.write_text(text, encoding="utf-8")
+        out[name] = p
+    return out
+
+
+def _verify(path: Path) -> dict:
+    """`vera verify --json`, refusing an internal error as an answer.
+
+    E699 is the envelope the compiler emits when it crashed.  A cell that only
+    asserted the obligations it wanted would pass vacuously on a crash — there
+    are no obligations to contradict it — so the gate is here, once, for every
+    cell in the file.
+    """
+    proc = _cli("verify", "--json", str(path))
+    try:
+        result = json.loads(proc.stdout)
+    except json.JSONDecodeError:
+        raise AssertionError(
+            f"verify emitted no envelope for {path.name} "
+            f"(exit {proc.returncode})\n{proc.stdout[:400]}\n"
+            f"{proc.stderr[-800:]}"
+        ) from None
+    internal = [
+        d for d in result.get("diagnostics", [])
+        if d.get("error_code") == "E699"
+    ]
+    assert not internal, (
+        f"{path.name}: the verifier reported an INTERNAL ERROR rather than a "
+        f"verdict — {internal[0]['description'][:200]}"
+    )
+    return result
+
+
+def _checks(path: Path) -> bool:
+    return _cli("check", "--quiet", str(path)).returncode == 0
+
+
+def _kinds(result: dict) -> list[tuple[str, str, str | None]]:
+    return [
+        (o["kind"], o["status"], o.get("error_code"))
+        for o in result["obligations"]
+    ]
+
+
+# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+# Fixtures
+# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+
+_POS = "type Pos = { @Int | @Int.0 > 0 };\n\n"
+
+#: #1421, verbatim: an imported `Option<Nat>` rebuilt as an `Option<Pos>`.
+_XMOD_LIB = """\
+public fn mk(@Int -> @Option<Nat>)
+  requires(true)
+  ensures(true)
+  effects(pure)
+{
+  int_to_nat(handle[Exn<Int>] {
+    throw(@Nat) -> { nat_to_int(@Nat.0) }
+  } in {
+    throw(@Int.0)
+  })

+"""
+
+_XMOD_MAIN = "import cb;\n\n" + _POS + """\
+public fn relay(@Int -> @Option<Pos>)
+  requires(true)
+  ensures(true)
+  effects(pure)

+  match cb::mk(@Int.0) {
+    Some(@Nat) -> Some(nat_to_int(@Nat.0)),
+    None -> None
+  }
+}
+"""
+
+#: #1424, verbatim: the same defect reached from one module.
+_SAME_MODULE = """\
+type PosInt = { @Int | @Int.0 > 0 };
+
+private fn mk(@Float64 -> @Option<PosInt>)
+  requires(true)
+  ensures(true)
+  effects(pure)
+{
+  Some(float_to_int(@Float64.0))

+
+public fn f(@Float64 -> @Option<PosInt>)
+  requires(true)
+  ensures(true)
+  effects(pure)
+{
+  match mk(@Float64.0) {
+    Some(@PosInt) -> Some(@PosInt.0),
+    None -> None
+  }
+}
+"""
+
+#: The rewrap happens inside a helper the caller passes a value to.
+_WRAPPER = _POS + """\
+private fn mk(@Int -> @Option<Pos>)
+  requires(@Int.0 > 0)
+  ensures(true)
+  effects(pure)
+{
+  Some(@Int.0)
+}
+
+private fn rewrap(@Option<Pos> -> @Option<Pos>)
+  requires(true)
+  ensures(true)
+  effects(pure)
+{
+  match @Option<Pos>.0 {
+    Some(@Pos) -> Some(@Pos.0),
+    None -> None
+  }
+}
+
+public fn f(@Int -> @Option<Pos>)
+  requires(@Int.0 > 0)
+  ensures(true)
+  effects(pure)

+  rewrap(mk(@Int.0))

+"""
+
+#: The refinement is a TUPLE COMPONENT, rebuilt on its own — the nested
+#: position #1360 exercised, with a refinement where it had a `Tuple`.
+_TUPLE_COMPONENT = _POS + """\
+private fn mk(@Int -> @Option<Tuple<Pos, Int>>)
+  requires(@Int.0 > 0)
+  ensures(true)
+  effects(pure)

+  Some(Tuple(@Int.0, 7))
+}
+
+public fn f(@Int -> @Option<Pos>)
+  requires(@Int.0 > 0)
+  ensures(true)
+  effects(pure)
+{
+  match mk(@Int.0) {
+    Some(Tuple(@Pos, @Int)) -> Some(@Pos.0),
+    None -> None
+  }
+}
+"""
+
+#: The same shape with NO refinement anywhere — the control.
+_CLEAN_CONTROL = """\
+private fn mk(@Int -> @Option<Nat>)
+  requires(@Int.0 > 0)
+  ensures(true)
+  effects(pure)
+{
+  int_to_nat(@Int.0)
+}
+
+public fn f(@Int -> @Option<Nat>)
+  requires(@Int.0 > 0)
+  ensures(true)
+  effects(pure)

+  match mk(@Int.0) {
+    Some(@Nat) -> Some(@Nat.0),

+# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

+#: nested type argument, with a division the chain's own predicates prove safe.
+_TUPLE_CHAIN = """\
+type Pos = { @Int | @Int.0 > 0 };
+type Small = { @Pos | @Pos.0 < 10 };
+
+private fn mk(@Int -> @Option<Tuple<Small, Int>>)
+  requires(@Int.0 > 0 && @Int.0 < 10)
+  ensures(true)
+  effects(pure)
+{
+  Some(Tuple(@Int.0, 7))
+}
+
+public fn f(@Int -> @Int)
+  requires(@Int.0 > 0 && @Int.0 < 10)
+  ensures(true)
+  effects(pure)
+{
+  match mk(@Int.0) {
+    Some(Tuple(@Small, @Int)) -> 100 / @Small.0,
+    None -> 1
+  }
+}
+"""
+
+
+def test_1421_a_refinement_chain_stays_unmodelled(tmp_path: Path) -> None:
+    """Stripping the WHOLE chain would be a false E526 — this is the witness.
+
+    The obvious reading of "a refinement contributes its base" is to strip the
+    chain, and it is wrong.  The predicate half of the rule stops at a
+    primitive base — `_translate_refined_predicate` reads `{ @Base | P }` with
+    `@Base` primitive — so for `{ { @Int | P } | Q }` neither predicate is
+    translated.  Strip the chain and the SORT succeeds while the predicates
+    stay absent: the payload becomes an unconstrained `Int` and
+    `100 / @Small.0` is reported `violated`/**E526** although `Small` proves
+    the divisor lies in `(0, 10)`.  A false positive on valid code, which is
+    the #854/#884 class this project treats as a defect.
+
+    So both routes refuse a chain together, and this program is the
+    discriminator: it reads `div_zero`/`tier3` on `release/v0.2.0` and on this
+    branch, and flips to E526 the moment `strip_refinements` loops.  That is
+    the mutation this cell exists to kill (review of PR #1431, F1/F4).
+
+    Conjoining a chain's predicates so the strip becomes correct is #1434.
+    """
+    result = _verify(_tree(tmp_path, {"p": _TUPLE_CHAIN})["p"])
+    assert result["ok"] is True, result["diagnostics"]
+    div = [
+        (o["status"], o.get("error_code")) for o in result["obligations"]
+        if o["kind"] == "div_zero"
+    ]
+    assert div == [("tier3", None)], (
+        f"a refinement chain stopped being refused — an E526 here is the "
+        f"unconstrained-Int false positive: {_kinds(result)}"
+    )
+    # The chain's own binding is honestly disclosed rather than proved.
+    assert ("refine_bind", "tier3_unguarded", "E506") in _kinds(result), (
+        _kinds(result)
+    )

problem_statement.title: [BUG] view_img displays the slice next to the one requested, and misreports coordinates on click
problem_statement.body:
`brainsprite.js` treats `numSlice` as a 0-based slice index everywhere it uses it — the sagittal draw (`case "X"`), the overlay value lookup, and the click handler, which clamps it to `[0, nbSlice.X - 1]`. The one exception is the coordinate readout, which computes `affine @ [numSlice.X + 1, ...]`.

`_json_view_params` compensates for that `+1` by sending `cut_slices[0] - 1`, even though `_get_cut_slices` already returns a 0-based voxel index (`apply_affine(inv(affine), cut_coords)`). The label then comes out right and the slice actually drawn is one voxel off.

### Reproduction

Put a marker on a single sagittal slice and ask for exactly its coordinate:

```python
import numpy as np
import nibabel as nib
from nilearn.plotting.html_stat_map import (
    _data_to_sprite, _get_cut_slices, _json_view_params,
    _get_brainsprite_html_ids,
)

n = 32
affine = np.diag([-3.0, 3.0, 3.0, 1.0])
affine[:3, 3] = [48.0, -48.0, -48.0]

mark = 20                                   # marker on voxel x = 20
data = np.zeros((n, n, n), dtype="float32")
data[mark, :, :] = 1.0
img = nib.Nifti1Image(data, affine)

world_x = (affine @ np.array([mark, 0, 0, 1.0]))[0]      # -12.0 mm
cut_slices = _get_cut_slices(img, cut_coords=[world_x, 0.0, 0.0], threshold=None)
params = _json_view_params(
    (n, n, n), affine, 0, 1, cut_slices,
    _get_brainsprite_html_ids("demo"),
)

num_x = int(params["numSlice"]["X"])
sprite = _data_to_sprite(data)
n_rows = int(np.ceil(np.sqrt(n)))
n_cols = int(np.ceil(n / float(n_rows)))

def tile_has_marker(tile):
    row, col = tile // n_cols, tile % n_cols
    return sprite[row * n : (row + 1) * n, col * n : (col + 1) * n].max() > 0

print("requested world x :", world_x)          # -12.0
print("cut_slices[0]     :", cut_slices[0])    # 20.0  (correct 0-based index)
print("numSlice.X sent   :", num_x)            # 19
print("marker in tile 19 :", tile_has_marker(19))   # False  <- drawn
print("marker in tile 20 :", tile_has_marker(20))   # True   <- wanted
```

The viewer labels that slice `x = -12` (the `-1` and the `+1` cancel), but the slice on screen is the neighbour. The error is one voxel: 3 mm here, 2 mm for a typical MNI grid.

The same mismatch shows up from the other side when a user clicks. The click handler sets `numSlice.X` to the tile that was clicked, which is correct, and the readout then reports `affine @ [numSlice.X + 1]` — one voxel past the slice being shown.

### Suggested fix

This can be corrected entirely in `_json_view_params`, without touching the vendored `brainsprite.min.js`: send `numSlice` as the true 0-based index and pre-multiply the affine by a translation of `-1` along each axis, so the viewer's own `+1` cancels. I verified that gives both the right slice and the right label at four marker positions, in both display conventions.

- I noticed this while working on #6134 and mentioned it in #6502. The fix touches the same function as #6502, so that one wants to land first.

@@ -3532,14 +3532,52 @@ def negative(x):
     return tf.negative(x)
 
 
+def _nextafter_16bit(x1, x2, dtype):
+    """`nextafter` for 16-bit floats, which `tf.math.nextafter` rejects.
+
+    Steps the IEEE 754 bit pattern by one, which is exactly a one-ulp step.
+    Computing in float32 and casting back does not work: a float32 step is
+    much smaller than a 16-bit ulp, so the result rounds back to `x1`.
+    """
+    b1 = tf.bitcast(x1, tf.int16)
+    b2 = tf.bitcast(x2, tf.int16)
+    zero_i = tf.constant(0, tf.int16)
+    one_i = tf.constant(1, tf.int16)
+    # Zero is tested on the bit pattern rather than with `==`, because
+    # bfloat16 subnormals compare equal to zero in tf's comparison ops.
+    abs_mask = tf.constant(32767, tf.int16)
+    is_zero_1 = tf.equal(tf.bitwise.bitwise_and(b1, abs_mask), zero_i)
+    is_zero_2 = tf.equal(tf.bitwise.bitwise_and(b2, abs_mask), zero_i)
+    same = tf.equal(b1, b2) | (is_zero_1 & is_zero_2)
+    # The bit pattern grows with magnitude for both signs, so stepping away
+    # from zero is +1 for a non-negative x1 and -1 for a negative one.
+    step = tf.where(tf.equal(x2 > x1, b1 >= zero_i), one_i, -one_i)
+    stepped = tf.bitcast(b1 + step, dtype)
+    # Zero has no bit predecessor, so its neighbour is the smallest subnormal
+    # carrying the sign of the direction travelled.
+    tiny = tf.bitcast(
+        tf.where(b2 < zero_i, tf.constant(-32767, tf.int16), one_i), dtype
+    )
+    out = tf.where(is_zero_1, tiny, stepped)
+    out = tf.where(same, x2, out)
+    return tf.where(
+        tf.math.is_nan(x1) | tf.math.is_nan(x2),
+        tf.constant(float("nan"), dtype),
+        out,
+    )
+
+
 def nextafter(x1, x2):
     x1 = convert_to_tensor(x1)
     x2 = convert_to_tensor(x2)
 
     dtype = dtypes.result_type(x1.dtype, x2.dtype, float)
-    x1 = tf.cast(x1, tf.float64)
-    x2 = tf.cast(x2, tf.float64)
-    return tf.cast(tf.math.nextafter(x1, x2), dtype)
+    x1 = tf.cast(x1, dtype)
+    x2 = tf.cast(x2, dtype)
+    # tf.math.nextafter supports only float32 and float64.
+    if dtype in ("float16", "bfloat16"):
+        return _nextafter_16bit(x1, x2, dtype)
+    return tf.math.nextafter(x1, x2)

problem_statement.title: keras.ops.nextafter returns Inf instead of max finite float32 when moving from Inf toward -Inf
problem_statement.body:
## Description

`keras.ops.nextafter` returns an incorrect result when moving from positive infinity toward negative infinity.

For the input below, the second element computes:

```text
nextafter(inf, -inf)
```

This should return the largest finite `float32` value, matching NumPy's behavior:

```text
3.4028234663852886e+38
```

However, Keras returns `inf` instead.

The Keras result is:

```text
[nan, inf, 0.0]
```

but the expected result is:

```text
[nan, 3.4028234663852886e+38, 0.0]
```

This looks like an incorrect infinity handling issue in `keras.ops.nextafter`.

## Minimal reproduction

```python
import os
os.environ["KERAS_BACKEND"] = "tensorflow"
os.environ["TF_CPP_MIN_LOG_LEVEL"] = "3"
os.environ["TF_ENABLE_ONEDNN_OPTS"] = "0"

import warnings
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")

import numpy as np
import keras

x = np.array([np.nan, np.inf, -0.0], dtype=np.float32)
y = np.array([1.0, -np.inf, 0.0], dtype=np.float32)

actual = np.asarray(
    keras.ops.nextafter(
        keras.ops.convert_to_tensor(x),
        keras.ops.convert_to_tensor(y),
    )
)

expected = np.nextafter(x, y)

print("keras:", keras.__version__)
print("backend:", keras.config.backend())
print("actual:", actual.astype(np.float32).tolist())
print("expected:", expected.astype(np.float32).tolist())
```

Output:

```text
keras: 3.14.0
backend: tensorflow
actual: [nan, inf, 0.0]
expected: [nan, 3.4028234663852886e+38, 0.0]
```

## Expected behavior

`keras.ops.nextafter` should return:

```text
[nan, 3.4028234663852886e+38, 0.0]
```

This matches NumPy's `np.nextafter` behavior. In particular, `nextafter(inf, -inf)` should return the largest finite `float32` value, not `inf`.

## Actual behavior

`keras.ops.nextafter` currently returns:

```text
[nan, inf, 0.0]
```

The second element corresponding to `nextafter(inf, -inf)` incorrectly returns `inf` instead of `3.4028234663852886e+38`.

problem_statement.body:
While working on #4003, I wanted to see how the new Metro Mobility Wallet flow would look like in the Admin but when I tried saving it, I got a `Template not found: eligibility/includes/selection-label--.html` error (even though I created a dummy template called `selection-label--metro_mobility_wallet.html`). So I guess that we may have introduced a bug in the Admin's form validation. As far as I can tell, [`self.instance.selection_label_template`](https://github.com/cal-itp/benefits/blob/main/benefits/core/admin/enrollment.py#L70) is not fully formed due to [`self.system_name`](https://github.com/cal-itp/benefits/blob/main/benefits/core/models/enrollment.py#L195) being empty. Something like the model instance hasn't been saved yet when it is called from `clean()`. You can also reproduce this if you try to create a new Older Adult or Medicare or any other existing flow, you'll still see an issue with the path to the template not being correct.

problem_statement.title: Three unreachable branches in is_separable (1118, 1124, 1230)
problem_statement.body:
Three branches in `toqito/state_props/is_separable.py` cannot be reached from any input. Found by @dchaudhari7177 while working on #1915 (see #1928), and verified independently.

Both helpers have exactly one call site, and at that site the dimension parameters are computed as

```python
min_dim_val, max_dim_val = min(dA, dB), max(dA, dB)   # is_separable.py:475
```

so they are always consistent with `d_a`/`d_b`. That consistency is what makes the branches dead.

### `_horodecki_low_rank_ppt_criteria`, lines 1118 and 1124

```python
if state_rank <= max_dim_val:
    return (True, "rank(rho) <= max(d_A, d_B) ..."), None, None   # line 1110
...
if state_rank <= rank_marg_a:      # line 1117 -> 1118 unreachable
if state_rank <= rank_marg_b:      # line 1123 -> 1124 unreachable
```

`rho_A` acts on a `d_A`-dimensional space, so `rank(rho_A) <= d_A <= max(d_A, d_B) == max_dim_val`. Any state with `state_rank <= rank(rho_A)` therefore also has `state_rank <= max_dim_val` and already returned at line 1110. The same argument applies to `rank(rho_B)`.

Empirically: 320 random density matrices across the dimension pairs (2,2), (2,3), (3,2), (2,4), (3,3), (3,4), (4,4), (2,5) never reached either line.

Note that `test_horodecki_rank_le_marginal_rank` in `toqito/state_props/tests/test_is_separable.py:373` is a bare `pass` stub aimed at exactly these two lines. It was presumably left unfinished because the case cannot be constructed.

### `_qubit_qudit_ppt_criteria`, line 1230

```python
if min_dim_val != 2 or prod_dim_val == 0:
    return None                     # line 1219
...
if d_a != 2 and d_b == 2:
    ...
elif d_a != 2:
    return None                     # line 1230 unreachable
```

Past the guard, `min_dim_val == 2` means `min(d_a, d_b) == 2`, so at least one of `d_a`, `d_b` equals 2. Reaching line 1230 requires `d_a != 2` and `d_b != 2` simultaneously, which contradicts that.

### What to do

Decide per branch whether the code is dead or the guard above it is too strong:

- If these are genuinely redundant, delete them. That is the reading the arguments above support, and it removes three permanently-uncovered branches plus the stub test.
- If instead any was meant to catch a case the earlier guard is wrongly swallowing, the guard is the thing to fix, and that would be a behavior change needing its own tests.

Either way this is a source change, so it does not belong in a test PR. Whoever picks it up should also delete the `test_horodecki_rank_le_marginal_rank` stub.

Removing the dead branches would also let `is_separable.py` reach full branch coverage, which #1915 otherwise cannot achieve.

problem_statement.title: Add an "auto" option for iOS simulator selection
problem_statement.body:
### What is the problem or limitation you are having?

At present, `briefcase run iOS` requires either a `-d <simulator ID>` option, or a manual selection from a simulator list. This is inconvenient for CI purposes when the available simulators can change.

It should be able to "auto select" a simulator when the specific image doesn't matter.

### Describe the solution you'd like


`briefcase run iOS -d auto` should select a good candidate simulator - use the most recent iOS version, selecting an "SE-class" device (i.e., iPhone 17e). This matches the default behavior of the CPython iOS testbed runner.

### Describe alternatives you've considered

We could also make `-d auto` the default behavior, and make a bare `-d` an option to "show the full simulator list". 

### Additional context

This problem doesn't exist on Android because (a) Android requires explicit creation of a simulator, and (b) Briefcase already has a syntax to "auto drive" the creation of an emulator for test purposes.

problem_statement.title: perf: renyi_entropy computes the spectrum multiple times
problem_statement.body:
### Summary
`state_props/renyi_entropy.py` factors `rho` more than once. Line 95 calls `is_density(rho)`, which factors `rho` via `is_positive_semidefinite` -> `eigvalsh`; line 104 then calls `np.linalg.eigvalsh(rho)` again. The `alpha == 1` branch (line 102) is worse: it delegates to `von_neumann_entropy`, which re-validates and re-factors a third time.

This is the same pattern recently fixed in `von_neumann_entropy`: compute the spectrum once and validate from it.

### Fix
Compute `eigs = np.linalg.eigvalsh(rho)` once, validate the density-matrix conditions from the spectrum plus `np.isclose(np.trace(rho), 1)`, and drop the `is_density` import. Mirror the `von_neumann_entropy` refactor.

Good first issue.

problem_statement.title: support group file exclusion under a single condition
problem_statement.body:
### Actual Situation

we have a single copier template for multiple types of deployments (thus multiple github actions pipelines), which lead us to a copier.yaml file that repeats the same condition per line on multiple lines, making it harder to update track. 


### Desired Situation

I want the copier.yaml exclude section to support group exclusions

### Proposed solution

So I'm proposing we support doing group exclusions:
```
- |
  {% if flag %}
  a.txt
  b.txt
  {% endif %}
- file-c
```
instead of

```
 - "{% if app_pipeline_disabled %}.github/workflows/deploy-type-b.yml{% endif %}"
 - "{% if app_pipeline_disabled %}.github/workflows/deploy-type-b.yml{% endif %}"
 - "{% if app_pipeline_disabled %}.github/workflows/security-check.yml{% endif %}"
....
```

+class ResponseWrapper:
+    def __init__(self, response: Response, seed: int | None):
+        self.response = response
+        self.seed = seed
+
+    def iter_content(self, chunk_size: int):
+        iterator = self.response.iter_content(chunk_size)
+        if self.seed is None:  # pragma: no cover
+            yield from iterator
+            return
+
+        # allocate data for two MPEG-TS packets
+        packets = bytearray(376)
+        view = memoryview(packets)
+        filled = 0
+        remainder = b""
+
+        # read packet contents, keep the remainder and the iterator
+        for chunk in iterator:  # pragma: no branch
+            needed = 376 - filled
+            if len(chunk) <= needed:
+                view[filled : filled + len(chunk)] = chunk
+                filled += len(chunk)
+                if filled == 376:
+                    break
+            else:
+                view[filled:376] = chunk[:needed]
+                remainder = chunk[needed:]
+                break
+
+        self._decrypt_packets(packets, self.seed)
+
+        yield packets
+        yield remainder
+        yield from iterator
+
+    @staticmethod
+    def _decrypt_packets(packets: bytearray, seed: int):
+        # translated to Python from their obfuscated JS
+        for num in range(2):
+            imul = ctypes.c_uint32((num + 1) * 2654435769).value
+            r = ctypes.c_uint32(seed ^ imul).value
+
+            if r == 0:
+                r = 1831565813
+
+            packet_offset = 188 * num
+            for offset in range(16):
+                r ^= ctypes.c_uint32(r << 13).value
+                r ^= r >> 17
+                r ^= ctypes.c_uint32(r << 5).value
+                r = ctypes.c_uint32(r).value
+
+                mask = r & 0xFF
+                if mask == 0:
+                    mask = 165
+
+                packets[packet_offset + offset] ^= mask
+
+

+
+
+class BigoHLSStreamReader(HLSStreamReader):
+    __writer__ = BigoHLSStreamWriter

That message uses `single=True` and specifies a `label` with the message. That means that the message is only ever printed once in a run, even if negative DPA is calculated for every block in the core. This is not great, and does not give the user an appropriate sense for the issue.

Additionally, it would be very helpful if the location of the negative DPA rate was provided in the warning message. As of now, the user has to dig down in the neutronics kernel output file or infer the location from the database.

problem_statement.title: Trampoline misses mutants when tests use `patch.dict(os.environ, ..., clear=True)`
problem_statement.body:
## Description

When a test uses `unittest.mock.patch.dict(os.environ, {...}, clear=True)`, the
generated trampoline reads `MUTANT_UNDER_TEST` from `os.environ`, finds it
empty, and forwards the call to the **original** function. Mutants reachable
only through such tests are then falsely reported as `survived`. This silently
lowers the mutation score of any project whose tests scrub the environment
(Docker / runtime detection, default-paths logic, env-driven feature flags,
etc.).

## Root Cause

`_mutmut_trampoline` re-reads `MUTANT_UNDER_TEST` on every call:

[`mutation/trampoline_templates.py` L121-L125](https://github.com/boxed/mutmut/blob/main/mutmut/mutation/trampoline_templates.py#L121-L125)

```python
def _mutmut_trampoline(orig, mutants, call_args, call_kwargs, self_arg=None):
    """Forward call to original or mutated function, depending on the environment"""
    import os
    mutant_under_test = os.environ.get('MUTANT_UNDER_TEST', '')
    if not mutant_under_test:
        # No mutant being tested - call original function
        ...
```

mutmut sets `MUTANT_UNDER_TEST` once in the forked child
([`__main__.py` L1052-L1055](https://github.com/boxed/mutmut/blob/main/mutmut/__main__.py#L1052-L1055))
before importing the test target, and the value never legitimately changes
during that child's lifetime. The per-call `os.environ.get(...)` therefore
serves no functional purpose given that lifecycle, but exposes the trampoline
to test code that scrubs `os.environ`.

## Reproducer

```python
# orchard/runtime.py
def is_in_docker() -> bool:
    return os.environ.get("IN_DOCKER", "0") == "1"

# tests/test_runtime.py
def test_is_in_docker():
    with patch.dict(os.environ, {"IN_DOCKER": "1"}, clear=True):
        assert is_in_docker()
```

If this is the only test exercising `is_in_docker`, **all** of its mutants
(`"0" → "1"`, `== → !=`, etc.) survive, even though the assertion would
catch them in a normal run.

## Current Workaround

Projects work around this with a per-test helper that re-injects
`MUTANT_UNDER_TEST` into the patched env:

```python
def mutmut_safe_env(**extra: str) -> dict[str, str]:
    env: dict[str, str] = {}
    mut = os.environ.get("MUTANT_UNDER_TEST")
    if mut is not None:
        env["MUTANT_UNDER_TEST"] = mut
    env.update(extra)
    return env

# in tests:
with patch.dict(os.environ, mutmut_safe_env(IN_DOCKER="1"), clear=True):
    ...
```

It works, but bleeds mutmut implementation details into every test that
needs `clear=True`.

## Proposed Fix: two options

### Option A: sticky cache on the trampoline (slightly recommended)

Remember the last non-empty value seen, so a wiped env falls back to it:

```python
def _mutmut_trampoline(orig, mutants, call_args, call_kwargs, self_arg=None):
    """Forward call to original or mutated function, depending on the environment"""
    import os
    mutant_under_test = os.environ.get('MUTANT_UNDER_TEST', '')
    if not mutant_under_test:
        mutant_under_test = getattr(_mutmut_trampoline, '_sticky', '')
    else:
        _mutmut_trampoline._sticky = mutant_under_test
    if not mutant_under_test:
        # No mutant being tested - call original function
        ...
```

A few added lines: one conditional that updates the sticky cache on non-empty
env and falls back to it on empty env. Each non-empty transition refreshes the
cache, so the parent's transitions through `"fail"`, `"stats"`,
`"list_all_tests"`, `"mutant_generation"`, and per-mutant names all keep
working.

**Behavioral difference vs. current code.** The parent process today
intentionally writes `MUTANT_UNDER_TEST=""` between phases (after
`run_forced_fail_test` at [`__main__.py:640`](https://github.com/boxed/mutmut/blob/main/mutmut/__main__.py#L640)
and after `mutant_generation` at [`__main__.py:994`](https://github.com/boxed/mutmut/blob/main/mutmut/__main__.py#L994))
as a "transition signal" between phases. With Option A, the sticky cache
ignores those resets and keeps reporting the previous mode. This is only
observable if the parent invokes user code through a trampoline *between* such
a reset and the start of the next phase. It does not affect the per-mutant
test runs themselves: those happen in `os.fork()`ed children whose env is set
once at fork time and never cleared, so live read and sticky cache are
equivalent there.

### Option B: import-time cache + live fallback

Snapshot once at module-import time:

```python
_MUTANT_UNDER_TEST_CACHED = os.environ.get('MUTANT_UNDER_TEST', '')

def _mutmut_trampoline(orig, mutants, call_args, call_kwargs, self_arg=None):
    """Forward call to original or mutated function, depending on the environment"""
    mutant_under_test = (
        _MUTANT_UNDER_TEST_CACHED
        or os.environ.get('MUTANT_UNDER_TEST', '')
    )
    if not mutant_under_test:
        ...
```

Faster than Option A (skips the per-call `os.environ.get` once the cache is
populated, measurable on suites with tens of thousands of trampoline
crossings). Relies on the trampoline impl being imported *after*
`MUTANT_UNDER_TEST` is set, which is true today but is a stricter assumption
than Option A.

## Verified in a real codebase

Reproduced and fixed in [orchard-ml](https://github.com/tomrussobuilds/orchard-ml)
on `orchard/core/environment/hardware.py`, where every test for
`configure_system_libraries` uses `patch.dict(os.environ, ..., clear=True)`:

| Setup | Killed | Survived | Score |
|---|---|---|---|
| `mutmut_safe_env` workaround active | 129 / 133 | 4 | **97.0 %** |
| Workaround disabled, trampoline unchanged | 114 / 133 | 19 | **85.7 %** |
| Workaround disabled, **Option A patched** | 129 / 133 | 4 | **97.0 %** |

15 mutants were falsely surviving without the workaround. Option A restores
the score exactly without it.

## Recommendation

Both options have tradeoffs.

**Option A** is minimal and works correctly in the fork-and-test path. Its
risk is parent-side: if user code is invoked through a trampoline between an
`""` reset and the next phase, the sticky cache would still report the
previous mode. I have not been able to find a code path in mutmut that
actually triggers this today, but the assumption is worth pointing out.

**Option B** is faster but has a sharper edge case: if the parent imports
`trampoline_impl` while `MUTANT_UNDER_TEST` is set to a non-mutant value
(`"stats"`, `"fail"`, etc.), the import-time cache freezes that value, and
forked children inherit it via copy-on-write. Their per-mutant env would then
be ignored. Option B is therefore only safe if `trampoline_impl` is
guaranteed to be imported after fork and after the env is set, which is not
the case today.

On balance I'd lean toward **Option A**, but I'm happy to implement either
(or a different approach you prefer).

+* `io.open`, `os.open`: support for `encoding` argument ([#120](https://github.com/pytest-dev/pyfakefs/issues/120))
+* `os.makedirs`: support for `exist_ok` argument (Python >=
+  3.2) ([#98](https://github.com/pytest-dev/pyfakefs/issues/98))

+* Support for mount points ([#25](https://github.com/pytest-dev/pyfakefs/issues/25))
+* Support for hard links ([#75](https://github.com/pytest-dev/pyfakefs/issues/75))
+* Support for float times (mtime, ctime)
+* Windows support:
+    * support for alternative path separator
+    * support for case-insensitive filesystems ([#69](https://github.com/pytest-dev/pyfakefs/issues/69))
+    * support for drive letters and UNC paths
+* Support for filesystem size ([#86](https://github.com/pytest-dev/pyfakefs/issues/86))
+* `shutil.rmtree`: support for `ignore_errors` and `onerror`
+  arguments ([#72](https://github.com/pytest-dev/pyfakefs/issues/72))
+* Support for `os.fsync()` and `os.fdatasync()` ([#73](https://github.com/pytest-dev/pyfakefs/issues/73))
+* `os.walk`: Support for `followlinks` argument
+
+### Fixes
+
+* `shutil` functions like `make_archive` do not work with
+  pyfakefs ([#104](https://github.com/pytest-dev/pyfakefs/issues/104))
+* File permissions on deletion not correctly handled ([#27](https://github.com/pytest-dev/pyfakefs/issues/27))
+* `shutil.copy` error with bytes contents ([#105](https://github.com/pytest-dev/pyfakefs/issues/105))
+* mtime and ctime not updated on content changes

--- a/armi/materials/material.py
+++ b/armi/materials/material.py
@@ -529,8 +529,16 @@ def getProperty(self, propName: str, Tk: float = None, Tc: float = None, **kwarg
             # only use cached value if the temperature at which it is cached is the same.
             return cached[1]
         else:
-            # go look it up from material properties.
-            val = getattr(self, propName)(Tk=Tk, **kwargs)
+            # go look it up from material properties
+            try:
+                # If this is an armi.materials.Material property.
+                val = getattr(self, propName)(Tk=Tk, **kwargs)
+            except KeyError:
+                # This is an armi.matProps.MatPropsMaterial property.
+                if Tc is None:
+                    Tc = getTc(Tc, Tk)
+                val = getattr(self, propName)(T=Tc, **kwargs)
+
             # cache only one value for each property. Prevents unbounded cache explosion.
             self._setCache(propName, (Tk, val))
             return val

problem_statement.title: Material.getProperty not correctly passing Temps in Celcius to matProps
problem_statement.body:
ARMI's `Material.getProperty()` takes in temperature in Celsius or Kelvin:

https://github.com/terrapower/armi/blob/ce01b794b0f128303adcf6faf072cc1e89e34c59/armi/materials/material.py#L517

And does the same thing all the other `Material` property functions do, which is convert things to Kelvin immediately:

https://github.com/terrapower/armi/blob/ce01b794b0f128303adcf6faf072cc1e89e34c59/armi/materials/material.py#L525

But there is an edge case where the material is called directly from `matProps`, and thus should be:

1. Converted to Celcius
2. Called `T`, because `matProps` doesn't care about other units.

This:

https://github.com/terrapower/armi/blob/ce01b794b0f128303adcf6faf072cc1e89e34c59/armi/materials/material.py#L533-L535

should become this:

```python
            Tc = getTk(Tc, Tk)
            val = getattr(self, propName)(T=Tc, **kwargs)
            # cache only one value for each property. Prevents unbounded cache explosion.
            self._setCache(propName, (Tk, val))
```

problem_statement.title: No mechanism on MCP and LangChain exceptions
problem_statement.body:
Errors captured by automatic instrumentation should have a mechanism so capture data is available, and the popularity of integrations can be determined.
See [https://github.com/getsentry/sentry-python/blob/e275c9e94323b429f39196881fb992d81a2e52ea/sentry_sdk/integrations/mcp.py#L425-L430]() and
[https://github.com/getsentry/sentry-python/blob/e275c9e94323b429f39196881fb992d81a2e52ea/sentry_sdk/integrations/langchain.py#L222-L231]()
